#7,384
The duel with Bradamante had the intended effect on the Picts. Ragnar might have lost, but that mattered little because of how well he fought. A fact that was further established with the following duels where Pict warriors sought to best Bradamante, only to be defeated with the same ease as his guard regardless of their own skills in battle. Of course, it bolstered the reputation of the Paladins as well. They were swiftly being seen as peerless warriors, but the further their reputation rose, the further they dragged Ragnar's reputation up with them.

And that mattered more. The Paladins were exceptional warriors, but that's all they were. They had no lands, no formal titles -- they were an order of warriors beholden to the Emperor. Ragnar, however, was a Prince. Son of the Allvaldr, and heir apparent to his father's empire, whose army was sweeping over the south like a farmer's scythe through wheat. The Paladins represented the Emperor, but one day Ragnar could become the Allvaldr, and few things were respected more than the ability to fight.

So, excuses were made for his defeat for him. 'He was too young.' 'He isn't a grown man yet.' 'If they fought again in a few years, surely he'd win.' Ragnar was sure that Ove had his hand in fanning the rumors like one would a flame, but it worked. The days following, the caution that the Picts regarded them with had faded a touch. There were stirrings amongst the clans in light of new information, but those discussions were kept far from prying ears.

While the alliances between the clans shifted underfoot, they couldn't approach to discuss finer details of any kind of alliance with them. His party, and that of the Paladins, were being closely watched. All the more so now that Ragnar had begun to tip the precarious balance of power within Alba. He had little doubt that King Causantín had spies reporting every time Ragnar breathed or ate, just on the off chance that he or anyone else in his party could be communicating with his detractors.

However, the game of politics wasn't so easily stifled. Instead, it was channeled and allowed to manifest in some ways to allow the king to exert a degree of control over the situation, and to force the bickering of politics to step into the light of day instead of lurking in the shadows. There were many ways to do it, but the most popular of them was a hunting trip.

"I hate hunting," Magnus remarked to him once they were seated on horseback, joining a large hunting party headed towards the royal forest. "Fishing is more honest."

"We aren't going to hunt anything. It's just an excuse," Harald pointed out. "We break into smaller parties to hunt game, and the King will watch from afar to see who approaches who. And every attendant will report every word that we say."

Ragnar agreed whole heartedly, which was also why he hated hunting trips like this. Worse, it wasn't a true hunt either. Dogs would flush out game, cornering it and then it would be bound so some lord could feel important shooting a stationary animal or skewering it with a spear.

"Father took us hunting once," Ragnar remarked as they trotted along with the royal party. "Real hunting. Just us, and him -- no servants. We had to track everything ourselves, kill our prey or go hungry."

Magnus nodded, "Cleaning and dressing it… cooking it too. Father can do a lot, but he can't cook." Ragnar shared a grin with his brother, the memory a fond one. Father didn't bring them to the old family home often, but each time he did, it was a welcome break from the capital.

Harald just shook his head. "My father's different," he admitted with a shrug. "He says that we've climbed too high to be caught doing the work of servants." That was a fair attitude to have about it. Many of the old blood in terms of nobility, few that they were, whispered amongst themselves that it was shameful to have princes and the Allvaldr hunting and preparing their own food. They said it was because Father was once a peasant and such callings come to those with lowborn blood.

They never said as much to his face, much less to Father's, but the whispers still reached his ears all the same.

The conversation lapsed as they continued down a well trodden dirt path towards the royal forest, which wasn't too far away from the city. When they arrived less than half a day riding, Ragnar saw that the camp was already erected and, from the size of the camp, one would assume that they took everyone in the city with them. Their own tents were swiftly brought up, and Ragnar noticed that theirs were far finer than those of the Picts. Thick dyed cloth that was further embroidered with elaborate patterns -- it was a tent worthy of being made into clothes that would in turn be worthy of nobility, and they noticed.

Regardless, it was then that the real purpose of the hunt made itself known as the party was broken up into three -- one spearheaded by the king, one by the Paladins, and one by them. As one would expect, the King's party was the largest, but there was also a disparity between his party and the Paladins.

Ragnar thought that things would honestly be much closer. Far closer. Both Astolfo and Bradamante were incredible fighters, and the Picts stood to gain much if they chose to ally with the Romans. But while some of the lesser clans did join their party, it was less than half the number that joined his, which was two thirds as large as the king's.

King Causantín undoubtedly noticed, but he said nothing of it as their hunting parties each entered the forest at three separate points. Ahead of them, scouting parties and dogs ran ahead, allowing the nobles to talk amongst themselves as they waited for game to be found and captured for them. Which was how Ragnar found himself in familiar company.

"When news of your father's arrival came, all of Alba held its breath," Lucas, the man who had welcomed them into the kingdom, began. They trotted along a well walked path, completely aimless and the hunting part of the trip completely forgotten. "Even here, we have heard tales of him. How he once stood before an army's archers with his hands spread wide, and the gods refused to let an arrow touch him."

"That story is true, according to him," Ragnar replied, his tone polite. "Though, the stories leave out the fact that most of the Frankish archers were already dead by that point."

Lucas laughed a little too hard to be natural. It was a very good, well practiced laugh. Ragnar imagined most would be deceived by it, but he had grown up around men that laughed like that. "I imagine that helped quite a bit, true. But had the gods wished him to die that day, it only would have taken one."

The purpose of the conversation wasn't to flatter his father or convey what respect Lucas had for him. It was about the gods. As in plural. A subtle way to make it clear that while they might not worship the same gods, Lucas and his faction weren't Christians.

"It's a frustrating story to hear, at times," Ragnar returned, pretending that he didn't notice. "My father speaks often about not tempting the Norns to cut your life thread short with recklessness, but his entire youth was spent recklessly."

"Such is the draw of destiny," Lucas replied, his tone perfectly amicable. "My sister likens destiny to a path in the forest -- you can walk the path that was laid for you, or you can attempt to brave the wilderness around it… but one way or the other, you'll end up in the same destination." He was deliberately mentioning his sister.

Maeve. "She sounds wise," Ragnar admitted, still not sure what to make of the girl. He hadn't seen her since that conversation and he didn't know if that was a good thing or not.

"Wiser than most," Lucas said, and at least there did seem to be an honest pride in his voice. "And it is the destiny of Alba that has her fretting these days. In particular, the vast army your father is sweeping over the lowlands with." And now the conversation approached the real topic that Lucas wanted to discuss. "By the day, it marches closer, picking through Northumbria like a swarm of locusts. King Ecbert is nipping at his heels, but neither seem willing to choose a battlefield."

Hm. While it could merely be a turn of phrase that he learned, Ragnar knew that locusts didn't dwell in Britannia. They were very prominent in the Bible, however. It wasn't definitive proof of anything, at least not yet, but it did mean that Ragnar would keep an ear out for any slips. While it didn't truly matter if Lucas was a Christian or not, if he was willing to lie about his religion that, at the very least, meant that he was a liar.

"The might of King Ecbert's army may be impressive by some standards," Ragnar said without missing a beat, "But it consists of half starved levies. Those in my father's army are veterans of the Mediterranean or the Great Conquest." An exaggeration, admittedly. But not an important one. "My father hasn't seen them off solely because he awaits your king's decision."

King Ecbert had amassed a considerable army over the days and weeks since they'd arrived. People displaced by the Great Raid and pockets of resistance that retreated rather than face Father's host both flocked to his banner. At the rate things were going, the king would manage to amass an army a hundred thousand strong by the end of the year. It was an army large enough that Britannia likely hadn't seen one so large since the days of Caesar's invasion.

But the fact that King Ecbert hadn't pressed the attack in favor of slowly building up his strength and letting Father ravage his historical enemies told Ragnar that Ecbert was exactly the kind of man Father thought he was.

"You speak as if our participation in the battle won't affect the outcome," Lucas remarked, a touch of a rebuke in his tone. "If not, what could your father possibly need us for?"

Ragnar hesitated to answer that question, uncertain if he should answer it with the truth, with lies, or avoid it entirely. But he decided to speak a half truth instead, "The isle of Britannia is a land that is easy to take but hard to hold. My Father has plans for these islands, but the shape of those plans are dependent on other people's reactions. Such as King Causantín, or Emperor Charlemagne."

Lucas didn't seem surprised by the admission, simply cocking his head to invite further elaboration. Ragnar indulged him, "As it stands, Father intends to ravage the South and take its wealth, before departing back home." Lucas' eyes narrowed ever so slightly, realizing that this invasion wasn't one of conquest. Yet, at least. "Once we withdraw the South will be destabilized, with its economy and nobility gutted. It would be beneficial for us to have an ally on the islands upon our departure, but it could be more beneficial to leave a garrison at a stronghold."

"Dependent on what, exactly?" Lucas questioned, and Ragnar saw he was somewhat unnerved. Tense. He felt like Lucas was catching a glimpse of the scope of the plans that some had for his kingdom.

"What Charlemagne does," Ragnar answered easily. "He's made a substantial investment in the South to fortify it against us. His overtures to your King and Alba as a whole are an indication that he has long term plans for Britannia as well. At the end of the Great Raid, Charlemagne could do one of two things -- he could cut his losses, or he could invest more into the islands."

What shape that investment took varied wildly. Charlemagne could continue to use Ecbert as a pawn to conquer the South, creating a unified England. He could conquer England with his own armies and claiming it as his direct domain. He could limit it to monetary support to help alleviate the following disasters that the Raid would leave in its wake. It could even be a mixture of all three.

"If it's the latter, then we would like to maintain a strong presence on Britannia, along with gathering support of stout allies. If it's the former?" Ragnar continued before offering a small shrug of his shoulders, "Such long term plans become unnecessary, but in the chaos to come, there are those we would prefer to see rise above it."

Lucas rode in silence for a long few seconds, gathering his wits and when he did speak, he spoke slowly. "And what opinion would the Allvaldr have about Alba becoming more than an ally?"

Ragnar kept his surprise off his face, but his eyebrows desperately wanted to rise high. To ensure that he didn't misunderstand, he tilted his head the same way Lucas had to invite elaboration.

"King Causantín is a weak king," Lucas spoke bluntly. "His rule is tolerated because of the betrothal he struck with my clan but no more than that. He is right about one thing, however -- your father and Charlemagne will both fight over Alba like two dogs over a mutton chop. And if this is to be so, is there not wisdom in choosing a master, before such a bloody affair can ravage our lands?"

So he was right. Lucas spoke of vassalage in the same vein as how Father brought Ragnar's grandfather into the empire. That was… surprising. And ambitious.

The point of the diplomatic mission was to gain an alliance. And Ragnar knew his father's plans for the future -- total conquest. Bringing one of the major kingdoms on the island would be a substantial boon towards that goal, and it would make maintaining a presence on Britannia far easier leading up to the conquest.

However, it was simply too good to be true. Ragnar wasn't certain if it was a trap exactly, but such submission would not be so freely given.

"I imagine so, when one values their people and kingdom more than their pride," Ragnar replied, resisting the urge to shift in the saddle. This felt like a conversation that he'd much rather Ove to handle. An alliance was just an alliance, not something they particularly needed one way or the other, but voluntary vassalage? That would have a significant impact on Father's future plans. "But one cannot help but wonder what price would be paid for one to swallow their pride in such a way."

"Your father is renowned for his repayment of loyal service," Lucas began and Ragnar felt a deliberate shift in the air. "King Causantín has his crown as the result of a compromise. Few truly desire him to be king, he was merely chosen because he was the least offensive to all of the Clans." Ragnar got the impression that Lucas was more than a little biased, but he ignored that in favor of zeroing in on what he was building up to.

'How easily he speaks of loyalty when he plots treason.' Ragnar wasn't surprised. And he knew Father would find such a thing viscerally offensive, but Ragnar had grown up surrounded by such people. Father filtered them out as much as he was able to, but the truth of it was that he was used to people looking at him and not seeing him, but an opportunity to get close to his father.

"Something I imagine would change with proper support," Ragnar replied evenly. The shape of the conversation had revealed itself. Lucas was making a bid to become king of Alba. In exchange, he would submit to Father's rule.

"Things have changed already," Lucas neither confirmed nor denied. "It is only a question of how great of a change there shall be and how much King Causantín struggles to keep a crown adorned upon his brow."

"A lot, I imagine. I've met quite a few kings in my time, and all treat their crowns as a part of themselves more dear than their own hearts," Ragnar said, earning a thin grim smile from Lucas. "However, if such a fight is to be had, it would be by their supporters."

Lucas inclined his head to Ragnar as they trotted along the path. "If such an event were to occur, then my clan would be counted upon. Others within King Causantín's camp are wavering in their support as well. I cannot say such a thing would be bloodless, but if handled decisively, most would think better of raising their blades for a fallen king." That was a rather optimistic view of things, but not entirely wrong. It fed into the same reasons why his father didn't simply have Charlemagne killed.

One part of it was Father's heartfelt respect for the Emperor as a rival. The other part was that the easiest way to ensure legitimacy was to vanquish the enemies of your predecessor. Which Father would undoubtedly be considered the greatest of by Charlemagne's successors. It was a rallying effect, and one that Ragnar expected would play out in Alba to restore the deposed king. Against Lucas, who many would point to and claim that he tossed away the pride of the kingdom for a crown.

There would be resistance, and it wasn't the kind that could be honestly settled with a battle. As much as Grandfather claimed credit for it, everyone knew that his unification of Norway was because of Father's initial conquest. Alba was an established kingdom with a history stretching back to before the fall of the Roman Empire, who they stoutly resisted until the Romans finally built a wall to keep them out of the south.

'A garrison would be necessary. Both to keep him honest, and to keep him on the throne.' Ragnar was putting the pieces together in the back of his mind, crafting the letter that he would send to his father with all haste. It would complicate things more than Father would care for, but if handled correctly, this was a substantial opportunity.

"And, of course, for such a thing to manifest, there would need to be… guarantees to ensure both sides uphold their obligations," Lucas continued.

Not unexpected, still he couldn't deny a shifting in his guts at that.

Marriage.

"That is understandable," Ragnar acknowledged with a nod. "However, I cannot speak for myself in such matters. The decision belongs to my father."

"I would expect nothing else-" Lucas began, only to be cut off by the sound of a horn blowing. He frowned in the direction of it, "That is… unusual. They'll scare away the game."

"An ambush?" Ragnar questioned as his bodyguards mustered and got into place, searching the trees for any sign of it. If there was an ambush, they had lost the element of surprise. But in the long silence that followed, Ragnar could hear the shouts of panic echoing through the forest.

"If it is, then it is not for us," Lucas remarked.

After a moment of thought, Ragnar urged his horse forward and they slowly approached the source of the commotion. Evidently, they weren't that far away from the king's party because it didn't take them that long to see traces of them in the form of an outrider.

Lucas called out for the rider to stop before they exchanged a handful of words, and based on the sound of it, it wasn't good news for Lucas because he went bloodless. Slowly, he turned to Ragnar, and he could see the Pict debate the merits of lying or not before he spoke. "Someone tried to assassinate the king."

"... What?" Ragnar blurted, caught flat footed.

"King Causantín has been wounded -- an arrow in his shoulder. It… seems as if he has been poisoned. He will likely die."

Well… that certainly complicated things, didn't it?

...

#7,407
To say that the clans of Alba were less than pleased with the attack on their king was something of an understatement. For all that they griped and undermined the man, the moment that he was attacked, they treated it as a personal slight. And for all they quarreled over petty differences and ancient offenses, they would stand united against a common enemy.

If they could agree who the enemy was, that is.

"He's still alive?" Ragnar asked no one in particular in the room. They had been relocated from the keep to an estate outside of the city. Though, calling it an estate would have been a touch generous even if it wasn't functionally a prison, albeit one guarded by five hundred of his personal guards. No accusations had been spoken out loud, but they had absolutely been thought.

"For now," Magnus answered. "It struck him in the back, and it seems like it struck a lung."

"Bad placement," Harald remarked. "But survivable."

A wound like that entirely depended on the strength of the man who was wounded, the skills of the doctor, and the will of the gods. King Causantín seemed like a hale man, but the clans had refused any offer of using their physicians to help treat the king. There was another factor at play as well, "He's fading unusually fast from the sounds of it."

"Poison?" Magnus prompted, and Ragnar shrugged. "If they were going to use poison, why not slip something into his drink? Why wait until there were so many people around?"

"Probably because they wanted to use the people as a cover," Harald guessed with a shrug of his shoulders, but he raised a fair theory.

"Have the dogs found a scent?" Ragnar asked, earning a cocked eyebrow from Harald, as if to say 'How would I know?' Ragnar sighed, scratching at his cheek and tossing himself onto the straw bed tucked in the corner of the farm house. "Ove will know. I suppose we have to wait until he returns."

Ove was currently with the clans, trying to smooth over any ruffled feathers and to see if there was still a way that they could get what they came for -- an alliance. He certainly had a task in front of him. Ragnar imagined that the near assassination of their king would complicate things, especially if King Causantín died after the fact. His heir was a young boy, so a conclave would likely happen to choose the next king amongst the clans.

"King Causantín, King Ecgfrith, King Æthelred… a lot of kings get assassinated on this island," Magnus said. "A response to our arrival, or something else?"

"I doubt that it's Charlemagne. A more unified Britannia is one that can resist us better. It wouldn't be in his interests to cause chaos for us to exploit," Ragnar voiced his thoughts before he glanced at Magnus. "King Ecbert?"

"Maybe," Magnus offered a shrug. "Charlemagne intends to use him as a meatshield, and Ecbert intends to use that support to make a play for the entirety of Britannia?"

"Does it matter?" Harald cut in with a frown. "We don't have any proof. Right now, half of the clans are convinced that we tried to kill their king and the other half only doubt it. Blaming some petty king in the South only makes it look like we're shirking blame." Another fair point by Harald.

"So the only way to clear our name would be to find the culprit?" Ragnar mused, his lips thinning at the thought. Something that would be a little difficult given that they were 'strongly encouraged to remain in the estate for their own safety.' In other words, the clans wanted them where they could see them.

Harald grunted from across the room but there was a long lull in the conversation before he broke it. "We don't have to bother with clearing our name." That made both Ragnar and Magnus look at him, so he continued. "When the king dies, there is going to be a succession crisis. We've started making some inroads with the clans… We could commit. All the way."

"A coup?" Ragnar uttered, sitting up and casting a nervous glance around the room. If anyone managed to overheard them, then they managed to get through five hundred of their bodyguards, so it wasn't a real concern but the mere thought made him nervous. "That…"

It was doable. Probably. It'd be messy. Very messy. There wasn't a possibility that Alba would be able to commit any forces to the inevitable battle against Ecbert, but that wasn't strictly a concern. The real issue was…

"We haven't received word from Father," Magnus pointed out. And they weren't likely to with the assassination. "I don't know what he would want us to do here. Beyond maybe just leaving entirely."

It was possible. Probable, even. Father had sent them to negotiate an alliance, and it was made quickly apparent that there were significant forces at play here when they found that a pair of Paladins had been waiting for them. If Father had known about them, then he probably wouldn't have sent them in the first place.

'Would this be a failure, then? Would he be dissapointed?' Would Father be relieved that they were smart enough to quit while they were ahead, or unhappy that they had not persevered, overcame the dangers, and succeeded despite the odds? Because Father always did. Either by force or cleverness, he always managed to succeed in the end. Was this another test for them to prove their worthiness? That they were their father's sons? If not by Father, then perhaps by the gods?

"... I don't know what he would want us to do either," Ragnar admitted. "But… I… don't want to disappoint him."

"... Yeah," Magnus sighed in agreement.

Father cast a long shadow, and he fully expected all of his children to surpass him. If not in every way, then at least in some -- be it as a warrior, a diplomat, a merchant, or as the Allvaldr. Ragnar had spent the entirety of his life trying to live up to that expectation. Father never failed to tell them that he was proud of them, but that wasn't the expectation that Ragnar had placed on himself. Father would sometimes get a look in his eyes when one of them did something that blew past his already high expectations. A gleam that went deeper than pride and became a genuine joy of what Ragnar's siblings were capable of.

"The way I see it, we have two real choices," Ragnar started, his voice low and even. "We can cut our losses in Alba and wait for an alliance once the dust settles… or we could follow up on the offer Lucas presented to us -- making him king in exchange for vassalage. Anything in the middle isn't worth the risk."

Magnus wavered, tapping his finger on his crossed arms. A habit that Aunt Jill hadn't managed to break him out of when Magnus was thinking hard about something. "They won't just bend the knee for a crown. The clans would need to be broken before they really accept such a thing."

"Which gives us leverage over whoever we make king," Ragnar pointed out. As he did so, he realized which path he was favoring. With a glance at Magnus, he saw that his brother was leaning the same way. "It'll require a lot of resources. Maybe a dedicated force, but we could weaken him enough to be dependent on Father but strong enough that we won't need to worry about him being usurped."

'It really is too much, isn't it?' The thought came unprompted when they shared a glance, realizing that they were committing themselves to a dangerous path. A path that Father may not wish them to tread and one that wouldn't be without its consequences. 'Overthrowing a kingdom just for one man's approval?'

There were other reasons, of course. Long term plans and advantages that would echo out over decades if not centuries. But…

Ragnar would be a liar if he said if any one of them was the reason he decided to walk the more dangerous path.


…
​

The preparation for what amounted to a coup was slow at first. Like them, most of the clans were 'encouraged' to remain indoors for their own safety. Though, to an admittedly less rigorous standard. Messengers had to run back and forth between the clans, and as the night wore on, several things became clear.

King Causantín wasn't long for the world. That, and whoever shot him in the back had been part of the King's own party as the hounds had tracked the scent that far before it was lost.

Ragnar had a theory on who it could be, but he didn't have enough proof to make an accusation one way or another.

Regardless of that, most of the groundwork for a coup had already been laid. It was only an issue of convincing those that had laid the foundations to commit to the act, even if they had to rush it.

Which was how Ragnar found himself sneaking out under the cover of darkness late into the night. Yet, it was impossible to completely obscure his arrival to Lucas' clan. Even if their departure was missed, someone would see or say something that would tip off his arrival. For that reason, Magnus and Harald would both approach other clans under the guise of trying to coax them into supporting the alliance even if the king died. Nothing that wouldn't already be expected of them.

After all, tonight was a night for plotting.

Ragnar arrived at a clan building within the city, the guards at the back entrance taking note of his two guards, but Ragnar pushed back his hood to confirm his identity. They said something in Gaelic, but stepped aside to let him enter what looked to be a pantry. He saw kegs lining shelves, and meats hanging on hooks to dry alongside bundles of herbs. The door shut behind him, and Ragnar stepped forward before the other person in the room revealed themselves.

They weren't who Ragnar expected to meet.

"It's not a trap," Maeve remarked, stepping out of the shadows. Then she blinked, tilting her head ever so slightly, "Ah, well, I suppose it is a trap, just not the kind you were prepared for."

Well, that wasn't exactly a promising start. Ragnar raised an eyebrow, inviting an explanation.

Maeve offered a sly smile, "We've been unchaperoned for five entire seconds. As far as anyone will care, you've gone and made off with my virtue. After all, how can a girl like me ever resist the charms of a noble prince?" She punctuated the sarcastic explanation with a dry laugh.

Ah. So, it's like that then? "I'll take that as a sign that your clan doesn't intend to uphold the betrothal?"

"Never a chance of that," Maeve confirmed with a nod of her head, taking a seat on a barrel and gesturing for him to sit on a crate across from her. "I don't dislike the poor boy, or anything like that. He's a sweet enough child. Brings me flowers sometimes," she mused softly, her smile taking a sad twist. "But we were never going to be married. If not this excuse to break off the betrothal, then it would have been another. The betrothal was just a way to buy a truce so that both sides could gain their strength."

Ragnar hummed, unsurprised by the information. "And I was a convenient excuse. A prince from a powerful empire, so reprisals are unlikely. It also puts you in a position to strong arm me for a marriage to solidify terms."

"Exactly right," Maeve confirmed openly and honestly. "There is a bit more to it than that, of course. Your father scares the hells right out of most of the clans, you know? We've been fighting against the Southerners for as long as there have been people on this island, and your father is walking over them like they're dirt under his heels. They'll bluster and beat their chest talking about gods and God, but the truth of it is, they know that if you really wanted our lands you could just take them."

She offered a theatrical shrug of her shoulders, "So, a son of the great Siegfried the Wolf-Kissed stealing away the virtue of a good and honest woman like myself is an indication of favor. Since all you boys prefer doing your thinking with your bollocks rather than your brains."

"Good and honest?" Ragnar echoed with a tilt of his head, and the smile he got at that felt a bit more genuine.

"'Course, marriage would be a stronger indication," Maeve continued as if he hadn't said anything. "Nothing manages to bind interests together like a few words, a ceremony, and smashing pissers."

"You forgot to add eloquent to your descriptors," Ragnar remarked.

"If one praises their virtues too much, they risk being seen as unvirtuous," Maeve replied, as if it should have been obvious. "But the point is, with a strong enough indication, all that chest beating and bleating like a bunch of angry goats becomes just that."

Marriage was something that felt so very distant yet had managed to loom over Ragnar's thoughts, especially of late. Father told them that he would try to make such a match for them where even if they couldn't find love, they could at least find happiness with their spouse. However, as princes and princesses, their marriages were less unions and more of a means to seal a contract between parties. Maeve put it best -- few things were more iron clad at the negotiation table than a marriage.

Promises and betrothals could be broken, but marriage and the intermingling of blood were final. By becoming kin, interests merged, assets were coalesced, and foes became mutual.

Ragnar never once thought that he would marry for love. He was prepared to marry someone he detested, even. So long as it served Father and the realm. That was his duty as a prince and as a loyal son.

"That won't serve my father's interests," Ragnar replied, making Maeve's gaze sharpen just a touch. "My father prefers stability. The fact of the matter is that, it does not benefit the empire if another party, such as the Romans, Abbasids, or even the Khazars are able to undermine a king in the way that our arrival has managed to."

Maeve made a show of thinking about it, "I suppose that makes sense." She acknowledged, leaving the door open for elaboration.

"When my father was forging the empire, he did so by creating kingdoms. Some smaller than Alba, while others were larger. The two exceptions to this was Norway, who offered my mother to him as a bride, and Saxony, where King Widukind conducted a purge of the problematic elements within his kingdom, so that Father could wipe the slate clean before he abdicated."

"Then why call him King Windukind?" Maeve questioned sharply, for what purpose, Ragnar could only guess at.

"Because he is a true king, and a man my father holds in the highest respect. He now serves as an adviser for my family," he answered. "The point being, with the power of the clans, it would be more in our interest to go with the latter example. And the easiest way to do that is if their chest beating and bleating became action so that we'd be better able to break their power."

Maeve did something unexpected as she kicked her legs back and forth against the barrel. She smiled. "Including my own? After all, a king with too much power on this far away island would be just as problematic as one with too little. Few things give someone a fatter head than a crown, after all. With enough resources and influence, some crowned idiot could sway the whole island in rebelling, and I imagine that would be quite the pain for the Allvaldr across the North Sea. Raising armies is expensive and time consuming, with one defeat could mean that the islands simply wouldn't be worth the cost to retake."

She was building up to something. Ragnar wasn't sure what yet, but her logic was sound. He just wasn't sure how honest he wanted to be.

By all accounts, she was right. To achieve what Ragnar wanted, then her clan's power would need to be curtailed alongside the others. Their powerbase would be wider, but shallower. But, he imagined that would be a hard negotiation point to sell them on. So, he had mostly been planning to undercut them in secret and by the time they realized, it would be far too late.

"The shape of my father's plans for Britannia are still undecided," Ragnar replied instead of commenting on her observations. "As you say, securing the islands will be a significant investment. There is no promise that future Allvaldrs will be as powerful as my father. In all likelihood, they won't be. So, in times of strife, it could be relatively easy for the islands to feel comfortable in rebelling."

Father, of course, had plans for such a thing. The North Sea wasn't a large one, but it was dangerous. Without warning, the skies could turn from cloudless to a storm, and the calm seas could rage until they dropped waves the size of mountains on unlucky ships. To secure the islands, they would need to project their presence upon them, and to do that…

Well, that wasn't important at the moment.

"Hmmm?" Maeve hummed, and he had the feeling she saw through his sidestepping of her observation. "So he might just decide to not bother with us at all? That'd be disappointing."

That wasn't the response he expected, "Disappointing?"

"I rather liked the image you painted for me," Maeve admitted and he felt like she was being honest, there. "Alba isn't a rich land. Not like the South is. What isn't mountains are hills. There's not much farmland, so we breed goats and sheep, and that keeps the land that we do have used for grazing. There probably isn't a single even road in the kingdom, and while the land isn't lacking in other resources, no clan alone has the resources to properly exploit them… and they're too proud to ask for help."

A loud dramatic sigh escaped her, "Pride really is a stupid thing. So many would rather choke on it than swallow it." Then her gaze settled heavily on Ragnar, "So, I wanted to see what the kingdom could become without all those unnecessary things getting in the way."

Ragnar felt a shift in the air that he couldn't quite understand. This started to feel less like a negotiation between his empire and her clan, and instead it felt… personal.

"There is another way to secure your grip on these islands," Maeve continued after a beat, leaning forward. "Hey, prince… what do you think about becoming king?"

"What?" He blurted, so caught off guard that the reaction slipped out. At it, Maeve gave him a vaguely disappointed look with a shake of her head.

"You didn't even consider it? That's no good. You're a prince! You should have a little more ambition," she scolded him. "It wouldn't even be that difficult to pull off. You marry me, and one or two other girls from the other major clans. The rest will rebel, of course -- you're a no good dastardly foreigner who covets the crown. But, with your father's resources and the loyal clans, their defeat would be all but certain. Strip them of their lands and resources, and you have the means of establishing your own base of power in Alba."

'This girl…

Maeve raised a finger, as if she were ticking off points. "With a loyal son and prince of the realm in charge of Alba, your father wouldn't need to worry about who controls 'Britannia.' And with you here, whoever else he places in charge of the various kingdoms he carves out, the presence of the royal family will be felt, reducing their willingness to act independently. Additionally, outright seizing the kingdoms means that you have a base of power for your war against the Romans when that finally starts."

… is a little too smart.'

Ragnar wasn't dull. He absorbed everything that his tutors had to teach him. He picked up languages with ease. He wasn't sure how smart he really was, but he did know that he was smart. Sometimes he even learned things faster than Father did. But this felt different.

"I'm sure your brother would take issue with that," Ragnar deflected… and at her smile, he was struck with a revelation. "He has no idea that I'm here, does he?"

"I love my brother," Maeve said, and that sounded honest, at least. "But he is a really oblivious guy. It's a lot of work covering up his shortcomings as it is, but as a king? That'd kill him." She let out a disappointed sigh with a shake of her head, "He's exactly the kind of guy that'd let all the power go straight to his head. The Alba that I want to see can't be real under his rule."

His thoughts must have shown on his face because she pointed a finger at him, "Don't go thinking that I'd betray my family on a whim. I'd do anything for them. It's just that in this case, what's best for them is not getting what they want."

"So, in this ideal Alba, I'm king, you are my queen, and Alba becomes a vassal to the Scandinavian Empire?" He voiced, trying to tell if this was simple ambition or something greater. Or worse. He hadn't even considered the possibility. It could work. Father was both the Allvaldr and King of Denmark. Should he be formally selected as Heir, then Alba would be his personal fief to give him a power base to work with.

Every point she made rang with a note of reason and truth. It wasn't a path forward he would have considered, but it was one. Especially when it completely removed the negatives of having to deal with a puppet king whose loyalty was dubious at best.

"That about sums it up," Maeve agreed with a nod, lowering her accusing finger, her gaze searching him for hints of his answer.

"Why?" He asked, summarizing all of his questions in a single word. He wasn't strictly against the idea. It felt like something that his father would approve of. Be proud of. But all of it hinged on Maeve, a girl whom he spoken to all of two times, including this one. And all he really knew about her was that she was dangerous.

Dangerous in the same kind of way that Aunt Morrigan was.

"Because I want more," Maeve answered so bluntly that it couldn't be anything other than true. "More for myself. For my family. For Alba." As she spoke, she stood up and took a step forward, looming over Ragnar before leaning in so close that their faces were practically touching. "So? How about it? Want to get married?"

It was exactly that moment that Ragnar began to suspect that there was something deeply wrong with him. Bradamante was one of the most beautiful women that he had ever seen, and she'd nearly killed him. Maeve, however, scared him on a level that felt instinctual, and in that moment, she seemed every bit as beautiful.

"Ah… if you wouldn't mind, I suppose."

He just needed to figure out how he was going to tell Father about all of this.

...

#7,442
Haldur hadn't stopped laughing since I broke the seal, read the letter penned by my eldest son, then started pacing. His curiosity had gotten the better of him and with a dismissive gesture, I let him read it. A mistake on my part because my brother had tears in his eyes and he was wheezing, entirely too amused with himself.

I had expected some difficulties navigating the diplomatic waters of Alba. While I wasn't too familiar with them in any meaningful degree, experience had taught me what to expect from the quarrelsome clans. Old feuds and infighting between different clans and inside of each of them, all trying to tear each other down -- not to rise higher, but because they would rather see their enemies in the mud with them than see them rise above them.

It was going to be a challenge for my boys, but I had confidence that they'd get the job done. And even if they failed, it would be a good experience for them. I thought I had prepared myself for every possibility -- success, failure, anything from Alba becoming steadfast allies to outright enemies. But the letter contained a possibility that I hadn't imagined and for the life of me, I couldn't tell if that was a good thing or not.

"Would you quit laughing already? You're my advisor. Advise." I grumbled at the red in the face Haldur who had tears in his eyes that he had to wipe away while stifling his giggles.

"Sorry, sorry -- it's just that, the boy was so mild-mannered. Between you and Astrid, I always thought he'd be a bit more brash," Haldur nearly started laughing again. "Then he goes and pulls a stunt like this! Now you know how the rest of us felt when we heard about your exploits. Mother's heart about went still in her chest when she heard what you got up to in Saxony."

I had to look away from my brother to hide the faint grin tugging at my lips but based on how he wheezed, he saw it all the same. "Shut it," I commanded him, having no expectation that the order would be obeyed. Picking up the letter, I read the contents again in the vague hope that I had misread the runes. No such luck there.

It was impossible for me to mistake Ragnar's handwriting, so I knew it came from him. It even read like his letters -- direct, including important details about the series of events around him, and then offering a few thoughts and his reasoning for his course of action. That action being a bid to become king and marry what amounted to a princess of the Picts.

A girl, who as Magnus described in his own letter -- 'As dangerous as she is fair, and she is the fairest girl in the kingdom.'

Which muddled things a bit for me. Ove's letter made it clear that the offer was genuine and had great potential within the kingdom, if for a price that could only be paid in blood. But Ragnar and Magnus weren't boys anymore. They were of the age where lust started to weigh heavily on the scales of their thinking, usually at the expense of common sense.

"The biggest issue I see with it would be his age," Haldur got himself under control so they could now discuss the practicality of such an arrangement. "He must have conducted himself well if the possibility is being entertained at all, but the fact is that he's too young to be king."

"They intend to make him a puppet," I voiced, a low growl in the back of his throat. Alba and the clans would bend the knee, but they intended to take my son's teeth from him. They intended to make him dependent on their support within the kingdom and entrench their own influence in the time it took for Ragnar to grow into himself.

"Aye," Haldur agreed. "But their attempts would help ease the transition. If we go in and openly put his butt on a throne, then it's a blatant power grab on our part. However, if one of them pushes him forward and acts as a form of regent, the whole thing will go over much smoother."

"The king was assassinated and it's a succession crisis. It's going to be rough no matter what," I pointed out, walking around the room as I reread the letter again. "With a strong enough force, we can circumvent those strings they're trying to put on my boy."

"At the cost of turning this into a conflict that couldn't be settled before our departure," Haldur pointed out, and I raised an eyebrow in his direction. He considered the point before nodding, "Aye, it's not likely to. Doesn't matter how much they like us, we'd still be putting foreign blood on their throne. And I don't think they like us that much to begin with."

"It's worth the risk," I voiced my thoughts.

"A kingdom served up on a silver platter? Of course it is," Haldur agreed. "But are you really going to let your boy stay on this island for years on end? Alone?" He asked a question, but his tone made it clear he knew what the answer would be.

"Absolutely not," I confirmed. Ragnar was too young. Far too young. He had his arm ring, but he wasn't a man yet. He wasn't ready for the burdens of being a king, especially in a kingdom so unsteady. "His mother would kill me."

Haldur snorted, "She's likely to do so anyways. You take the boy on his first raid and he comes back married."

He meant it as a jest, but the idea inspired a thought. "We go through with the marriage. Secure the alliance against the anglo-saxons. Then we depart as planned, but we leave a garrison force to uphold our interests until Ragnar is ready to assume the throne."

Haldur frowned, having his doubts. "I imagine the situation is going to be very different five years from now. King Causantín isn't even dead yet and they're squabbling over who succeeds him. Five years from now, I imagine they would have settled on someone."

"I doubt that," I replied. "The kings of this land have been dropping like flies this season. I don't think that will change after our departure." A plan was starting to put itself together in the back of my mind. It wasn't a possibility that I expected to drop into our laps, but Ragnar was right to attempt to seize control over it.

"I hope that isn't a declaration of intent?" Haldur raised an eyebrow at me, and I chuckled.

"Not of mine. Ecbert's," I voiced, setting Ragnar's letter aside before I took a seat near a balcony. Our forces were slowly combing the northern lands of Britannia towards Alba. Northumbria hadn't managed to offer any true resistance to slow us down.

"You honestly think he's behind it all?" Haldur questioned, and I shrugged.

Our progress with the raid had been steady. Faster now that word of us had well and truly spread. The situation in Northumbria was a farce. King Osbald, who took the crown after King Æthelred of Northumbria had been assassinated, lasted all of three weeks before being deposed by the now King Eardwulf. Something King Osbald took issue with and he was now rallying the nobility and other forces within the petty kingdom in a bid to reclaim his crown.

By all accounts, his bid to become king again wasn't going great. Actually, it was going quite poorly. But the situation was such an obscene mess that the nobles who didn't flee their estates or holdings with as much wealth they could carry simply threw open the doors for their raiding parties in the hopes that the rumors of our merciful nature were true. The nobles who fled of course flocked to Ecbert and Wessex, as the weak flocked to those that were strong.

Out of all of the monarchs on Britannia, Ecbert was the only one who could be called strong. And, day by day, his strength was growing. The nobles who fled took as much of a town's treasury as they could, alongside their own personal wealth. All that wealth was being served up to Ecbert on a silver platter, alongside worthwhile courtiers entering his court because, even if they might be cowards, they were smart enough to know that there was no hope of reinforcements, much less victory.

"His intentions become clearer," I replied with a nod. "He has the means to offer a proper battle, and he knows it. Yet, he does little more than nip at our heels and offer the occasional skirmish. Despite there being calls to attack and some even labeling him a coward for not being more aggressive."

Haldur tilted his head, "You think its all just a ploy then? Smoke and mirrors?"

"Not entirely," I replied. "If he senses the possibility of victory, then I imagine that he will pounce on it. I don't believe that he intends to offer a proper battle. I think he's preparing to usurp Mercia and even Northumbria from their kings. He gets the wealth and his pick of nobles from their courts, and when we depart, he will be in a perfect situation to usurp their crowns."

It was exceedingly pragmatic. Ruthlessly so. Ecbert was turning himself into the face of resistance against us all while undermining it. And I suspected that I wasn't the only one who had figured that out. Otherwise, there were far more effective places to send two Paladins than Alba. I had known Astolfo hailed from Mercia, and there he would have been a strong rallying figure. But in Alba? As a representative from Rome and a petty kingdom that Alba had quarreled with since the Roman Empire fell?

That was a move that could only be explained by Charlemagne losing faith in his pawn. That was a move determined to prevent me from gaining further advantage on Britannia.

"And us having a strong ally on the islands wouldn't be helpful to that goal," Haldur followed my line of thought. "That's no promise that he will interfere, however."

"He will if he has good reason to," I refuted, making Haldur tilt his head. "As it stands, Alba is a far-off threat for Ecbert. However, if it were to encroach on what he intends to make his new borders…"

Haldur understood instantly. "You wish to divide Northumbria," he guessed and I confirmed it with a nod. In terms of landmass Northumbria was the greatest of the petty kingdoms, though Mercia boasted a larger population. Well, it did. I was uncertain if that was still true. "That would certainly help soothe the bitter taste of swallowing their pride."

It wasn't a perfect balance, but it was enough to satisfy our goals. Walking over to a nearby table, I pushed back a few papers to reveal the map that I had been building little by little. Our scouts and raiding parties were filling in the great blank that my Map had been when we first arrived, revealing mineral deposits and soil fertility. While it was still incomplete, it was enough to reveal that Britannia was a rich land for farming.

Expanding Alba significantly would overstretch it, especially with an unruly populace. That would make it unsteady and prevent the solidification of power in the crucial years. Then, upon our return, should Ragnar truly wish it, he would be in the perfect position to become king. Likewise, Ecbert wouldn't be able to consolidate his own power on the island by the time we returned with the intent of conquest.

Yet, to the Picts and Alba as a whole, it would be seen as a most generous gift. An expansion of their borders beyond what they had ever managed in their history.

A true poisoned chalice.

"When shall the Picts receive their gift?" Haldur questioned and I offered a thin smile.

"When they offer my son a bride."


…
​

It took three days for King Causantín to die. For most of that time he was delirious with a fever, and when he wasn't, he was slumbering like he was already dead. Ragnar hadn't been permitted to offer his respects to the ailing king in person, but from the rumors that swirled, the king didn't die a good death, nor a gentle one before his body failed him.

Three days felt like a long time. Longer still to die. But, in the grand scheme of things, it was hardly any time at all. Enough time for a letter to be sent to Father about the marriage offer but not enough time to receive a reply. Meanwhile, things in Alba were… unstable.

"Are you stupid?" Magnus asked his favorite question over the past few days once more.

"Probably. I mean, at least a little bit," he replied, giving his brother a flat glare. One that Magnus had grown immune to since they were boys. "Any particular reason why you're asking again, or is it still about Maeve?"

"It's absolutely about Maeve," Magnus replied with a disappointed shake of his head. "You met the girl once, and you're tripping over yourself to marry her."

"Be fair, Magnus." Harald said with absolutely no intention to help, "the offer came with a kingdom attached to it."

"Another thing," Magnus continued, seated at the top of a hill to watch Perth from afar. The city was in a frenzy, not unlike an anthill getting kicked open. "Are you really planning to live here? Away from Denmark? It won't be for another five years before Father conquers these islands. You'd be alone in hostile territory. Were you even thinking at all?"

"Oh, he was. Just with his-" Harald started to quip and Ragnar waved them both off.

"Enough of that," he protested, giving them both a mild glare. "The match… It's a fine one. I'll leave the details for Father to hammer out." Meave had left the storeroom very pleased, but he hadn't seen her since. Yet, the movements of such a marriage were set into motion. Ove was discussing what such a union might bring to Alba and the Scandinavian Empire.

It hadn't yet reached a point that it couldn't be called off, but without ample reason to oppose it the marriage would go ahead. Meaning, quite soon, he would be a married man. It didn't feel real yet. He expected to be plagued with doubts and uncertainty after giving his consent to such a match, because Magnus wasn't wrong. Maeve wasn't someone he knew well, but she did feel like someone that he understood.

"There's no way that he'd leave you behind when it comes time to return. Your mother would actually kill him," Magnus continued all the same. "So, at the very least, you'll be coming back with us."

"Which means I'll probably be married soon," Ragnar reasoned. He wasn't sure what the future held, but he had a feeling that it involved a scolding. He didn't mind the thought. It felt… kind of good, to make a decision like this, regardless of what the circumstances were. It was the feeling of taking control of his own fate with his own hands.

However, before the pair could fuss over details, Ragnar caught sight of something interesting. A party was gathering up at the entrance of Perth -- at first, Ragnar assumed it was another clan that intended to return home to prepare for the succession crisis, but that thought was proven wrong when he saw familiar plate armor. It was the Romans. They were leaving, with Bradamante and Astolfo at their head.

"Seems like they know that they've lost," Harald remarked.

"I'm more surprised that they're being allowed to leave," Magnus added. "As it stands, they're the ones that suspicion is falling on for the king's assassination."

"More like the Picts realize that they couldn't keep them here even if they tried," Harald replied. He had the right of it, more or less. With the king dead, the clans of Alba weren't ready to make their stance between Scandinavia or Rome clear. So, it was simply easier to let them go.

The Romans, for their part, realized that if they lingered too long that opinion would change and they would become a natural scapegoat.

Still, it seemed like a shame. Enough so that Ragnar began to move forward before his mind really began to register what he was doing. It was just such a shame, he felt. The Romans weren't exactly stealing away in the dead of night, but they weren't receiving a proper send off that they were due either. And that was simply unacceptable.

Ragnar made his way down the ridge and towards the city -- his approach was hardly stealthy, so the Romans saw his approach long in advance. They weren't greeted with any warmth. Just frosty glares that bordered contempt, which made Astolfo's easy going smile that much of a contrast.

"Oh! Prince Rags is here to see us off? What an honor," Astolfo said, and in another, Ragnar might take that as sarcasm. But, Astolfo wore an honest smile.

"I thought someone should," he admitted. Astolfo smiled in a way that told Ragnar that he knew that wasn't all that he came down here for. There was a question that he wanted to ask, but wasn't sure if he really wanted the answer.

He had been caught off guard by the Romans' presence. He had been so focused on what their arrival meant for the negotiations that he'd never stopped to think about why they were there in the first place. After all… why send two Paladins to a place like Alba at all? One would have surely sufficed, but not sending any would have worked just as well.

There was no gentle way to phrase the question. "Were you sent here to kill me?"

Astolfo didn't tense at the question. He didn't look surprised either. "Ah… well, not in so many words, but more or less, yeah," he admitted with an almost casual ease.

That was the only thing that made sense. The Romans had to know that any alliance with the Picts would be short-lived. It simply wasn't practical to maintain and the leadership of Alba would realize that as well eventually.

"Then why didn't you?" He asked, his gaze sliding to Bradamante, whose expression was impassive. They'd had the means. They'd had the opportunity. And they most certainly had the motivation. Yet, he was still alive, and unless they struck him down now, that would continue. Meaning that they had accomplished nothing on this trip and they would return as failures to their Emperor.

It was Bradamante who answered, "My Emperor laments that he did not slay your father when he had the chance." She started, not exactly disproving his point. "He came to him, a boy your age, as a spy. One whose presence had been betrayed by an ally in his own camp. Your father was alone, surrounded, and not yet the warrior that he would grow into."

Then something in her eyes softened ever so slightly. "Emperor Charlemagne laments this opportunity, but I believe that even should God allow him to go back in time, he would make the same choice. For my Emperor is not a man who would carelessly order the death of a child who had not yet done him any wrong."

"You take after your old man a little too much, Rags," Astolfo remarked before he saddled his horse. "I think you have it in you to be a great Allvaldr one day. And whatever happens between our nations… we can hardly call ourselves respectable adults if we go making that your problem before you're old enough, can we?"

Bradamante mounted her horse and the Roman delegation began to move forward while Ragnar struggled to muster a response. What could he say to that? A mere thank you seemed so underwhelming. "I…" He started, only to falter as he looked between the two.

"Take care, Rags!" Astolfo said, urging his horse forward and giving an enthusiastic wave goodbye. Bradamante offered a slight inclination of her head before she followed her senior Paladin, leaving Ragnar to watch them go.

Leaving so much unsaid. And, as he watched them go, he truly hoped that he never saw either of them again…

Because Astolfo's warning from before rang with a fatal truth -- that the next time they met, it would be on the battlefield, and they wouldn't part as friends.

...
