#7,455
Hjalmar saw the island of Mann spring up from the heavy fog that clung to the lazy sea. They approached at half speed, him and fifteen thousand warriors spread across around a hundred and fifty ships. The men were eager to get solid ground under their feet again, and he shared their eagerness. He let out a whistle to signal a lad with a strong pair of lungs, prompting him to blow a horn to signal their arrival and that they were on the same side to the town that had sprung up on the barren looking island.

"The man can't help himself," Hjalmar mused with some amusement. "It's as if he's compelled to build cities."

A growing town welcomed them at a natural harbor along the coast. He, alongside several of his commanders and their ships, sailed straight towards the docks that seemed busy while the rest of the men would disembark outside of the town. They were greeted with a large man that vaguely resembled King Hoffer, though that was mostly in how large the man was, at the end of the dock. His legs wobbled just a bit, but he didn't make a fool of himself walking down the deep dock towards the welcome party.

"Hjalmar the Bold," the man greeted him with a wide smile. "I am Hoffer the Short. I rule this town in the name of the Allvaldr. Well met."

"If you are the shortest of your family, then you have the blood of giants in you," Hjalmar greeted the man. The Bold, he called him. It took everything he had not to laugh at that. It made him sound so much grander than he really was. It also put expectations on him that he didn't care for. Why not Hjalmar the Exceedingly Pragmatic? Sure, it was bit of a mouthful but so were half the titles people insisted on being called.

Hoffer laughed a little too sharply for his amusement to be entirely genuine. "We likely do, but I'm the shortest of my brothers. They called me such as a boy, and now everyone calls me so as a man." Ah. Well, now he felt bad. "Welcome to Geymsla. A few moons ago, it wasn't even a fishing village. Now it boasts eight thousand people, be they warriors or thralls."

"The Allvaldr really does work fast," Hjalmar mused as Hoffer welcomed him to follow. He had been a much younger man when he joined the army on the eve of the Conquest. There, over three years, he saw countless plain and unremarkable villages. Then, older and a little more seasoned, he saw towns and cities in the Mediterranean. That experience made the Allvaldr's touch obvious when it came to the layout of the town.

The shapes of the buildings and roads, how they were laid out for easy navigation and mobilization if needed. Where there were clearly defined places for markets that didn't impact the flow of those coming and going… there was a clean organization to the town that often felt lacking in others towns. But, when he considered the population and the number of houses he had seen…

"Aye," Hoffer nodded, sensing his realization as they walked through the streets. Hjalmar saw what he meant about most of the people being thralls, as he saw work crews turning the muddy roads into one's covered in cobblestone. "Most of the buildings are storage. Hence the name." Which did admittedly explain the name -- Geymsla meant storage in Norse.

Hoffer was giving him the tour it seemed and Hjalmar appreciated it. The town had a natural flow to the work that he quickly took notice of. Men brought spoils from the ships, and depending on what they were decided which of the storehouses they were brought to. From there, they would be dumped, organized, and then categorized with appropriate dues being marked down.

From there, Hjalmar saw men carrying barrels and crates full of artifacts made of precious metals. He recognized their type immediately -- crosses, bibles, candlesticks, utensils, and adornments. Laborers tore out the precious jewels in them if they had any, organizing them in piles, before separating the metals that were then melted down into ingots of silver and gold. Once cooled and weighed, they would be stacked up into crates and hauled off to another storeroom. This one under guard by two hundred men, all Ironclads.

"It's a shame to smelt them down," Hoffer admitted while they watched the process unfold. "But we wouldn't be able to carry back half of the spoils if we didn't. We just wouldn't have the room."

"There are worse problems to have," Hjalmar replied. He had encountered a similar issue before his departure from the Mediterranean. Which had him following in the Allvaldr's footsteps -- while most of his forces sailed around the coast of the Roman Empire, a large contingent marched up the Dnieper River with a vast amount of their wealth. It was necessary as even with more than a hundred ships, they just didn't have the room. "I take it that the raid has been a success so far?"

"Enough so that I feel bad for his boys," Hoffer said with a grin. "How do you surpass a man like that?"

'You don't,' Hjalmar figured. 'You just get really good at pretending that it doesn't bother you.' However, he couldn't say that. Especially with unknown ears listening in. "His eldest are part of the raid, aren't they?"

Hoffer nodded, "His eldest boys. Ragnar and Magnus. Eh, well, they might never step out of their father's shadow, but the blood shows. Ragnar snagged the heart of a Pict princess! You lot arrived just in time for the wedding."

Well, that was something of a relief. He had never seen a royal wedding before and he was probably important enough to merit an invitation. Though, he wasn't sure if he wanted to go exactly. Going to the wedding meant meeting the Allvaldr and that would likely involve an explanation about what he was thinking withdrawing from the battle outside of Rome, and taking thousands of Norsemen from King Hoffer as they collectively realized that their unchecked rampage was over.

That was a conversation that felt like it could go really well or extremely poorly for him.

"I suppose I should find a gift for the lad, then," Hjalmar mused. Luckily, he had several boat fulls to choose from. "When and where is the wedding?"

"Glasgow. It's not too far from here, a day's sailing up the coast with the wind at your back," Hoffer answered. "You should have enough time to rest and water your men before you depart my fair city." Meaning he had about three days to prepare himself to meet the Allvaldr once again?

That felt like entirely too much time and not enough.


…
​

Geymsla really was a warehouse rather than a town, and he saw it in action for the two days the men got to unload the cargo and enjoy themselves after many long weeks at sea.

The Allvaldr had swept through Mercia and then Northumbria like a farmer harvesting a crop, making sure that every last grain was accounted for. The massive army he brought was splintered into hundreds of raiding parties, some larger while others were as small as a band of five. They dispersed across the petty kingdoms, looting everything of value down to farming tools. All of that loot was brought to what were now two forts that had been built on the coast, where a similar process of cataloging the spoils occurred to ensure that those that brought it in were credited with their due.

It was then packed off, sent to Geymsla, where it was categorized again, sorted, smelted, or sold at the market that had sprung up. Pretty women or strong backed men were sold at thrall markets, fine goods were hawked by merchants -- things on the mainland, be it the Eyrie or Britannia, for which Irish and Britons were venturing out to the Isle of Mann to buy back what was essentially stolen from them. The Allvaldr even took their charcoal to feed the ever burning furnaces that even still couldn't keep up with demand.

His own wares were similarly categorized, evaluated, and sorted with individual warriors being credited their due. It was a clever little system to push against fraud, either from anyone overevaluating their due or the harbor master undervaluing it to cheat them. Most of their spoils were packed off, some of the men buying and selling at the market.

However, it was hardly as if the Irish or Britons were opening a door, inviting them in and letting them ransack their homes. There were constant skirmishes across the islands. Raids going wrong, ambushes, sheer dumb bad luck -- there were no grand defeats, but there were no grand victories either. Just little by little, the natives of these lands were picking away at their strength. Especially in the bottom half of Northumbria, where their raiding parties were being hunted by King Ecbert.

But any progress that they had made was immediately undone with the arrival of fifteen thousand warriors. And after a brief recovery, they were eager to go back to sea if it meant arriving in time for the royal wedding. Or, rather, the festivities that would follow the wedding.

A guide led a portion of their fleet up the coast to prevent them from getting lost, as Britannia had hundreds of rivers that would lead them down winding paths. The one that they wanted had a large mouth that started to steadily narrow before Hjalmar saw any signs of the city beyond a fishing village located upstream.

Glasgow had been a small town. He saw the traces of it that lingered after the Allvaldr got his hands on the city -- a wall had been quickly erected, grounds were cleared l, while a sea of tents could be found outside of the walls from the Picts and the army that was attending the royal wedding.

His own army would be funneling up the river in batches to avoid overwhelming the small dockyard. However, Hjalmar along with his peers arrived first. And it was there, they were greeted with a familiar face.

"Isulf," Hjalmar greeted his old squadmate back during the Conquest with some warmth. "You look well." While Hjalmar and Ulfar had been chosen by the Allvaldr to go to the Mediterranean, Lokar and Isulf had chosen to remain in Scandinavia to serve there. Trym, however, was a bit like moss that had grown on Hjalmar as the man followed him all the way down to the Mediterranean and back again.

"Same to you, Hjalmar. Ulfar," he returned evenly. Hjalmar didn't take it personally. Isulf was a standoffish man by nature, but he never failed to have his back when it counted. "The Allvaldr welcomes you both and invites you to the palace."

Nothing unexpected there, so Hjalmar offered a small nod before following Isulf. They didn't have to go far. The town wasn't exactly big to begin with, though Hjalmar did see that it was full to the point of bursting. As they walked through the dirt streets, he saw a similar reaction to what they got in Geymsla -- word quickly spread about their arrival with people crowding the streets to get a look at them as they passed, cheering them on as victorious conquerors.

It was a good feeling. And he hoped a good indication of how the Allvaldr felt about what transpired in the Mediterranean.

The palace was more of an estate, and an unimpressive one in comparison to what he saw in the Mediterranean or back home. Still, it served as the lodging for the Allvaldr with walls, a courtyard, and a large building that sat in the heart of it. They didn't enter the estate itself but walked around it, taking them to the gardens.

There, for the first time in five years, he saw the Allvaldr, and he was exactly as he remembered. Unreasonably large with a barrel chest and thick arms, his blood red hair was pulled back out of his face and cut short so that it only brushed his shoulders. His beard was also cut short so as to not hide the scar on his neck. He wore what Hjalmar now recognized as an Arab inspired style of dress with knee high boots, trousers, and elaborately embroidered folded tunic that came down to his knees and was held in place with a blood red silk sash.

"Allvaldr," Hjalmar greeted him alongside his peers, all of them dropping to a knee in his presence.

"Rise," the Allvaldr commanded easily, turning to face them. Then he gestured to two short men that stood nearby, and upon looking at them, Hjalmar realized that they weren't short men but very tall boys. "These are my sons, Prince Ragnar and Prince Magnus. They were eager to meet the heroes of the Mediterranean."

A knot of tension around his heart came undone at his tone, but he was still reeling from the revelation that the two boys were the eldest princes. Both favored their father in looks, including the blood red hair, but they seemed to have inherited their mother's eyes as Ragnar's were a different shade of blue while Magnus had green eyes. They'd also clearly inherited their father's size because if they kept growing as they were, by the time they could grow a beard they'd be a head taller than most.

"We are honored," Hjalmar spoke first. "And we express our congratulations on your marriage, Prince Ragnar."

"I am glad to see that you arrived in time to attend," Prince Ragnar replied in a warm if practiced tone. "My marriage is one cause to celebrate, as are your victories in the Mediterranean."

The interaction was brief. Barely an exchange of pleasantries, but Hjalmar didn't last this long without being able to read people and his immediate impression of Ragnar was that he was cut from the same cloth as his father. They carried themselves in the same way, but Ragnar didn't carry himself as a boy his age should. He carried himself as… well, a prince.

"Victories tempered by a defeat, alas," Ulfar spoke up at Hjalmar's side, both of them standing.

Prince Ragnar inclined his head. "That is true, I suppose. Tell me, how is my Uncle?" He questioned lightly, gently probing at the topic that Hjalmar wanted to avoid. Then, Ulfar, the bastard, glanced at Hjalmar to answer since he was the one who spoke to King Hoffer last before their departure.

Hjalmar thought back on the meeting. How listless King Hoffer had been, slouching in a chair with dark bags under his eyes.

"He seemed…" The temptation was there to lie, but it was hardly as if the royal family couldn't find out. And if he wasn't in trouble now, he would be then. "Defeated, I'm sorry to say. He took the loss outside of Rome quite hard."

Prince Ragnar nodded sadly, but Hjalmar was looking at his father, who wore an even expression that didn't hint at his thoughts.

At least until he spoke, "I'm afraid that was unavoidable." The Allvaldr spoke up with a sigh in his voice. "Hoffer's plan was sound enough, but he misjudged the timing."

"Like I did?" Prince Ragnar questioned, earning a thin smile from the Allvaldr, who rubbed the top of his head affectionately.

"Aye. At least a little bit," The Allvaldr replied, and that felt like a private conversation they were referencing that he didn't have the context for. "Hoffer was right that the kingdom required significant territorial gains to avoid his islands being eventually swallowed up one by one. And Italia was the perfect location to expand to. He also sought to fracture the restored Roman Empire before the foundations had time to settle, which was wise. However, his mistake was thinking that he needed to accomplish both goals at once."

"What should he have done?" Prince Magnus asked, his brow furrowing.

However, the Allvaldr gestured to Hjalmar to answer, making him still for a moment. But, after swallowing the lump in his throat, he voiced the answer to that very question that he had been asking himself since the battle.

"Raiding the north of Italia and Rome would have been enough. We shouldn't have fought at all," Hjalmar voiced his thoughts. "The North was devastated after the raids. The people and lords there would have seen Charlemagne as weak and as a sovereign who couldn't fulfill his obligations to protect them. The whole area would have become a hotbed of sedition, forcing Charlemagne to expend resources to keep the area pacified. And if he couldn't, then Charlemagne would have lost Italia all the same and with it, the symbol of Rome."

It would have taken longer that way. Years. Maybe even a decade. But the Allvaldr would undoubtedly have ways to poke the resulting beehive to make sure that Charlemagne suffered more for it. Maybe by supporting others to revolt in the Roman Empire, who would be emboldened by Charlemagne's distraction. Maybe by way of Hadi of the Abbasids launching his invasion to reclaim all of Hispania and possibly even beyond it.

The point being, it would have taken time, but if King Hoffer had focused on fracturing the Roman Empire, he would have gotten what he wanted eventually.

"Essentially correct," The Allvaldr replied with a nod of his head. "Of course, Hoffer's motivation for rushing is valid. Charlemagne is rather adept at turning rebellions into means of strengthening himself, so it was possible that anything other than a decisive defeat on the battlefield would be recoverable for him. There is also the consideration that while he was king, the kingdom was new and his authority untested."

Hjalmar thought of the mercenaries that had made up the army. Most of them hadn't cared that Hoffer was king or of the fate of the kingdom. They bent the knee and fought under his banner because it was their way of getting rich. Even before the defeat, there had been plenty who decided that they were rich enough and simply vanished in the night with their wealth.

King Hoffer had likely felt the pressure of his army vanishing underneath him as time went on. Or feared that influential mercenary captains would eventually challenge him for his crown. He'd likely thought that he had to do it then or never.

"Though now we do find ourselves in a similar situation," The Allvaldr continued, his gaze taking the measure of him, just as he had before he sent them off to the Mediterranean. "In the coming years, my son will become King of Alba, and that has changed the nature of the plans that we discussed five years ago. Rather than vanishing for another five years, it is my intention to maintain a strong presence on Britannia until we return to finish the conquest as planned."

Not entirely unexpected. The Allvaldr had made it clear that he expected things to change when Charlemagne began to react. And he had been fairly confident the events in the Mediterranean would have an effect on things.

With a gesture, the Allvaldr instructed them to follow alongside his sons, and he led them into a study that looked like it had been repurposed for his use. It might have been a store room since it had a big enough door that the Allvaldr didn't need to duck his head to pass through. There, he brought out a map that seemed impossibly detailed.

He had seen Roman depictions of Britannia, and it looked like a misshapen mass floating in the North Sea. The one before him was marked not just with villages and towns, but rivers, forests, and farmland. It almost felt like too much information.

"Until my son assumes the Alba throne, we must safeguard our interests on Britannia. To this end, I have amended my initial plans for the partition of Britannia," he said, gesturing to a border marked with a thicker line of ink. "Alba will be expanded down to the Hadrian's Wall, while Northumbria and Mercia will be cleaved in two to form a single kingdom."

The partition would make Alba, this new kingdom, and what was currently Wessex roughly equal. In size, at least. He didn't know what the divide would be in population, farm land, and such things. Though he did expect Wessex to be the richer of the kingdoms on account that they bordered the channel between the Roman coast and Britannia.

"Meanwhile," The Allvaldr continued, "All of the Eyrie will be unified under a single banner." Which was the smaller, but still considerable island to the west. "The groundwork for these two kingdoms will be staged from the Island of Mann and Alba over the next five years before we conquer the islands outright. And, when that time comes… those that have safe guarded my son's and my empire's interest will be entitled to a suitable reward."

Crowns.

The Allvaldr was talking about making him a king. A King of a land full of people that the Allvaldr had robbed to the point he took their firewood.

Hjalmar found his mouth as dry as the deserts of Egypt while Ulfar leaned forward with a hungry gleam in his eye, but he found his voice first. "I… don't suppose I could refuse such an honor?" Especially as one of the things that he had heard about this damned island was that its kings had a habit of dropping like flies.

There was a twinkle in the Allvaldr's eyes before he reached out and rested a hand on Hjalmar's shoulder, before delivering his answer in the form of a single word.

"No."

Yeah… he should have figured.

...

#7,480
Astrid was probably going to murder me once I returned home, but I had accepted such a fate at this point. There was no avoiding it. So, I endeavored to enjoy the time that I had left and watched from above the festivities surrounding my son's wedding.

The location of Glasgow was something of a compromise. Perth was the center of power in Alba, but the kingdom itself was far too destabilized at the moment with the assassination of their king. That, and it would be seen as weakness on my part to allow them to host the wedding. For similar reasons, they were reluctant to come to the stronghold of power that I'd established on the Isle of Mann. Glasgow was just close and unimportant enough that it served as a suitable compromise.

At least in theory, since the small town was completely unequipped to handle the thousands of people that camped outside of its newly erected walls, most of which were my warriors. Hjalmar and Ulfar's army of fifteen thousand men had settled in quickly, but there were still hundreds to thousands that trickled our way after they finished their raid on a town or village. Comparatively, the Picts sent a small party but in terms of wedding guests, it was a small army on their own.

The friction I expected began almost immediately. The Picts were a fractured bunch, but Ragnar was right that they could broadly be placed in two groups -- the Old Picts, which he was marrying into, and the New Clans. Which were Gaelic clans that came from the Eire or Wales, or even Northumbria, before the Romans had imposed their culture upon the defeated clans. The New Clans, though the name was a misnomer on account that they had held the lands for centuries by this point, had seized the lowlands of Alba as far back as when Rome made their attempt at conquering all of Britannia.

The Old Picts were all in on the marriage, celebrating it much like a lifeline tossed to a drowning man at sea. Something that I could watch as Ragnar went through the steps of a traditional dance with his bride, Maeve. I would have liked to know her better before consenting to such a union, but it had only taken one meeting to confirm what Magnus had to say about her -- she was like Morrigan.

Not entirely, of course. Maeve boasted no magics and had grown up a princess of the old clans rather than a half-starved child in the woods. Yet despite their differences, they carried themselves with the same aloofness while their eyes and ears drank in every detail. She had been all smiles for the meeting, every word careful and measured, enough so that she would have been right at home in the Roman court at Constantinople.

Watching her dance with my son, I couldn't help but worry just a bit. The girl was young, clever, and beautiful, but I had spent enough time with those that harbored ambitions to recognize the signs. Ragnar was sincerely convinced that she was honest with her desire to transform Alba from squabbling clans to a single united kingdom. However, I couldn't help but suspect that her motivations ran deeper than that.

"He's a lucky lad," Haldur remarked to me, leaning by my side as we watched the festivities rather than indulge in them. Such was the price of a crown. "And he's a clever one. She's not likely to completely wrap your boy around her little finger."

An amused huff escaped me despite my solemn thoughts, "He has more ambition than I thought he had in him." Until he'd sent that letter informing me of his bid for the throne of Alba, I had always thought Ragnar to be more… passive. He was the type to sit back, observe, and react. There wasn't anything wrong with it. I vastly preferred it to rash stubbornness in fact.

He was like I had been when I was the his age. Before Horrik did what he did, forcing me into a more proactive role if I wanted my vengeance. So it really had come as a surprise when he made such a move, stepping well outside of the realm of responsibility that I had entrusted him with to make strides to incorporate another kingdom into the empire.

"Hardly a bad thing in an heir," Haldur remarked, and it took the edge off my good mood. Things were better than they ever had been between us. For all of the warnings that my mother had given, and for all of his small power plays to gauge where we stood with each other… My relationship with Haldur had only been better when we were both young boys. Probably before I could speak in full sentences.

But then he would do that.

An idle remark that wasn't so idle. It was a test to see if my stance had changed in some way so he could use the information as some kind of leverage. The worst part was that I doubted Halur even realized it. It was just his nature. And while I couldn't blame a scorpion for being a scorpion, I could find it irritating when it stung me.

Still, it made me confront a decision I had been holding off on -- the decision of who my heir would be.

I watched the pair dance on, and despite their youth, neither were unaware of the danger of those watching on. Most of that danger stemmed from self-interest -- when things changed, it invited the opportunity for people to change their fortunes in turn, to climb higher on the social ladder, just as much as it presented a risk that could see them fall. Some, however, glowed a malevolent red to my eyes.

Maeve's betrothal to the late King Causantín's son and heir was broken with the very same breath that they announced her wedding with my son. That was the only reason why things didn't descend into outright factional warfare. As much as the clans may bluster and gripe, they knew quite well that they stood little chance in open battle against us, so they wouldn't try. And that was exactly my concern. Knives in the dark were far harder to defend against than an axe in a shield wall.

"Maybe," I replied. Ragnar had proven himself with this gambit, but he had also stepped foot into a realm that he wasn't ready for. If the pair's initial plan was carried out, I had little doubt that both would perish the moment my ships left the shore. Still, it was a spark of ambition that I hadn't expected from my eldest. In five years, he'd be a man grown and far better prepared to handle the challenges of being a king. And those challenges would further prepare him for becoming the Allvaldr. "What about your boy? Have you settled on a match for him?"

My gaze found Harald speaking amongst a small group of Norsemen and Albish women. There was no mistaking their intent, and the girls didn't seem to mind it.

Now it was Haldur's turn to still, wondering if I was asking as his brother or as the Allvaldr. In the end, he offered a shallow nod. "Aye. It hasn't been announced yet, but we're in talks with King Ihala's daughter."

The blocs were already starting to form, but they were forming along the lines that I'd expected. Haldur was the King of Sweden while King Ihala was King of Finland. Their kingdoms were neighbors, they shared similar economic interests as despite being located on the eastern border of my Empire, Finland was far from the economic heartland.

There was a sudden tension between us that was difficult to articulate. Haldur was bracing himself for my reaction -- either to accept the match or to reject it. My powers as the Allvaldr were yet to be defined, and interfering in such a marriage could be within their limits if I chose to.

But I didn't. Instead, I offered a shallow nod, "A fine match. She's a pretty girl. Clever too. I don't think my son will be the only one wrapped around his wife's finger."

The tension bled out if Haldur, even if he did try to hide it with a chuckle that sounded more relieved than amused. "They got it from us, and we got it from Father."

That earned a sad smile from me, my gaze lingering on my son and nephew for a moment longer before I looked over to Lucas. He was mingling with both Hjalmar and Ulfar, considering them both peers already. Peers that he would be dependent on to keep his crown long enough for my son to take it -- though, he wasn't yet aware of that.

Both men were reliable. Trustworthy. They had done everything that I had asked for and more. I would have preferred things to have gone differently back in the Mediterranean, but that was simply the way of things. Hoffer had attempted to do too much at once, and tried to win the battle instead of the war.

Hjalmar, I was inclined to make King of the Éire. It wasn't a rich land, but it was a vast one, and it could be quite powerful if properly harnessed. Ulfar, I intended to make king of the territories of lower Northumbria and upper Mercia. A middle kingdom that I didn't intend to ever feel like their footing was quite secure.

Britannia wasn't a territory that would be easy to hold. The small islands already boasted a population that was comparable to the entirety of my empire. The North Sea wasn't so easily crossed, and the channel between Wessex and the Roman Empire could only be safely traveled a few months of the year. In the end, taking them would be the easy part. Holding them would be quite different.

The easiest way to ensure that none of the kingdoms ever managed to gain enough strength was to ensure that they had evenly matched rivals and that they were trapped in a steady grinding conflict.

But those were thoughts of a more distant future. Today, my son was getting married… and there were battles yet to come before these islands fell into my grip.


…
​

"We cannot allow this!" A former lord of Northumbria shouted, red in the face with veins bulging in his neck. "These Northmen have swept across our kingdom like a pox, and now they have taken root with the barbarians of the north! Something must be done, King Ecbert! Something beyond words of caution!"

Pepin watched from the shadows as the assembly of lords and ladies gathered in a hall that had once been the throne room of Mercia. It was no accident that King Ecbert had chosen it as the venue for the mixture of lords in exile. Many from Northumbria and many from Mercia itself.

Ecbert was a master of perception. Pepin had already known as much. He'd spent years with the petty king by this point, but it was always a delight to see a master at work.

Ecbert was seated upon the throne of Mercia in full regalia -- a crown adorning his brow, a scepter in one hand, while the other was left resting on the arm of the throne with an open palm. The king of Wessex looked like the ideal king. An image that was further enhanced by two of his father's Paladins, who stood at the bottom step of the throne, presenting themselves as an impenetrable shield to the crowd of frustrated nobles.

Imagery was important, loath as Pepin was to acknowledge it. It was the very thing that kept his twisted form from the throne that should be his by rights, but he understood it. More than what you said, more than what you did, appearances mattered most for kings. And what the former Mercian nobles saw was the king of Wessex seated upon their throne as if it was the most natural thing in the world.

"Peace, Lord Osmær. Peace," King Ecbert uttered, his tone placating. "I am not unaware of what the Northmen have done to our homes. Nor am I somehow unaware that fifteen thousand of the hardened warriors that maliciously sacked the capital of our shared faith have reinforced the Emperor of the Pagans."

"Peace!" Osmær shouted, his tone incredulous, as if he couldn't believe the word had just come from Ecbert's mouth. A strange thing, because that was exactly what he had been saying for months now. "I've bloody well had enough of peace! War is what we want! War against those thieving godless bastards that are stealing our wealth, our women, and our homes!"

There was a general clamor of agreement. More forceful. Such meetings weren't uncommon. By this point, they happened nearly every day. As the Northmen continued northward, all but stripping Northumbria of every ounce of silver and gold, and every peasant with a pretty face or strong back, the nobility of the kingdom continued to trickle to Ecbert.

They brought gifts and tribute to curry favor, trading away the last of the precious wealth they had managed to flee with in the hopes that Ecbert would restore their position. As he was the last king on Britannia who wasn't insane, stupid, or dead. A bastion of strength in a long dark night, and Ecbert was keenly aware of it. It was an image that he'd deliberately cultivated, and why their march across Mercia and Northumbria was so excruciatingly slow.

Wessex had grown fat off the suffering of its neighbors. It gorged itself on the skilled craftsman who managed to escape the Northmen's grip. Its treasury overflowed from the offered wealth of desperate nobles. But, more importantly, it had the right family names with ties to the right lands and the right nobles who were just smart enough to see Ecbert's true intentions and were wise enough to bow their heads all the same.

The mob before the king weren't those chosen few. They were the ones who looked at Ecbert and bought the lie that he was selling them.

That he was in any way a savior.

"I understand your frustration, my lords," King Ecbert offered placatingly, but the mob was not in the mood for platitudes.

"How could you? Wessex hasn't been touched! Your lands and your people haven't seen so much as a hair of the Northmen!" A voice amongst the crowd shouted out, emboldened by the general ire.

What Ecbert had been doing wasn't without its risks, however. His armies marched slowly, swelling in size until they reached the point where they weren't slow just because they were dragging their feet. Their numbers had swelled to the point that the sheer logistics of moving so many people down a single mile of road with any kind of efficiency was enough to bring grown men to tears. Merely setting up camp took the better part of the day.

It certainly didn't help that the army was full of inflated egos, rash fools, and those thirsty for revenge. It was that easy, purely because King Ecbert was using it as a chamber pot for the nobles that he had no use for and his political rivals.

"This is true," Ecbert acknowledged freely. It wasn't an argument he could counter easily. "But have I not committed the full weight of Wessex to the cause of ridding ourselves of these Northmen? Am I not here, before you, far from home and declaring for all to hear that we will give battle, and we will win through strength of arms and the glory of God?"

He raised a hand to forestall a clever remark or frustrated retort. "What I offer is caution, my lords. Our enemy is one emboldened by the Devil himself, and like the Devil, he taunts and infuriates us all so that when the time comes, we will be blinded by our wrath and stray from the path that God has laid for us."

Such words had a dwindling effect the more that they were used, and Ecbert recognized that he had wrung them for all of their worth.

So, he stood up, "We have been patient. We have mustered our strength and assembled an army the likes of which this land has never seen before. Across England, the devout have cried out and offered prayers to God Almighty towards a single purpose." With each sentence, he descended a step, Pepin watched as a cautious hope ignited in the eyes of the frustrated nobles. "We must tread carefully in the days to come. We cannot rush forward. We must instead hold fast, take one step at a time, all to ensure that every damned Northmen in our home will be gathered up."

His voice rose, "There will be no prisoners! No mercy! Not for these heathens, who have so savagely ravaged our lands and our very faith!" The mob truly was as smart as its dumbest member, and they were hearing what they wanted to hear. "The time is nigh, my lords. I promise you this. We are but days away from our promised battle, and you have my word that I shall fight beside you when that day comes!"

Lies, of course. King Ecbert was a man who had an extreme awareness of himself and his capabilities. At least, that was Pepin's estimation of him. He was no warrior. No general. He might be on the battlefield, but it would be as a figurehead. His son, Æthelwulf, was cut from a very different cloth. He possessed a level head, sound reason, and an awareness of intrigue, but not a talent for it. He was a warrior, and it would be he who led Ecbert's armies against the Northmen.

Osmær's shoulders sagged, the fight bleeding out of him. "How much longer must we wait, my king?"

In response, King Ecbert smiled, reaching out with a hand and resting it lightly on his shoulder. "Prince Ragnar is getting married. Godless or not, such a union should be celebrated… and I believe that we have just the gift for them, do we not?"

Pepin watched it all from the shadows. How the mob was satisfied with a handful of false words and even falser promises. How his father's paladins watched on, playing the part of the steadfast guards of the king, but in reality were blades pointed at his neck. And, despite himself, Pepin was genuinely impressed with the petty king of a land that by all rights shouldn't matter.

Because he had set the stage masterfully, and now it was time to raise the curtain.

...

#7,491
Ragnar had expected something to change once he got married. What, exactly, he wasn't entirely sure. Maybe for the world to look a bit differently. Or maybe for the world to look at him differently. But, upon waking up in his empty bed, everything felt so very… normal. As if it were just any day rather than a pivotal moment in his life.

It was a strangely disappointing feeling that he wasn't quite sure what to make of. All the same, he rolled out of bed to find that a servant had prepared an outfit for the day, and he began to dress himself. It could be something of a chore at times, especially with the knots and buttons to hold the outfit together, but Father had little respect for those that couldn't even put on their own boots and neither did he.

Once he was dressed, he stepped out of the room that he had been sequestered inside of. They had been granted a manor for the sake of privacy within the city, though calling it a manor was exceedingly generous. Still, it was a building with more than one room, which made it the closest thing the city had to one.

Maeve was seated by the hearth, a knife in her hand as she carved out shafts for arrows. Her gaze flickered up, and they stared at each other for a beat too long, before her lips quirked up. "I thought you'd be the type to rise before the sun does," she remarked to him, resuming her whittling.

"I don't usually stay up so late," Ragnar defended himself, casting a glance at the rays of light pouring through the windows. It wasn't quite noon, but it wasn't far off either. "And when I do, I'm used to someone waking me up." If not Father or one of his brothers, than a servant.

"Hm. I asked them to leave us be for the day," Maeve told him, and that would explain why they were the only two in the building. "We're married now, but… truth be told, I don't have a clue what you're like when you're alone."

Ragnar stilled for a moment before he decided to approach the hearth. "That's because I'm not usually alone," he admitted. There was always someone nearby -- a bodyguard, a servant, one of his siblings, or a parent.

"Hm. I meant more that I don't know what you're like when you're not being a prince," she clarified. "We got married because of politics, but I wanted to leave them at the door for a bit."

"How greedy," Ragnar acknowledged, making her smile grow a fraction.

"Aye, a bit," she admitted. He was a prince of an empire, and now she was the wife of a prince. Politics would be part of their lives until they died. Ragnar had known and accepted that from a very young age, and it didn't really bother him. Not truly. But, as he sat in a carved chair, the conversation lapsing, he could admit that he wasn't prepared for… this.

The silence. The absence of expectations. The simple fact that he lacked an easy answer to her question -- who was he when he was alone?

Maeve continued to whittle away at the arrow shaft, checking its straightness with a glance, before she broke the silence.

"I'm the one that killed King Causantín," she informed in a tone that didn't at all reflect the weight of the crime that she was confessing to.

Ragnar took in a slow breath, blinking at how the admission of regicide was delivered rather than the confession itself. Mostly because… "I thought as much," Ragnar admitted. Maeve cocked an eyebrow in his direction, asking a silent question. "Your brother all but offered your hand. Your absence for such an offer was strange."

She seemed to ponder that for a moment before nodding in acceptance, so Ragnar continued. "I knew that whoever had killed him had been amongst his hunting party," he said, picking up one of the completed arrows. "Outwardly, you had no motive to kill him, so you weren't seriously considered as a suspect by anyone. But when we met for the second time in the storeroom, I began to suspect you as the assassin."

He rolled the arrow between two fingers before presenting it to Maeve, "I didn't know for certain, of course. But I suspected."

There was a glimmer in her eyes that Ragnar wasn't skilled enough to decipher as she took back the arrow. "Not going to ask why, are you?"

"I wouldn't think you'd confess to murder without giving a reason for it," he pointed out.

"I might. It's not like you can do anything about it now," she pointed out, but she seemed satisfied with his response.

"That'd be a bit too cruel, wouldn't it?" As she said, confession or not, there was very little that Ragnar could do with the information now that they were husband and wife. Formally accusing her after they had been married wouldn't just tarnish his own image, it would shatter the budding relationship between Alba and Scandinavia, putting to rest any possibility of an easy vassalage. To do so would be pointless, stupid, and completely invalidate all the reasons they got married in the first place.

Maeve smiled in a way that made heat crawl up his neck, but she answered all the same. "I don't have one really good reason to do it, but I have a lot of little ones."

"Compelling ones, I hope?" She had murdered a king, after all. And it had taken him days to die.

"Some, maybe. Others, I doubt that they would make much sense to you since you aren't from here." Maeve admitted, being startlingly honest. "Pride has always been important to the clans. We've spilled more blood in the name of pride than we ever had for the gods or good sense. But the biggest point of pride of all is our supposed victory over the Romans."

She snorted, "As if we actually won. My ancestors twisted our history until the truth was barely recognizable. We were on the cusp of defeat. Half of the clans were fighting amongst themselves while the other half had already submitted to the Romans. Then their Emperor went and died, and all of a sudden, the Romans had better things to do than finish us off. But, if you listen to any tale or poem -- they tucked their tails between their legs, built a big wall to hide behind, and cowered behind it until their whole empire collapsed."

Maeve picked up another arrow to start whittling. "Like with the Romans, we knew that you were coming long before you actually arrived. And the clans pointed to our victory over the Romans, deluding themselves with the thought that if we managed to do it once, then we'd be able to do it again."

Ragnar said nothing, letting her speak and get whatever it was that weighed on her off her chest. Nor did he offer any confirmations that his father would have undoubtedly finished what the Romans started centuries ago. From what he saw of them, they had little chance of defeating them in a pitched battle.

"King Causantín was the cautious sort. Always checked his footing before he took a step. I liked that about him," Maeve admitted, and it was a strange thing to hear her compliment the man she'd murdered. "But even with my engagement to his son, he just didn't have the support to drown out the fools. He knew it, so he would have gone with whatever they said because that meant he kept getting to be king. Even if it led Alba into a war that we wouldn't have been able to survive."

Meaning that King Causantín had been predisposed to the Romans? That didn't seem right-

Ah.

He meant to betray Father. Possibly in battle or in the immediate aftermath of it. Such a tactic wouldn't have worked against Father, but King Causantín wouldn't have known that much.

"So, you killed him," Ragnar acknowledged.

"So, I killed him," Maeve agreed. "I… didn't mean for it to take days. I was nervous, so my aim wasn't what it should have been." Well, that was a relief. If she liked King Causantín and still sentenced him to die a slow death, he couldn't imagine what she'd do to the people she disliked.

"Hm," Ragnar hummed in acknowledgment, earning a reproachful glance.

"That's all you have to say?" Maeve remarked, clearly expecting more. Her guard was up, as if she were expecting condemnation.

The issue was… that was about the sum of his thoughts. "I appreciate you telling me," Ragnar said, and that wasn't what she wanted to hear based on how her eyes flattened. "But…"

He wasn't even sure how to phrase it. It was something he always kind of felt, but never put into words. "My father believes in honor. Usually to the point it acts as a detriment to his ambitions. He'll guard himself from intrigue, and he'll keep a keen eye on the plots that surround him, but… to him, assassination, blackmail, extortion, and other dark acts are tools that he refuses to engage with. Even when he does stand to gain from it."

Now Maeve tilted her head. "And you don't?"

"Assassination and war are extensions of diplomacy rather than failures of it," Ragnar replied. "I don't intend to go around murdering people for the sake of convenience, of course. They are tools to use when the situation calls for them. What you described… I feel that it fits that condition." So there was no anger in him that his wife had murdered King Causantín. There was no real surprise either, because he'd already had suspicions, but it hadn't been worth it to confirm them, especially since she had gotten away with it.

"And how do you know if the situation calls for it?" Maeve pressed, her tone betraying her interest.

To that, Ragnar shrugged. "I don't know yet. I've killed on the battlefield, but I haven't ordered someone's death. I feel like that will be different, somehow. Until then, I'll learn from my father and my aunts." Aunt Jill in particular. Father shied away from intrigue, while Aunt Morrigan specialized in it. Aunt Jill seemed like a fair middle ground to try to emulate.

"Huh," Maeve returned, seemingly mollified by his response. "How practical of you." That felt like a compliment, so Ragnar decided to take it as one.

"Why the sudden confession, anyway?" Ragnar asked, knowing that it couldn't be a surge of guilt or anything like it.

"Mostly because I thought you should know. My brother knows that I did it, and if he thinks he can use the information against you, then he will," she answered, almost dismissive of the fact her brother planned to extort them. He was in a position to. It wouldn't take much twisting to paint them -- he and his family -- as the aggressors. That it was their idea all along.

Of course, Maeve and Lucas would suffer for it alongside them, but the narrative of the situation would twist from his father taking advantage of the situation to being its mastermind.

"The rest? Well, I thought you'd answer a question honestly if I was honest first," Maeve continued. She lowered the whittling knife and the half finished arrow. "I'm your wife now. Sooner or later, you'll be the King of Alba. That's all but set in stone. But there is a higher crown that you can claim, and people expect you to take it."

He didn't mean to, but Ragner found himself tensing, knowing exactly what she was going to ask.

"Do you want it? Your father's crown?" Maeve asked him directly, pinning him with a measuring look that told him that he shouldn't even try lying. "Enough to take it if needed?"

Ragnar worked his jaw for a long second, his gaze drifting from her to the hearth that sat near. When he did speak, he chose to be honest.

"I don't really care about being the Allvaldr, or my father's heir," he admitted. "My father… he sleeps once every few days, did you know that? And even then, there are hardly enough hours in the day for him to do everything that he needs to. And that's with my mother and aunts helping him. It's an endless amount of work and he constantly deals with people that he wouldn't piss on even if they were on fire. Most days, I don't think even he wants to be the Allvaldr. He just has to be because otherwise, Charlemagne would have swept over us like the tide and eradicated our faith."

"That doesn't answer my question," Maeve pointed out. "What do you want?"

"I…" Ragnar faltered. "I just want to live up to my father's expectations," he admitted after a second of hesitation. "If I become the heir, then that feels like a sign that I am. If I don't, then it feels like I fell short somehow. But actually being the Allvaldr? I don't really care one way or the other."

It felt almost shameful to admit. That his father was going to spend his life building an empire that could stand for a thousand years, and Ragnar… didn't really care about it. Or, he didn't care as much about it as he cared about disappointing his father.

What he didn't appreciate was Maeve snorting in amusement, making him narrow his eyes, but she waved off his ire. "I'm not laughing at you. Not really. I'm just not sure you realize how rare that is. Most princes and lordlings can't wait for their fathers to die because it means they get a title they aren't prepared for. Then they go on to have kids that they know don't care about them, so they don't care in turn."

Maeve leaned back in her seat, humming with contentment. "That's not the answer I expected," she admitted. "But I think that I like it. No ambition for the sake of it, but you're a little too dutiful for your own good."

That made a knot between his shoulders come undone that he only became aware of once it vanished. "And now?" He prompted, wanting to know what she intended to do with the information.

"Now?" She echoed before shrugging, "I think I'll enjoy our marriage."

A small breath of amusement escaped him, "Well that is a comfort. I'd hate it if assassinating royalty became a habit for you."

A slow grin tugged at her lips that she couldn't quite wipe away, "See to it that you stay on my good side, and it won't."

The conversation lapsed and this time, it felt far more comfortable.


…
​

"Look who finally decided to join us," Harald remarked upon seeing Ragnar enter Father's office. Ragnar felt everyone's attention shift to him, and he wasn't sure what to make of the smiles. Or the pats on the back. They were treating him as if he had taken a great stride in his life, but things still felt normal, even as he took his place by his father's side.

Father rested a hand on his shoulder, giving it a reassuring squeeze, but moved on with the discussion that they all had been summoned for.

"Ecbert and his lords are committing to an offensive," Father began, and that stifled the cheer in the room. "He's gathered all the strength of Northumbria, Mercia, and Wessex. Our scouts report that he has an army more than a hundred thousand strong. Closer to a hundred and fifty, I imagine."

"How?" Harald blurted, earning a reproachful glance from Uncle Haldur. Chastised, he continued all the same. "Forgive me for speaking out of turn, uncle, but… how?"

"By putting spears in the hands of farmers," Uncle Haldur answered, earning a nod from Father.

"Most of the army consists of refugees from our raid," he informed in a hard tone. "Or those that seek religious revenge for the sack of Rome." At that, many eyes slid to Hjalmar, who stood near the center of the table in a seat of honor.

He met the glances and offered a small shrug, "Sorry."

That earned a few chuckles, the tension in the room easing just a touch. Father put a great deal of faith in the man. Ragnar was inclined to trust him just for that, but he couldn't say that he knew him particularly well. He did have a sharp sense of humor, though. Of all the gifts that he'd received for the wedding, the pope's strange hat was among his favorites.

"They will be ill trained, poorly equipped, and disorganized," Father continued. "But I won't lie to you. They don't need to be any more than that when there's that many of them. Short of holding an entrenched position, we don't have a hope of withstanding the sheer weight of their numbers, and fighting from an entrenched position would see us besieged."

"We must face them," Lucas replied, a sense of urgency lurking in the back of his tone. He realized the truth of it -- such an army could not be assembled and not be used. Even if Father ordered the end of their raid, that army would be marched up to Alba for its alliance with Scandinavia.

Given that it would one day be his future domain, Ragnar was inclined to defend it.

"We will," Father assured those at the table. "We must. The Christians are creating a narrative, and for better or worse, we must play our part in it." There were many at the table that didn't know what to make of that, but Ragnar did.

The sack of Rome, and the raiding of Britannia, all followed by the rise of a 'pagan' empire to the north. Father had had him read the Bible cover to cover, so that he could understand the thinking and motivations of their enemies. One lesson stood out -- Christianity thrived in the face of oppression. The more the Romans had tried to grind out the sparks of their faith, the more kindling they fed them until it became an uncontrollable flame.

Charlemagne was using that same sense of adversity and righteous rage to bind his fragile empire together. It was an easy rhetoric to establish. To the South and West were Muslims. To the North were 'pagans.' And to the East were the Khazars, who practiced Judaism or Tengrism. Christianity was quite literally surrounded and under attack on all sides.

"What we must do is be on the offensive," Father continued. "We harry them to a battlefield of our choosing. We destroy their supplies enroute, break the will of their men before they have a chance to fight. Against such an enemy, we cannot fight them as one cohesive whole, but in a thousand small battles before we finish them."

It was a fine speech. Those at the table thought so as well.

But, deep down, Ragnar began to wonder…

What game was Ecbert playing at?

#7,514
"A shame that your father recalled the Paladins," Æthelwulf remarked to Pepin, the prince of Wessex riding alongside Pepin's carriage. It was a bit gentler on his twisted spine for long journeys, and it was hardly as if the army they marched with was outpacing it. "It would have been a dream to fight beside them."

Æthelwulf smiled at the thought, completely ignorant of what the recalling of Astolfo and Bradamante meant.

Ecbert did, though he hid it with patient smiles and a farewell feast. Charlemagne had made a decision after years of investment into England. A decision made after reading reports from countless spies as well as Pepin's own.

Despite the vast army that so slowly marched North, one that was baying for the blood of the Northmen, Charlemagne had foreseen the conclusion of this war and decided against risking his Paladins in a battle with a foregone conclusion. His father felt that while bloodying the Northmen was still a possibility, outright victory wasn't, so his most valuable pieces were being pulled off the stage for another day and another battle.

"They were needed elsewhere," Pepin replied.

"I would have thought your father would have recalled you as well," Æthelwulf remarked with a gentle probing, not sure what to make of his continued presence in these foul islands.

"I have spent years preparing for this battle. It seems only right that I see it through," Pepin replied, giving an answer that he knew Æthelwulf would respect. And respect it he did based on the quirking of his lips and the firm nod in response. The truth was a far crueler thing. Something that Pepin had prepared himself for the moment he set sail for Britannia.

Charlemagne had not recalled him alongside Astolfo and Bradamante. He was to stay in Ecbert's court as an advisor until Charlemagne decided otherwise. It was banishment in all but name. He was to stay on the islands, out of sight and out of mind, likely to be forgotten until his dying day. And likely even after.

His wretched affliction was a stain on the legacy of a Frankish King, but for a Roman Emperor? The stakes were higher and the margin for error was nonexistent. Charlemagne simply couldn't afford to have a deformed son at his court, even if he was forced to dwell in the shadows.

"I've long awaited this day," Æthelwulf replied, gazing off in the direction of the Northmen. Where Prince Ragnar celebrated his wedding. A beloved prince, by all accounts. One who understood his duties and the expectations placed upon him. Kind to the servants, clever enough to hold his tongue and listen, and a brilliant warrior. It almost felt like a mockery that he was sent by God to punish Charlemagne's hubris, while Emperor Siegfried was rewarded at every turn by the gods he worshipped. "Father spoke of patience, but I will admit, my own was nearing its end."

That was a sentiment that most felt when Ecbert decided at long last to commit the army that he had amassed. There was much rejoicing, with priests burning incense and chanting prayers throughout the mass of bodies, some hundred and sixty thousand men strong. If Pepin listened, he was sure that he would be able to hear priests chanting their prayers as they marched.

"I hope that spirit remains once the battle begins," Pepin replied. He had his doubts. The men were ready to fight. They were practically chomping at the bit. They felt they had God's guiding hand on their backs and that He was pushing them forward to a fateful confrontation with the Northmen.

But few things were as fragile as morale. It only lasted until the first setback, and the reports that Æthelwulf interrupted his reading for idle chatter left Pepin uncertain of what it would be, but convinced it was soon to come.

Siegfried would have known long in advance that even with his veteran force, he couldn't hope to overcome such a disparity of numbers. He would have plans in place when Ecbert did decide to move. He'd had months to prepare for such a battle, and Pepin was attempting to see his plan through the scouts and spies scattered across Northumbria.

"How long do you think it will be?" Æthelwulf questioned with the brashness of a young man eager to prove himself and to step out of his father's shadow.

To that, Pepin glanced up at the darkening skies overhead. "I doubt that it will be long… but I fear that the Northmen will see us long before we see them." It was clear that wasn't what Æthelwulf wanted to hear. He was dreaming of glorious battles that would see his name etched into the bedrock of history. But, even with an unwelcome answer, Æthelwulf thanked him for it, as it was a direct answer, unlike what he received from his father at the very head of the army.

Being a cripple had its advantages, loath as Pepin was to accept them. He was an unsightly creature, so when most weren't gawking at his deformity, they were quick to avert their eyes and pretend that they didn't see him at all. It made it easy to maneuver in the camp once they stopped for the night.

He walked through the sea of tents with so many men crammed into them that they were practically spilling out. Some lacked shelter entirely, content with a bedroll, a pitchfork, and the clothes on their back as they lay in the dirt between tents to protect them from a strong breeze. Others forewent sleep entirely, gathering around campfires to play games or sing songs.

But it was what Pepin didn't see that worried him. The camp was so vast that building defenses for it was essentially impossible without deforesting the local hunting grounds. Instead, there were watch towers dotted along at steady intervals with patrols of foot soldiers to ensure that no one was sneaking into the camp unnoticed.

And it was what he heard that concerned him.

Ecbert's tent stood out amongst the sea of tents. A sign of importance to differentiate himself from the impoverished lords with whom he surrounded himself. There were so many noble tents, it felt like a third of the camp was dedicated to them. When he ventured near, the guards posted outside of the tent allowing him to enter with glances of ill-disguised disgust, he could hear it.

Arguing.

"My lands have been ravaged by these heathens, and I will have my due in blood!" A voice shouted out, and from the shadows, he saw the red faced rage of a noble around a large table. His proclamation was met with jeering and dismissal.

"All our lands have been ravaged! It doesn't grant you the right to lead the left flank!" Another shouted back at him, and the voices that had jeered earlier were now roaring with agreement. While the first noble's supporters jeered back.

At the center of it all was Ecbert. His expression was calm and dignified, but Pepin knew the man well enough to know that he was at his wits end with the conversation that had gone in circles for days on end.

Glory was a powerful motivator. And so was shame. The nobles who gathered around Ecbert now were the same nobles who had abandoned their lands with what wealth and strength they could muster. They wanted to wash away the perception that they were no more than clever cowards, and the previously well-established plans were cracking under their fervor and eagerness to fight.

Old and new rivalries flared now that they were taking the fight to the Northmen. They didn't want to be placed under the command of another, or they coveted a position that another had and the glory that would come with it. And the old divide between Northumbrian and Mercian lords was rearing its ugly head worse than ever.

Some days, the lords felt as if they were one wrong remark from fighting each other before they fought the Northmen.

Ecbert took great care to not make a wrong remark, "Peace, my lords. Peace!" He stresses, raising a hand to calm down the squabbling nobles. "We have enemies aplenty outside of this tent. There is no sense fighting amongst ourselves."

It was to his credit that they did quiet down. His authority over them was new and untested in many ways, but Ecbert was at least respected by all the men in the tent. Or at the very least they understood that he held the keys to their future, so it was best to still their wagging tongues when he said so.

"I understand your eagerness," Ecbert uttered in a calmer voice for a quieter crowd. "But do not let it overwrite your good sense. A plan is in place, my lords. Deviation now, in the final hour, is most unwise." He was right. Everyone in the tent knew that he was right. Few things were more dangerous to an army on the eve of battle than to change the commander.

However, the lords didn't care about what was right. They cared about themselves and their ambitions.

The nobles argued around Ecbert. Not directly protesting his decision, but calling out insults to each other to voice how little they cared for the current arrangement. An arrangement they had previously agreed to, but nobility was quick to forget favors and remembered slights for generations. Ecbert sat in his throne, his irritation slowly simmering and Pepin wondered if he was going to see the restrained king lose his temper for the first time.

But then a messenger arrived, covered in a sheen of sweat with so little breath that he had to gasp to get out his message. "Riders, my king! Riders in the night! We're under attack on the west wing!"

The reaction was immediate. Fear and bluster. Pepin saw through it all. A battle that they had clamored for had arrived early and without warning. Their confidence that no one would be mad enough to attack such a force was shattered. Ecbert, to his credit, was decisive.

"Water! Get the man some water!" He demanded, standing up, and a servant pressed a cup into the messenger's hands, and he drank deeply from it. "Now, my good man, you say the Northmen are attacking the western flank? How? How many? Why were they not seen by our patrols? How deep are they in our camp?"

The messenger bowed his head, "I do not know their number, your grace, but they are in their thousands. We suspect that they ambushed our patrols, but they do not cut deeply into our camp. They harry our outskirts."

A distraction.

"A distraction," Ecbert concluded alongside Pepin's thoughts. "They seek to burn our supplies! Double their guard, and call for our riders! We can crush their cavalry here and now! Deus Vult! God wills it!" The warcry was echoed out by the nobles, who rushed out of the camp for their share of the glory. Leaving behind only Ecbert and Pepin.

Through the tent fabric, he could hear the camp coming alive as word was spread. Orders were being barked out, shouts of defiance and anger echoed through the air. It was superficial. And pointless. Siegfried would not attack with such confidence if such simple countermeasures would work.

Ecbert sank into his throne, his gaze going to the shadows where Pepin lurked in. There was a heavy silence in the tent, Ecbert visibly chewing on the situation before a sigh escaped him. "Why in God's name would he attack? Why wouldn't he simply leave? What does he hope to gain by fighting a hundred thousand men?"

The questions revealed the truth of it. The same truth that Pepin had long since realized. And the truth that his father had recently understood.

Ecbert, at no point, actually intended to actually fight Siegfried the Wolf-Kissed.

He amassed his army and influence, delaying and delaying, in the hopes that when the army swelled large enough, Siegfried would decide fighting it simply wasn't worth it. Because it wasn't worth it. They had ravaged Mercia, Northumbria, and the Eire. They had more wealth than they could hope to carry back to Scandinavia even if they made three trips.

Any sane man would look to what they had gained, look to the army that saw to chase them off, and simply decide to leave. To stay and fight was an unnecessary risk. A pointless risk.

That course of action would have left Ecbert in his position of supreme influence. He would be the man who chased off the Pagan King. The heathens that had ravaged their homes, pillaged their wealth, and rode off with their sons and daughters. All without needing to actually fight the renowned warrior king, who had never lost a battle, even when faced with longer odds than he currently did.

"Because his plans have changed," Pepin answered. How, he could only guess. The marriage with Maeve of Alba was certainly an indication, but not a clear answer. "Even if those plans end at ruining yours."

Ecbert offered a thin smile, "I had a similar thought. I'd hoped you would voice an alternative." No such luck there. "I suppose I should be honored that the great Siegfried the Wolf-Kissed is going out of his way to crush my ambitions."

That was one way to look at it.

Ecbert leaned back in his seat, adopting the mask that he wore so well, "No matter. If he seeks to fight, then we must simply win." Pepin watched the king as he stood with a sense of purpose, and he bowed his head low since he could not do so naturally.

Because, despite never planning to fight Siegfried, he would have made plans just in case.

Pepin fell into the king's shadow at a distance as he emerged from his tent, organizing their defenses. Most of which were already well underway, but Ecbert understood the value of being seen as the one in charge. The messengers flowed too and from him from every corner of the catastrophically large camp -- their supplies had triple the guard placed to defend them while their cavalry were mustering. The west wing was being harried, and from where Pepin stood, he could see the glowing flames as tents burned.

"Your Grace!" A messenger shouted, dropping to a knee before Ecbert. "Lord Æðelbeald has charged out with his forces!"

Three hundred of their horsemen with two hundred supporting infantry.

"Recall him! Now!" Ecbert snapped, launched into a flurry of activity alongside the half panicked and enraged camp. The vast army, for all that it was a slow, lumbering beast, meant that while they built up their numbers, they had time for training, during which they were drilled in formations and arms. It looked like a good third of them forgot that training upon hearing of the attack, but most didn't. And those that didn't were the stabilizing force in the army that stopped the panic from overwhelming their good sense.

The messenger faltered, "He is already engaged with the enemy, Your Grace."

"Damn him! Get word to Lord Cenric and Lord Eadræd -- they are to engage in support and withdraw with Lord Æðelbeald!" Ecbert ordered naturally because he understood well enough what Siegfried was doing. It was the only way he could hope to defeat such a vast army. "Lord Pepin, do remind me how many horsemen Emperor Siegfried possesses?"

Warhorses were a special breed of horse. They had to be raised from birth for the battlefield -- conditioned to not flinch away from a colliding charge or the chaotic sounds of battle. More often than not, a good warhorse was worth more than the man that rode upon it.

"Fifteen thousand, King Ecbert," Pepin answered. "Most taken from the lands of Northumbria and Mercia." Warhorses didn't travel by sea in long voyages, so the reinforcements that came from the Mediterranean wouldn't have any. Siegfried arrived with roughly five thousand. The other ten thousand were taken from various noble houses and stables throughout the two small kingdoms that he'd raided with impunity.

"And do remind me, how many do we possess?" Ecbert said, looking down at the frozen stiff messenger.

"Two thousand," Pepin answered. Wessex was not a large kingdom, even if it was a rich one. Throughout it, there were perhaps a thousand horses that were worthy of being called a warhorse. The remaining thousand they possessed came from the small nobles who flocked to their banner. Siegfried had swept Mercia and Northumbria clean of anything of value, and that included the horses. Leaving them with a mere two thousand, unless their men were willing to ride into battle with panicked work horses and mules.

"If Lord Æðelbeald, Lord Cenric, or Lord Eadræd take issue with this order, dutifully remind them of that. We do not have the forces to waste, especially when we know that the force harassing us is not the entirety of their strength!" Ecbert snapped and sent the messenger off running with a stern look. "And someone find my son before he does something rash!"

Ecbert did not venture to the battlefield, for he knew he would be of little use there. Instead, a steady stream of orders came from him as he tried to get a grip on the vast army that was stirring with anger at the attack. Formations were solidified and given the order to march, reinforcing the right wing.

But, no sooner than they arrived, horns blew to signal that the battle was over. For the briefest of seconds, Ecbert's expression betrayed him. A thinning of the lips, his face paling in the light of the torches -- he understood that it could not be a victory. All the same, his presence was required, so whatever his misgivings might be, he set out on top of a horse.

The damage to the camp was considerable, but a far cry from how bad it could be. Dozens of burnt tents with bodies laying in the packed dirt between them, if the burning tent hadn't collapsed upon them. Pepin would have to wait for reports, but he would estimate no more than a hundred had perished. If that. More would be injured, some losing their ability to fight.

It was… a lackluster night raid from such a famed warrior.

"If he did not attack our supplies, then what did he do?" Ecbert questioned, more to himself than anyone else. There was a quiet but growing dread that seemed to creep up on the king as he gazed out into the darkness, knowing that a wolf prowled in the dark. His grip on his reins tightened, and again, he whispered, "What did he do?"

It would take them three days to realize, and by that time, it was far too late.
