#7,535
"If we are God's chosen instrument to vanquish the heathen and his legion of demons, then why does He punish us so?" Æthelwulf asked his Lord and Savior, on his knees with his hands clasped together. Normally, when praying, he would strike himself with a whip as penance for unworthy thoughts and doubts. Yet, the heathens had attacked their force with near impunity, and their Lord Father, God Almighty, required every able soldier so he restrained and limited himself to kneeling on small stones.

He knelt in his tent before a cross, completely alone. A measure that his father had taken to ensure that he didn't fall to the sickness that ripped through the camp like a wild fire.

It had been in the aftermath of the first raid that they found rotting meat and other filth in their food supplies, with many only discovering what had been in their cooking pots when they reached the bottom. Many had gotten sick, their bodies attempting to purge their humors with a flux. They were racked with such pains that most couldn't do more than raise their heads from their beds.

It was regrettable, but they had thought that would be the end of it by morning the next day. Many were still weak, struggling to keep food down, but they were recovering from their purge. Others, however, did not. They fell ill with fevers, their bodies continuing to purge, even when they had nothing left in them. Father ordered those that were sick to be sequestered from those still healthy, but it came too late because by the third day, the number of sick had jumped. Most didn't even know that they were ill until they bent over to pick something up and found they couldn't control their bowls.

Now, five days later, it felt like more people were sick than not.

"It is the Devil's work," Æthelwulf continued. "I know this. But… why do you not protect us? Why has this trial been foisted upon good Christians?" He continued, his head held low. Doubts clawed at him. He had never doubted his faith. He loved God with the entirety of his heart, and he was certain that He would be at their side on the battlefield, making victory a promise.

But now doubts coiled in his guts like a nest of vipers. For more than a week, they had suffered nightly raids from the heathens. Sometimes they harried their flanks, other times their center or rear. Twice, they had carved a line through their formations to accomplish specific goals -- to destroy their food supplies and to kill or steal their horses, be it war horses or pack animals.

In the former, they failed. Father had spread the supplies throughout the camp, foreseeing the Heathen King's attempts, but it did mean that they still lost a portion of their supplies. Their raids on the warhorses were far more effective. They had burned their feed, forcing them to graze, which left them isolated to be picked off. Or they baited them to give chase before shooting the horses from underneath their riders with a hail of arrows. Of the two thousand warhorses that they'd started the march with, they had less than five hundred now.

His heart was wavering. He did not doubt the power of God- never that. But he doubted that it was His plan for them to emerge victorious. And he could not see why God would allow such a thing… and that… that scared him.

"My lord," a voice from outside the tent spoke up. "Your meal has been delivered."

A rebuke for interrupting his prayer was on his lips, but the man couldn't have known he was praying. No one had been allowed in his tent in days, and Æthelwulf had been forbidden from leaving it.

"My thanks," he told the man. "I will break my fast after my morning prayers." He heard a muttered response through the fabric, leaving Æthelwulf to turn his gaze to their Lord and Savior hanging from a jeweled cross, His visage so life-like it was as if he were gazing upon Jesus Christ himself. "My apologies. For… for my doubts. For the interruption. I just…"

His lips thinned and his head lowered, "I am a weaker man than I thought."

It was easy to have faith when it wasn't being tested. And their faith was being tested.

Making a cross, he bowed his head low once more and uttered, "Amen," before raising to his feet. Fetching his breakfast, Æthelwulf spied a familiar shadow cast upon his tent. "Lord Pepin," Æthelwulf greeted his father's twisted advisor and disgraced prince of the now Roman Empire born anew.

Æthelwulf wasn't certain what to make of Pepin. By rights, he should be the prince of an empire whose history stretched back more than a thousand years. Yet, he was cast adrift to distant shores because of his twisted shape. There was part of him that felt pity for Pepin. Another part that felt a measure of disgust at his disfigurement.

But both parts were smaller than the one that feared the hunchbacked prince. Pepin was smart in the way his father was smart. In ways that Æthelwulf knew that he wasn't. Yet while his father could rely on charming smiles and his position, Pepin had nothing, and he felt all the more dangerous because of it.

"I have come with news, Prince Æthelwulf," Pepin sat outside the tent on a box, his voice low. "Another hundred and thirty died of this pox last night. Another twenty this morning, with more to come by noon."

A hundred and fifty souls lost before they could draw the blood of heathens and avenge their ravaging. "And the afflicted?"

"Your father's containment has slowed the spread, but it has made us vulnerable in other ways," Pepin answered.

Æthelwulf clenched his hands into fists. "The losses from the raid?"

"Three hundred. More wounded," Pepin answered, his voice grim. He understood exactly what that meant. "The isolated sections of camp… they are vulnerable and they suffer for it. Siegfried rains arrows down upon them while concentrating his strength to strike where we are vulnerable."

Meaning that the only reason why they hadn't lost more to the pox that tore through the camp was that Siegfried had killed many of the sick. Their strength was being bled from them drop by drop. Since the raids began, perhaps five thousand had perished. An absurd number, but when considering the whole of their army, it was barely a dip in their numbers.

"Killing us isn't the point," Æthelwulf repeated a point he felt like he had made a hundred times by now, but no one was truly listening. "He attacks our morale. Not us. He is delivering the message that he can attack us with impunity and that we are too weak to defend ourselves. How long is it before the army fractures and we lose more men to deserters than we do to sickness or battle?"

"I am afraid that we are already well on our way, Prince Æthelwulf," Pepin replied, and he was one of the few who understood their poor positioning. "A band of thirty village men attempted to sneak out during the raid. We found their heads on stakes outside of our camp. At the very least, Siegfried seems to be helping us with our deserter problem."

To an untrained eye, such a thing might seem like madness. Æthelwulf saw what it was, however -- it was a statement. They were huddling up in their pens like sheep, while he was the wolf that stalked outside. That all they could do was huddle together and hope that they were the ones taken in the night.

"And my father?" Æthelwulf started, frustration welling up from his chest to the back of his throat. "What does he have to say to this mess?"

"He is of split-" Æthelwulf didn't need to hear the rest. It was the same answer he had received every time he asked. An answer he was sick of. As sick as he was of the canvas walls of his tent.

"Enough," Æthelwulf decided, standing up. "I have had enough of his indecisiveness."

Pepin had an answer ready, telling Æthelwulf that his response was no surprise. "Your father is currently in a council meeting. Half are attempting to convince him to pursue battle and the other half peace." The latter half were a growing voice. They were those who had lost their faith in their righteous cause. They were those who let themselves be consumed by doubt over why God would allow them to be hobbled and suffer so.

"Then perhaps one more voice is needed," Æthelwulf said, knowing that he was being manipulated. He could feel the strings on him as he stormed out of his tent, breathing the closest thing he had come to fresh air in days. It was a question of who was pulling them, but even if he was being manipulated to a goal -- that didn't mean the goal was unworthy.

He marched to his father's tent, which had been moved to be kept isolated. A secondary palisade was erected around it with guards set paces apart, just to ensure that no one managed to slip by them in the middle of the night. Be they Englishmen or Scandinavian. The guards made to stop him but he waved them off with a hand, storming into his father's tent to see that it was a storm of arguments.

Lords were shouting at one another until they were red in the face, spit flying and they beat on the wood table with their fists like it were the enemy. At the head of the table was his father, his expression an impassive mask. He did not seem surprised to see Æthelwulf, who announced himself by slamming his hands on the other end of the table.

"We attack!" He joined his voice into the storm of arguments, and his declaration was met with a chorus of agreement and denials. "We attack while we still have the strength, Father. Before he bleeds us anymore. Before cowardice and doubt infect our men alongside this pox he has cursed us with. We attack! We have to! Or we have failed in our duty as men and Christians! We will have failed God Himself!"

He wasn't good with words. Not like his father, King Ecbert of Wessex, was. He always knew what to say and how to say it. He could tell a man to go to hell and make them look forward to the trip. It was a talent that Æthelwulf found entirely lacking in himself. However, where his father spoke flowery words, never making his true thoughts known to anyone but himself… Æthelwulf was direct.

He was like a blade, cutting right to the point. In his father's eyes, that was a weakness. But being blunt had its own strengths.

"We," Father began, his voice decidedly even, "are being baited into a trap, my lords and son. There is no battlefield nearby where we can use the one true and genuine advantage we have. We must delay a battle, press on until we find more advantageous grounds."

"And when we arrive, we will have half an army!" A lord called out, and the argument almost resumed, only to be forestalled by his father raising a hand.

"I am not blind to the cost," Father replied. "However, as I have said time and time again -- if we are to commit to a battle now, then we would be doing so on Siegfried's terms."

"Let him dictate! God wills our victory, so we will be victorious!" The faction that desired war was building momentum, stamping their feet and their voices becoming a chorus of approval. "The Heathen doesn't have the stomach for a true battle! If he did, then he wouldn't stalk about in the dark! He's a coward!"

Æthelwulf didn't think he disagreed with anything more viscerally in his entire life, but he didn't raise his voice to disagree. Instead, he looked across the table imploringly at his father, gripping the edges of it with white knuckles. They had to fight. They had to. Win or lose, God's will or not -- if they did not fight, then they would lose their honor. Their pride.

To slink away from the Heathens now, after they had ravaged Mercia and Northumbria so thoroughly, would cost them everything that they had built. It would leave a stain on their family name that would never wash out, even after a thousand years.

"A Heathen, absolutely. A coward? Perhaps. But there is one thing I will never accuse Siegfried of, and that is being a fool," Father rebuked. Another hand forestalled an argument. "However," he continued with deliberate slowness, "I find the arguments compelling. All the more so because they come from my son."

It was then that Æthelwulf realized that it was his father's strings that had been on him. He was a prop for the argument. An excuse for Father to commit to a course of action without a loss of face with the opposing side.

"If we cannot reach a favorable battlefield, then we must change our approach to the battle," Father continued, spreading his hands wide. "What I suggest is thus -- we divide our army in two. Two smaller armies of seventy thousand will have greater maneuverability and like the jaws of a trap, we can lure the Heathen in."

"Of course, the stronger of the two armies -- our soldiers that have been spared the pox, our proud lords, and what cavalry we still possess. The other… it will possess our ill and our weakest. Its purpose is to serve as a deterrent on one flank, rather than to win the battle." It was a serviceable solution to their issues. Even if they were laden with a plague, seventy thousand men was still seventy thousand men. They alone outnumbered the enemy, but their presence on the battlefield would force Siegfried to divert forces to secure that flank, leaving even fewer men to deal with the true threat.

"I know your hearts well, my lords, so allow me to make myself clear -- I will lead the weakened army. It is not a position of glory, I know, but we do not fight for glory." Father continued, fuelling the mutters that flared up but turned into whispers of amazement. Respect. They saw his acceptance as a sacrifice, giving away what they deemed invaluable for the sake of victory.

It couldn't be further from the truth.

"Though, I do hope you will not begrudge me if my son holds a position of honor in the left wing in my stead," Father continued, and the thumps of approval were all the answer that was needed. Æthelwulf met his father's gaze, who inclined his head to him. Æthelwulf returned the gesture, elated, but with it came a heavy weight on his shoulders. The left wing was the pivotal wing. The wing that often decided the fate of the battle, possibly even entire kingdoms.

He would not command it, which was something of a relief, but the burden of leadership was still there.

The meeting continued on, the momentum was behind the faction that favored battle, so those that favored negotiation found themselves boxed out of the conversation. Plans were discussed, altered, discarded, reworked, and then implemented. They spoke at length at the few advantages that they did have and among the few was they had more archers than the Heathens several times over.

What took place in the tent was quick to spread amongst their people. Upon hearing that they would fight the Heathens, many shook off the air of despair that hung over them. They gained a sense of purpose beyond waiting to fall ill and die.

Father, despite all appearances, had been quietly preparing for the day. Bows and arrows were made, armor was repaired, as were weapons. By noon, Father gave the order to march out of the camp they had huddled inside for days. And despite all of the concerns and gumption the lords showed, none argued the fact that the terrain was poor for them.

There were flatlands, but there were hills jutting out almost at random, and even in the flatlands, there were subtle dips and elevations. Which was something of an advantage as it would hamper the Heathens' cavalry. Somewhat.

The Heathens had already selected their battleground, forcing them to come out to meet them. The battlefield did favor them. Intensely so. They secured a steep hill, one side of which had nearly vertical cliffside. A position that they'd further reinforced with ditches and earthworks.

Æthelwulf swallowed a swell of bitterness, knowing that their hesitation had allowed the enemy to entrench themselves. All the worse, by the time they arrived, the Heathen army already stood in formation, allowing the afternoon sun to shine down on them -- their armor glimmered in the light, and Æthelwulf felt a clenching in his stomach at the sight of it.

He wore armor. A steel helm, a chain mail hauberk, and a padded gambason underneath. He was amongst the few that did, as it was a luxury available to only the highest lords amongst them. It was a harsh contrast in comparison to the Heathens. All on their front line wore full sets of armor -- chainmail and plate, the same that was reserved for Charlemagne's Paladins. They stood shoulder by shoulder, flags flapping in the wind bearing a double headed raven that marked them as Siegfried the Wolf-Kissed's army.

Their cavalry was split in two groups at the base of the hill in a lopsided manner. One side had nearly ten thousand according to the reports, while the other had about five. In either case, they had no hope of advantage there. Æthelwulf sat on top of one of the few horses that they had left in a company of five hundred. As it was, their cavalry would only truly be useful to escape rather than fight.

At the very head of the army sat Siegfried himself, on top of a warhorse that seemed to have been bred with purpose to be large enough to carry him. He wore armor in a similar style to that of his men, all except for the black wolf pelt that was closer to the size of a bear that hung off his shoulders and a crown that was hammered into his helmet.

The Heathens allowed their army to form up into what amounted to a crooked V formation. Æthelwulf expected to see the Heathen line shuffle in response, but no one seemed to move a muscle in the enemy formation.

They stood across from one another for what felt like eternity, but in reality couldn't have been more than a minute.

And then a horn blew and every single carefully crafted plan was shattered into countless pieces when the Heathens did the very last thing Æthelwulf expected. That anyone expected.

They charged.

...

#7,562
Ragnar's father had taught him, and all of his siblings, the importance of morale in a battle. That whole supplies and leadership mattered a great deal, they mattered so much in part because they fed into the confidence of an army. When warriors were well armored, well fed, and under the command of trusted and tested leadership, they would simply perform better. They would fight harder, last longer. They would hold their nerve despite long odds because they would believe that victory was possible.

The past week and a half, Father had been slowly killing the Anglo-Saxon's confidence. Their morale. The disease that they inflicted upon them burned through their camp like wildfire, they kept them awake with nightly raids to make sure they didn't rest easy, and they burned their supplies so they would be forced to march on an empty stomach. Now, on the eve of battle, Ragnar found himself seated upon a horse amongst eight thousand on one wing of his father's army.

The enemy was spread across the battlefield, and despite it all, Ragnar felt trepidation rise in the back of his throat. They seemed genuinely endless as they marched onto the field in relatively disciplined ranks, creating an awkward V shaped formation by extending one line and taking advantage of the natural terrain. At the head of the larger army was King Ecbert, who was marked by his few horsemen on the field as much as he was by the flags and the crown he wore. The other army was led by lords of high standing and fanatics united in their hatred for them.

He had seen them in camp during the raids. The sea of tents and the people walking between them had been many, to the point he didn't even try to count them. But it was another thing entirely to see them on the battlefield, ready to fight. His own confidence wavered, just ever so slightly, because everything that they had done… had been done out of necessity. Despite their having better arms and armor, in spite of their having more experience in the field of battle, King Ecbert and his assembled lords could win. They could win by sheer virtue of numbers.

It wasn't a matter of morale or experience. That many people, if properly directed, would break them. Their lines would crack, any escape route would be closed, and almost like a sand castle in the face of high tide, they would be swept over, and nothing would remain of them by the time the tide receded.

Which is why they bluffed.

"Steady yourself," Father warned him and Magnus. "And stay close to your guards. Neither of you have anything to prove, so don't take any unnecessary risks. Keep your shields up and don't let go of your weapon when the time comes."

Experience, Father called it. They needed to learn what it felt like to be part of a true charge before they would be expected to lead men into one. Ragnar doubted that he would even need to draw his blade, but his heart was thumping in his throat.

"We'll be careful, Father," Magnus was doing better than him apparently, because he found his voice. Their father offered a small nod, showing that he heard the words, and that was all the time that they had before a horn blew. The sound echoed in the air and set something unstoppable in motion as the entire army began to march forward, abandoning their entrenched position.

The sound of everyone taking the same step forward at once echoed out across the field, the enemy across it stupefied by what they were doing. They had arrived on the battlefield with the full expectation that they would be the aggressors, and now they found themselves on the defensive. Every plan that they had went up in flames, and from where Ragnar sat, he could see the mess of messengers running back and forth between the lords of the troops of men. Each having a different idea of what their response should be.

Some had their archers march ahead of their portion of the army, intent on assaulting them with arrows for every step that they took. Others wanted to continue on with the plan and meet them in the middle with a charge of their own. Ragnar could almost trace the argument as passengers ran back and forth between lords, each demanding that the others follow their lead.

It caused confusion to sweep over the army, buying their advance invaluable time, but caution won out over aggressiveness. The archers began to emerge at the front of the vast force before they unleashed the first volley. It was a sight to see.

Father kept the number of archers in the army at around five for every hundred men He preferred sharp shooters to pick off important targets, quality over quantity, and until that moment, Ragnar had never doubted the decision. Yet, as hundreds… thousands of arrows were released into the air, becoming a wall of falling arrows, he began to question the approach. Yet, it wasn't anything that they weren't prepared for. The infantry continued to march in step, simply raising their shields overhead and layering them over one another, trusting that those at their right shoulder would protect them as they protected those at their left.

There wasn't anything he could compare the sound of thousands of arrows thudding into wood at the same time or bouncing off of armor to. It was something so unique that Ragnar felt like he would never hear anything like it again, at least until the Anglo-Saxon archers let loose a second volley. It slowed their advance, but it didn't stop it. Their infantry still crossed the field under the storm of arrows, enduring a third volley, and then a fourth, before the archers began to retreat behind their line of soldiers and their frontline leveled pikes at them.

It was only at a distance that Ragnar could realize how small their army was in comparison as they approached one wing of the enemy. How hopelessly outnumbered they were.

And that was the entire point of the charge that struck the Anglo-Saxon's with a roar and the clash of steel. It was to solidify their own resolve and will to fight. To show the men that there was no need to fear the enemy's vast numbers. That they could take the fight to the enemy and win the day.

It also would weaken the enemy's confidence. Their faith would be shaken from the fact that Father and his army were willing to be the aggressors. It would fracture their belief that their numbers would be their salvation. At least, that was the hope. Ragnar believed it because his father was certain of it, but he wondered if the enemy that looked down at them saw how small they seemed in comparison to the vast army that felt like it could effortlessly swallow them up.

But they would choke on them. That much Ragnar was certain of.

Their frontline consisted of Father's veterans. Some who had been with him since his time in the Mediterranean, who had fought in a hundred battles against longer odds than this and possessed an unshakable faith in Father and his strategies. They met the line of pikes and pushed forward, reaching the men behind them before cutting them down as a farmer would cut through stalks of wheat. The Anglo-Saxon's weren't prepared for the deadly impact, and it showed. The first line faltered and before the second line could step forward to take their place, they too fell.

The raw disparity between their arms and armor was almost as vast as the disparity in their experience. Their men could take blows and shrug them off to continue fighting. Their armor was forged in war, designed to do exactly what they were doing -- stand in the face of the enemy and cut their way through.

Yet the Anglo-Saxons were not cowards. Far from it. They stood on the field with hate in their hearts -- if not for the sacking of Rome and the looting of their churches, then because their own homes and families had been ravaged by their raids. And if not for that, then Father had given them plenty of reasons for their ire over the past week and a half. They surged against the frontline, throwing themselves at them to not just stall their advance but to push them back. To tear at their armor with tooth and nail if that's what it took.

It was enough to rouse the second army. The sickly army. With King Ecbert there, the chain of command was clear and they were able to act on his orders on a more uniform scale. And that was exactly what Father had intended.

Another horn blew and Ragnar's heart was in his throat because that was the signal for the cavalry charge. Just as there wasn't a sound quite like thousands of arrows striking shields, there wasn't anything like the sound of thousands of horses galloping at once. It was just the rhythmic noise of hooves digging into dirt. His vision became obscured by those before him, but he was counting the seconds until their arrival, waiting for the first sound of it.

He knew the plan. Father had known that the Anglo-Saxons would divide their force and present the stronger of the two as the face. When they went on the offensive, King Ecbert would see the opportunity to simply close the awkward formation to surround their infantry. They would meet the out of position flank with thirteen thousand horsemen ranked five men deep across a wide area. The flank would buckle under the impact, allowing the infantry to withdraw in a controlled manner.

Ragnar could see it unfolding behind his eyes, but his imagination couldn't capture the true impact of the charge when the first line struck the mass of Anglo-Saxons. More than the men screaming in pain or fear, it was the way the horses that cried out that cut through the sounds of war like a knife. It set his teeth on edge, but he didn't have the time to dwell on it because his horse followed through on the charge and he found himself trampling people under his hooves.

Everything that his father said echoed in his ears, yet all the same Ragnar found himself striking out. His guards were at his sides, stabbing down with their spears, and Ragnar did the same. The Blessing his father gave him let his spearhead punch through the guard of the Anglo-Saxons, stabbing at their throats and chests where he could. All the while, his warhorse followed the flow of the herd that began to cut to the side, the outer layer of the charge stabbing out at the enemy before they began to pull back.

Ragnar couldn't help but to glance over his shoulder, and his throat closed at the sight. He only had a narrow view of it, but it was a sight that he knew would be repeated everywhere they struck. And what he saw was a line of dead and dying men -- they laid where they had been trampled, bones shattered and many had enough strength left to scream and cry as they bled out into the dirt. Others were mercifully dead, struck down and serving as a warning to the others that survived the charge.

He saw naked terror in their faces. They had thought themselves prepared for it, but they had experienced the single worst thing that they could have imagined. The parts of the army that had been spared the charge were recovering, but they had to push through those that had survived it. It was a horror that he knew would only grow when the charging mass of horses slowly spun around to deliver a second charge into their recovering flank.

The second was more devastating than the first, somehow. Ragnar expected them to be better prepared for it, but their charge cut through them like a knife. There was a part of him that expected them to just run. To abandon the fight entirely because they knew they had no counter to their overwhelming cavalry. That what just happened to them was going to happen again and again and again. The answer to that only revealed itself when they formed back up in ranks, positioned to cover the retreat of their infantry.

They had hit them hard. Brutally hard. More men had been killed in that charge than the entirety of some of the battles Ragnar had fought in. Yet, they had only hit a relatively small portion of the whole.

They felt it, certainly. The aftershocks of the charge were rippling out, and despite their infantry withdrawing, the pursuit was short-lived and died when those who were eager to give chase found they were alone in it. That allowed their men to retreat to the fortification that they'd built days in advance, and their cavalry to retreat to their starting position.

Just with one thousand fewer horsemen. They broke off in secret, abusing the sheer mass of their numbers to hide their departure so they could join another two thousand horsemen that waited in secret. After all, the difference in appearance between seven thousand cavalry and eight thousand was negligible.

"What will happen now, Father?" Ragnar questioned, watching the enemy recover from the unexpected blow. Men were being dragged off the field while others moved up to take their place. They were trying to hide the damage as much as they were trying to tell how badly they were hit.

Father sat on top of his horse, Gram slick with blood, "They will attack." He was absolutely confident of it. His doubt must have shown on his face because Father favored him a smile, "They have no choice but to attack. King Ecbert knows that if he lets that be the tone of the day, then half of his men will flee in the night. So they will attack, even if they know they will spill blood for nothing, because they can't afford to do anything less."

His father said it, and so Ragnar would believe it, but it took time for his words to prove true. The enemy was licking their wounds, reorganizing themselves, but within the hour they marched. Archers walked forward first, coming to a stop at the edge of their range before they began to unleash a volley of arrows. Their men were in formation, and Ragnar himself was well covered by a number of shields, just in case.

Their archers were supported by their marching infantry, slowly getting into place in established ranks. However, they were content to sit on their hands and wait until the archers ran out of arrows before they made a move.

It was then that Father took action. Their own archers approached under a cover of shields. One that was the length of their body that could be propped up with spokes in the ground, while another would stand behind them with a second shield to cover them both between shots.

Father was amongst them with a monstrosity that he called a greatbow. It was styled after a metal bow that one of Charlemagne's Paladins had used a long time ago, only expanded upon to make full use of his strength. It was near his height in length and what he notched into the bowstring was less an arrow and more a thin javelin.

It wasn't the most effective weapon. Father had admitted as much. However, it was a uniquely terrifying weapon, and that was its true purpose. Killing the enemy was just an added benefit.

Their archers began to trade volleys with the Anglo-Saxons, felling them one by one with deadly aim. And it was then that Father unleashed the first shot of his greatbow, unleashing the long thick arrow at those across the field. Rangar tracked the giant arrow, making sure not to blink, and if he had, he would have missed it striking a man in the chest with enough force that it knocked him off his feet and sent him slamming into the man behind him. Both were dead before they struck the ground.

Those nearby the fallen stopped to stare, completely missing the next volley they were meant to unleash. However, word only began to spread when Father unleashed the next arrow, this time striking a man in the throat and it struck with such force, it took his head off. The other archers in their army did great work, felling them with every gap between volleys, paying no mind to how their shields became filled with arrows and splintered wood.

They didn't have as many, but they did have better archers. Two thousand of them were amongst the army, and they did great work. Every arrow they delivered was fatal, and in three volleys, more men had died from their archers than from their cavalry charge. The Anglo-Saxons felt it keenly. Their archers began falling back, convinced that the next volley would mean their death.

Arguments broke out on the backline, commanders trying to get them for unleash another volley with threats and promises. That lull was enough for Father's archers to shift their attention to the standing army behind them, dropping soldiers standing in the line. It was impossible to miss. Especially when Father unleashed an 'arrow.'

Ragnar honestly expected them to pull back. To retreat, reassess, and maybe try to attack from a different angle. But perhaps King Ecbert sensed that they couldn't afford that. Instead, they charged forward with a warcry spilling from their lips. Their formation collapsed with men running forward, accepting that some of them would fall to arrows. And they did. Without needing to duck between volleys, their archers unleashed three more before they were forced to retreat between the lines of infantry.

For a third time, Ragnar found a sound that was like no other. The sound of tens of thousands of voices shouting out as they clashed against their entrenched lines felt so loud that they could be heard around the world. They trampled over the dead, jumping into the ditches and rising up, because they could do nothing else with so many pushing them forward.

And for all they had bloodied the Anglo-Saxons, for all they tormented them and afflicted them with disease… They fought with a desperate fury, tearing at their frontline that met them with axes and spears. The ditch was filled with corpses in hardly any time at all, some of the dead forced upright simply because there were too many people around to let them fall.

Ragnar watched it all from his place on horseback. He watched how their line bent under sheer numbers and fury. Arrows rained down from above, the archers on their backline and the Anglo-Saxons continuing to shoot. Neither side seemed to notice. There was an itch to take action. To rally the cavalry and to deliver a charge into their flank. All the more so when he saw their frontline being overwhelmed, their shieldwall buckling by sheer weight of numbers.

Yet, he received no command to do so. And no matter how terribly things seemed to be going, Ragnar told himself that it was all going according to plan.

Then, almost without warning, a horn blew on the enemy side and the attack slowed to a halt. Their backlines and archers began to peel back after barely more than an hour of fighting, prompting those behind them to retreat with them. For all their fury, the retreat was orderly. A cry of victory spilled from Father's army at the sight, but they made no move to pursue.

Ragnar found that he couldn't join them as he surveyed the battlefield, seeing hundreds- thousands dead. Most of them the enemy, but their ditches were filled with corpses, the field were littered with them… by all accounts, they had won the day.

Yet, Ragnar couldn't help but feel like they had survived it.

...

#7,589
"Repeat yourself." There was a waver in King Ecbert's voice that Pepin heard. A tremor of disbelief that echoed out in his tent, around the table full of the lords that answered to him. "I fear I must have misheard you."

The messenger shifted uneasily before clearing his throat, yet his gaze did not rise from the ground even as he complied with the order. "S-six thousand have perished, your grace. Another fair thousand are injured. Aid is being given, but with the sickness…" The messenger understood the dire news that he delivered. Enough so that he knew he risked his head to deliver it. Kings weren't particularly known for how well they received terrible news, after all.

Ecbert, to his credit, did not lash out. "I see. That is… most unfortunate. Thank you for your efforts, young man. If there are further developments, do bring them to my attention." It was a dismissal that the messenger was glad for, rising to his feet and bowing his head low before he all but fled the tent. Ecbert clenched his jaw but still restrained his reaction. "Come morning, will will have ten thousand dead. Possibly more, depending on how many the pox claims."

A well and truly unthinkable number. An absurd number. Pepin had thought himself prepared and well warned about the absurdity of Siegfried. Yet, he had underestimated the young Emperor- the Allvaldr. Ten thousand dead in a single day of battle was astounding. His father had fought in battles with comparable numbers, and the casualties were in the hundreds.

'The difference in experience and armor,' Pepin deduced while the tent became its own battlefield. Siegfried's warriors were just that -- warriors. Veterans of a hundred battles against their farmers and cobblers. But the biggest cause for the lopsided and downright sickening casualties was the difference in arms and armor. Plate that could turn away a blade against their soft cloth armor, if they even had that much.

The mental component was another point of difference. For all their fervor and hate, it was beyond daunting for the Anglo-Saxons to see their comrades beat their weapons against a seemingly unstoppable foe before getting cut down. To say nothing of that monster Siegfried himself.

'Warfare has changed.' Pepin wasn't sure if anyone else in the tent realized that. Since Cain first picked up a rock to bash in the skull of Able, humanity had been waging and perfecting war. They developed spears to stab at the enemy from afar, bows to shoot at them from outside of the spear range. Tamed horses so they could enter and leave the enemy range. They developed armor to turn away blunt weapons, then blades. They formalized it. Refined it. And now, the next step of warfare had been revealed.

Plate armor on a professional army.

It was something that his own father had been developing, but he couldn't produce it en masse as Siegfried had. Simply because what Siegfried did was raid neighboring kingdoms, steal all of their iron down to farming scythes and the nails holding up a peasant's home. Then he fed that surplus of iron into his steelworks -- dozens if not hundreds of blacksmiths then worked all day and night to endlessly produce arms and armor for their soldiers. It was a wholly unique approach that was afforded to Siegfried due to the nature of his people.

It was something that could only be copied by the older empires. Such as the Roman Empire and the Caliphate. Empires with vast resources, populations, and robust logistics to create and support such an army. Worse, it was going to be a necessity. As Siegfried had amply proven…

The days of levied forces were dead. Ill equipped and poorly trained peasants simply couldn't hope to contest such a force. While Pepin doubted that levies would entirely go away, as they could be used in smaller more specialized roles, or to support a standing army rather than to be used to provide one.

But that was a thought for a future they very well might not get to see.

"My lords! My lords! Calm yourselves!" Ecbert commanded, and with far greater difficulty than normal, the table full of nobility obeyed. "I will confess, I find these losses as disturbing as the rest of you, but should we lose ourselves to panic, the battle will be lost before we take to the field again!"

A lord spoke up, "Ten thousand is catastrophic… but it's a small portion of the army, isn't it?" It felt like madness, but he wasn't wrong.

"Pressing the fight was the correct decision. Our morale is as high as it can be," another seconded. Again, he wasn't wrong. Yet, he wasn't entirely right either. The common soldier knew that there had been terrible losses, but they didn't understand how terrible. Their expectations were tempered by the belief, which has been deliberately spread, that they had been on the cusp of victory. It would not take long for that particular lie to run its course and for those that believed it to realize it was a lie.

"It won't last," another refuted. "Between the dead and the pox spreading, if this draws out long enough, we'll lose the one advantage we have when our army is too busy shitting themselves to death." Quantity was a quality of its own. The losses of ten thousand men was enough to be a decisive defeat. However, they still had more than a hundred thousand levies. They could afford to lose the same amount each day for ten days, provided the army didn't lose its nerve.

Which it absolutely would.

Something Ecbert understood quite well. "Tomorrow," he proclaimed. "We must win tomorrow, or we cannot win at all."

There was a chorus of agreement with one speaking out, "We press the attack. Commit entirely to offense. Both the hale and the ill. We'll sweep over them and surround them!" That earned a chorus of cheers, hope rekindled in their hearts that victory was still possible.

And when the meeting was adjourned, Pepin retreated to his tent before once more finding himself on a battlefield inside of a carriage. The battlefield was a place of horror in the early morning with a dense fog clinging to the ground. It gave the seemingly countless corpses that were left to rot in the field, either laying where they were slain or gathered in piles outside of the ditch before the Scandinavians, an ethereal quality that made his hair stand on end.

Through the dense fog, he could make out the ready ranks of the Scandinavians. Their banners flapped weakly in a low wind, condensation gathering on their arms and armor. Despite how many people stood on the battlefield, it felt unnaturally quiet. Unnervingly so. As if both armies were so tense that they didn't dare breathe.

The silence was only broken by the sound of a horn, King Ecbert giving the order, and a war cry that followed was every bit as deafening as the silence had been. For a moment, Pepin couldn't even hear himself think, though he felt it -- the ground trembling underfoot, through his carriage, and into him. More than a hundred thousand men stormed across the battlefield, and it felt like an earthquake.

Across the field, the Scandinavians were ready. A trade of arrows wouldn't favor them, and Siegfried foresaw that conclusion. Siegfried's archers stood elevated behind the army, and they met the charging tide with thousands of arrows. It was impossible to miss in those conditions, but from his vantage, Pepin could see the uniquely deadly aim of the archers. Hundreds of men were struck and simply collapsed like puppets with their strings cut -- even if they weren't dead when they fell, they soon were when they were trampled by their comrades behind them.

A second volley was delivered, and it was no less deadly. Neither was the third or the fourth. Or the fifth-

'The mud,' Pepin realized. The battlefield was complete upturned dirt from the conflict yesterday from so many men stepping on it. It hadn't rained, yet the morning was humid, and that wetness was seeping into the dirt, which slowed their advance. Perhaps not by much. It was no thick muck that threatened to claim every boot initially for those at the forefront, but for those that came behind them? When their lifeblood soaked into the earth and the already upturned dirt was further mixed with hundreds of feet ahead of them?

It staggered the army. Allowing the archers to unleash not just a fifth volley, but a sixth and a seventh in short order. They focused their aim, weakening the wall of bodies that they faced, which in turn allowed the infantry to act.

They kept their nerve despite the odds. That, more than anything else, was what Pepin focused on when the lines of infantry shifted before unleashing a wall of spears into the mass of charging men. A pila, Pepin realized with dark amusement. Siegfried was using Rome's own tactics against them. That amusement didn't last long when his stomach clenched, the screams of men dying and in agony reaching his ears and the scent of blood became so thick he could taste it.

By the time their army struck the Scandinavian front line, Pepin expected their charge to be blunted. To break like a fragile spear. He wouldn't blame them for it. After witnessing that slaughter yesterday, he wouldn't have stepped foot on the field. But they met the Scandinavians with defiant roars, and it was at that moment Pepin realized he had underestimated Anglo-Saxon army.

There were few motivations more potent than hate and love, and they didn't feel any love for those who had ravaged their homes.

So they fought on, overcoming the piles of corpses and the ditches that were soon filled with them, all clashing against a frontline of interlocked shields. The clash rang out, almost like a clap of thunder, and it served as a rallying cry. There was no grand display of tactics. No clever ruse. It was a simple overwhelming force that pushed against the frontline, threatening to shatter it or move it. And, after long minutes of fighting, the full might of the army exerting its weight, it was the latter that unfolded.

The front line of the Scandinavians retreated a step to avoid buckling, but soon found themselves taking a second in the face of the surge of morale. Inch by inch, step by step, Pepin watched as the Scandinavian retreated from their position and the army steadfastly chased them.

"They're abandoning the high ground!" Someone shouted out, taking it as a sign of victory. And the Scandinavians were -- Pepin watched the well entrenched position be steadily overwhelmed, forcing them to retreat down the hill and into the fading morning mists. It was better than what they could hope for.

Yet…

'Their formation is still solid.' Pepin was not a military man. He was not a hardened soldier or a brilliant tactician. He just had sharp eyes and a sharper mind to make up for his twisted spine. And what he saw was their army pressing on, chasing after their success in the efforts to break the Scandinavians and surround them… yet it was what he didn't see that began to worry him.

"King Ecbert," Pepin spoke up from the carriage, meeting the king's eyes to find his expression could have been carved from granite for all the emotion that it showed. "Their cavalry."

"I know," Ecbert replied. "But I'm afraid that it is too late."

It took a split second for the meaning of the words to settle. Then he looked to the army that chased the Scandinavians off the hill that they fortified, into the valley beneath it. With grim understanding, he realized the truth -- they had effectively lost control of the army. It was too vast, too unwieldy, and too drunk on progress. They were convinced the next step would be the one that broke the enemy. Even if King Ecbet warned of the coming cavalry charge until he was blue in the face, their army wouldn't be able to respond.

Because it had become a mob. An armed, furious mob that wanted blood.

Still, runners were dispatched in an attempt to reign in the army. To establish some semblance of control over it before they heedlessly walked into a trap. Yet, if any progress was made to the goal, Pepin didn't see it when the trap was sprung.

A horn cut through the air like a knife, followed by the sound of galloping horses. They almost appeared as specters, erupting from the fog, streaming forth into the sides of their army. Pepin couldn't see the entirety of the impact, only how their forces shuddered under the unexpected blow.

However…

"I hear horses," Pepin realized, his heart rising to his throat before he shuffled to the other side of the carriage, ignoring a red hot spike of pain in his back from the sudden movement before he ripped open a window. He wasn't the only one who had noticed, but it was far too late to do anything.

More horsemen appeared from behind their backline, and they weren't in small numbers. There were thousands of them. Had their scouts failed so utterly that they missed such a force? Or had they walked into a much grander trap than they realized? Pepin supposed it mattered little as their horsemen, all nobility and their chosen few guard, started to react. They circled around, some breaking off from the force to flee while others were gathering their resolve.

Prince Æthelwulf was doing what he could to rally them, barking out orders between lines of prayer. He was a warrior to his core. More so than his father, who watched the oncoming charge with the expression of a man who knew he had been outplayed, and accepted the consequences.

Yet, despite the Prince's valor, it wasn't enough to make up for the difference in numbers. The Scandinavian cavalry swept over them, clashing against those who would fight and tearing those who wouldn't off their horses so that they couldn't flee.

Pepin didn't try to fight or escape. His carriage wasn't particularly suited to either, nor was he. Instead, he watched as the nobility were swiftly captured and subdued, the rest of the cavalry holding off what remained of their reserve forces. Which were those so ill they could barely stand and would likely be dead come morning. The capture was efficient. Practiced. Well executed, with Prince Æthelwulf being brought to the ground and secured with ropes, while spears were leveled in Ecbert's direction.

His gaze landed on the apparent leader of the charge that trotted up to his carriage. He was a large man with dark hair and a neatly groomed beard tucked under a helm that he took off to meet Pepin's eyes. It was the first time that they met, but he knew the man -- King Haldur, brother of Emperor Siegfried. "You must be Prince Pepin," Haldur observed, a calculating glint in his eyes.

Pepin held his gaze for a long few seconds before laughter spilled forth from his lips.

It seemed that only his enemies acknowledged that he was a prince.


…
​

"They're breaking," I observed in a cold voice, looking across the battlefield. I had underestimated the religious fervor that would carry the army forward, but I had prepared for it. As it was impossible to fully repel the weight of so many people, I instead planned around getting pushed back. Abandoning the high ground would convince the enemy that our fighting retreat was genuine, allowing us to lead them where our cavalry was hidden. The mass charges on the side, combined with a dedicated push with our infantry had the intended effect.

They were being squeezed and panic was setting in.

Some at the back were breaking off to run, but many more still fought -- one part because of fervor, but mostly because they still believed that they were on the cusp of victory. It took time to put that delusion to rest. And by the time that it was, when the common soldier looked around for guidance from his superiors, he found them all dead by our sharpshooters. It was only then that the army began to disintegrate, breaking apart to flee.

Something I would not allow, sending my cavalry after them. The battlefield was littered with corpses, some of them stacked so high they stood as tall as I did. Yet more would die in the coming hours as I cemented my victory. This land was always going to be a problematic land to rule from afar, and the greater the casualties were, the better. Not only would it mean fewer rebels in the future, it would discourage those who might think to pick up a spear.

It would be an example to point to, proving such actions were futile.

My men unleashed a victorious war cry, knowing that the day was won. Our losses were light. Extremely so given the number of men we'd faced, but the armor we wore wasn't infallible. The shield wall fractured in some places, some of my men getting pulled out of the line and swarmed like ants. However, our losses were around a hundred dead. A few hundred more wounded.

"I thought we were going to lose," Ragnar admitted next to me, a note of quiet awe in his voice. He stared out at the field of the dead, and it was not the first time he had seen such death. Though it was the first time Magnus had, and he seemed pale at the sheer volume of bloodshed. He kept his composure, however. And that was the important part.

I chuckled, urging my horse forward and my sons followed along with their guards. "We almost did," I admitted, earning a sharp look from Rangar. "If our line had faltered, we would have lost. If any part of the army failed to do what it was told, it would have had a cascading effect that there would be no stopping."

I glanced at my sons, expecting an elaboration as we rode through the battlefield. There were corpses scattered across the hill, and already the bodies of our own were being pulled from the piles to be burned with honors. Their arms and armor would go to their next of kin, along with their bones.

"We won because of our discipline?" Magnus found his voice, and it was when we rounded the hill that the scattered corpses became piles. The stench of death was thick, the thin mist obscuring them ever so slightly. Still, it was a great killing field. I estimated that we had killed roughly ten thousand yesterday. Today, perhaps as many as thirty thousand.

It really spoke to their absurd numbers that there was enough of an army left over that if they regrouped, they would still outnumber us.

"Our training. Our armor and weapons. Experience played its part too," I confirmed with a soft nod, spying our destination. The noble prisoners who were smart enough to stay on the backlines. The prisoners that King Ecbert wanted to keep close. His son among them.

The prisoners were huddled together, but as king, Ecbert was afforded additional luxuries. He sat on top of his horse, his crown still resting on his brow. He wore a decidedly neutral expression, watching our approach. Then, when we arrived, he threw on a well-practiced smile.

"I don't suppose it would be too late to negotiate terms?" He asked, as if he were in a position to negotiate.

As if he hadn't sent a runner in the dead of night with terms carried in a letter. A deal struck in the shadows, known only to myself, King Ecbert, and the messenger. A deal that made King Ecbert as much of an accomplice to our victory as our soldiers because I agreed to those terms.

King Ecbert was a man who knew he'd lost the war, so he was determined to win the peace. And that made him dangerous.

However, I played my part in the deception.

"No. I don't suppose that it is."

...

#7,621
Ecbert didn't believe in God. Neither did he believe in the Devil. But, he supposed if either Heaven or Hell were real, then he would undoubtedly be consigned to the latter. His ambitions were of this world -- a supreme Wessex and an England united underneath it. His son, Æthelwulf, was a dense lad. He was incapable of the delicate political maneuverings, so if England was to one day conquer Alba and the Éire, then they needed momentum that could be carried forward to his generation and beyond it.

It was an ambition that he dedicated himself to in his entirety. The closest he had ever come to believing in God was when Emperor Charlemagne had opened his coffers to Wessex in the name of securing their borders and expansion. It had seemed entirely too good to be true. While he still doubted the existence of God, there was increasingly more proof of the Devil.

Odds were he was seated across from him.

"Allvaldr Siegfried," Ecbert uttered the name that had darkened his shores and cast years of careful plans into utter disarray. "My congratulations on your victory. I hope that it was at least hard won?"

Siegfried at least looked the part. To the peasants, a king was the closest they would ever get to God, and it was the greatest con in history that a crown made a man in any way special once it was placed upon his brow. Ecbert was under no delusion that he was any better or worse than a peasant toiling in the field. He merely had the great fortune of being born to the right father and being a bit cleverer than most.

The man who sat across from him looked as if he were more of a god than a man. Large. Almost unseemingly so. A mane of blood red hair that was smoothed back, his beard cut short. He wore a king's ransom in armor, while the head of the beast that rested on one shoulder seemed to be staring right into Ecbert's soul. Likewise, he had never been under the delusion that victory against such a man was in any way possible.

You don't win the kind of victories that Siegfried did and be a fool. If he was going to fight their oversized army, then it meant he was confident that he could win. And if he had to place a wager on himself or Siegfried, then the answer was obvious.

Thus Ecbert decided that if he couldn't win, then he would control how he lost.

"You made us bleed for it," Siegfried acknowledged. His boys stood at his sides, and both of them were going to grow up to be little monsters. Or not so little, given their height. The one on Siegfried's right, Ragnar, would be King of Alba one day. King Lucas was an interim king. Ecbert was quite aware of the man. His reign would end with him dead in a few years or revolt, and both fates were being avoided by ongoing support by Scandinavia. An empire didn't expend resources like that to rule indirectly.

Not Siegfried.

And certainly not Charlemagne.

"I suppose that is the most that could be hoped for given the circumstances. I must say, well played," Ecbert inclined his head to Siegfried. He personally wanted to strangle the man, but Ecbert could admire a master at work.

Siegfried repaid him the same courtesy, "It was a bargain well struck." The boys at his side kept their expression neutral, but there was a slight shift in their posture that betrayed their displeasure. "You have upheld your end of it. As shall I."

There was a knot of tension that bled out of Ecbert at that. It had been a risk. A dangerous one. But he would not survive without taking risks- not when he was being crushed by two overwhelming influences. Siegfried and Scandinavia on one side, Charlemagne and Rome on the other. So, he plotted. He schemed.

And he walked a tightrope.

"The terms?" Ecbert prodded, keeping his expression warm but neutral.

"You shall remain King of Wessex, with everything south of Hadrian's Wall being your sphere of influence," Siegfried confirmed. Mercia and a vast swathe of Northumbria, both would fall under his dominion. A unified England, even if it wasn't the borders that he had envisioned. The battle had gone perfectly.

The problematic elements he had accepted in his court for the sake of wealth and appearances had been culled. They had thanked him for the opportunity to be in the vanguard, and if they weren't dead already, then they would be soon enough. If not by disease deliberately spread to them, then by an assassin's dagger in the dark. The lords that he would rule over would benefit enough from the windfall that even if they suspected, they wouldn't dare make an accusation.

England was within his grasp.

"Your son, Æthelwulf, will become a guest at my court, alongside the sons and heirs of several of your nobility," Siegfried listed off the cost of what he gained. It was a loss. Truly. Æthelwulf was in a pivotal moment in his education. Yet, there was an opportunity there.

Æthelwulf was but a few years older than Ragnar and Magnus. A friendship between them would benefit the fledgling England quite well. Politics would always be politics, but there was a possibility that England could gain a lull. A brief period of time to firmly establish itself and its independence from both Scandinavia and Rome. Failing that, there were few friendships that were stronger than being the only familiar faces in an unfamiliar land.

Ecbert had learned as much when he was abroad in Charlemagne's court. Fools he wouldn't have pissed on if they were on fire were fast friends. At least until he learned Frankish.

They would form a bedrock of loyalty when his son was returned to him.

"A weregild of five hundred pounds of gold and silver will be paid separately, with each ransom to be capped at a maximum of twenty pounds of gold and silver." The cost stung, but the truth was his treasury could endure it. It was a necessary cost as well.

As far as his nobles were aware, he was on a lonely hill, negotiating their freedom with the Devil himself. Too good of a deal would arouse suspicion. Too bad of one would be ruinous. But one that was just good enough, with himself shouldering much of the perceived burden? Sparing them from ruinous ransoms that would have taken the last bits of wealth they had left in this world?

Debts could be every bit as valuable as loyalty. If leveraged correctly, of course.

"Lastly, a truce lasting five years between the forces I leave behind in Alba and Britannia at large." That last term was the one Ecbert resented the most. Five years wasn't a lot of time, but it wasn't a small amount either. Those five years could be spent undermining Alba, but to make matters worse was the knowledge that Siegfried was leaving token forces behind to maintain his influence. "At the end of the truce, your son and other noble hostages shall be returned. So I vow."

It was not a good peace deal, but it wasn't ruinous either. Especially given their current circumstances. He had been forced to thread the needle between Charlemagne and Siegfried, and while he hadn't managed to do so flawlessly, given the circumstances at hand…

He would maintain his independence from Siegfried and Charlemagne. Charlemagne had all but sought to buy out the crown and England itself. The wealth he expended on Ecbert's realm demanded a return. The very same kind of debts Ecbert intended to leverage against his nobility would be leveraged against him in turn. It would be a slow death for England. Trade concessions, rights, then England would become a junior partner before its independence was eroded like a sandcastle in the face of the tide.

Ecbert had maintained appearances that he was upholding his end of the bargain. Charlemagne had doubts, of course, otherwise he wouldn't have instructed the Paladins to offer gentle reminders of his obligations. Yet, the fact that neither had taken to the field told Ecbert all that he needed to know and compelled him to send that first message -- victory was impossible, even with the Grace of God on their side.

He would have preferred not to fight the battle at all, but apparently, Siegfried was the kind of man who saw that he was outnumbered four times over and considered it a good time. Unfortunate, but by securing terms in advance, he could prevent his realm from being outright conquered. Even better, with so much of Wessex's strength retained, and after such a bloodletting, Charlemagne would be inclined to make further investments as Ecbert had followed his will to the letter.

"As do I," Ecbert swore. There were other details, of course. They had managed to capture a few dozen Northman raiders over the various skirmishes, and all would be returned to Siegfried. "There is one additional matter that I would like to discuss. Lord Pepin, son of Charlemagne. What is to be done with him?"

He had developed a soft spot for the hunchback. There were precious few who could match him in wits and enjoyed a game of chess as much as he did. However, Ecbert understood that Pepin was largely outside of his ability to help. He was an advisor sent by his father, but he was foremost the son of the reigning Roman Emperor. His freedom was Charlemagne's responsibility.

But he would do what he could. Even if it was merely saying a few words in Pepin's defense.

"He is being held ransom by my brother. A letter has already been dispatched to his father," Siegfried answered, and that soothed the worst of his concerns. The Paladins hadn't confessed their intentions towards Siegfried's children, but they didn't need to. It was a relief to see that Siegfried was not as vengeful as the stories made him out to be -- else Pepin would suffer a most undeserving fate for the actions of his father. "We shall depart from your lands before we receive an answer, so he will accompany your son and the other hostages to our homeland."

"I see," Ecbert uttered, offering a nod of acceptance. Pepin's departure would be a loss, but so long as he wouldn't be killed… pressing the matter would require far more leverage than he currently had. "Then I shall pray that you return home safely. And quickly."

Siegfried offered a humorless smile that didn't reach his eyes. "I thank you for it, King Ecbert."

With that, the negotiations were concluded.


…
​

"You didn't lie," Magnus observed once King Ecbert departed from the tent, content that he had secured everything he cared about -- the future of England. And he had, for a time.

"I didn't need to," I agreed. The plans that I'd made before the raid had begun had already adapted once. They could do so again. "Ecbert places more value on the perception of being King of England than the reality of it."

For the next five years, Ecbert would bear the aftermath of the raid. It would be he that brought order to the towns and villages, many of which had everything of value ripped away. We took not only their wealth, but their tools to smelt down into armor. Life would be hard in Brit- England for the next few years. And as much as that ire would be directed at us for committing the deed, it would be directed at Ecbert just as much depending on how well he handled everything that came next.

I didn't know if he would succeed or fail. Or if he would fall somewhere in the middle. If he was smart, he would focus his efforts on the most valuable stretches of land, but even that would have significant repercussions down the line when the truce ended.

The seeds to take over all of Britannia had been planted. In five years, it would come time to reap what we had sown. And I suppose time would tell who had gotten the better part of the deal we made, simply because there was no doubt in my mind that Ecbert knew exactly what I intended.

"Are we done with the raid, Father?" Ragnar asked, and I rested a hand on his head and ruffled his hair.

"Aye, we are," I confirmed. It was still fall, and the window for our departure was closing. Unless we wanted to winter in Britannia, the raid had achieved everything that I wanted it to. The wealth that we had secured would fuel the projects I sponsored across Scandinavia and the victory solidified the legitimacy of the empire. The raid, and the battle that followed, would be a shining example that I could point to as an argument in the years to come at why the unification was necessary and why the individual kingdoms were greater when they were part of a larger whole.

The captured soldiers, which still numbered in the tens of thousands even after the route, were dispersed across Northumbria and Mercia to make their way home in defeat. Once there wasn't a possibility of Ecbert reneging on the bargain, I gave the order to return to Geymsla with our noble prisoners.

To say they were sullen was an understatement, but that would mellow with time.

My army marched to the forts that we used on the mainland, setting sail back to Geymsla while also destroying the forts to ensure that they couldn't be used against us. It was only when we arrived back on the small Island of Mann and Geymsla itself that the celebrations began in earnest. A feast butchered the animals that we couldn't take with us and the island couldn't support while thanks were offered to the gods with sacrifices.

I played the role that was expected of me in public, making no small number of toasts and bestowing gifts upon those that had proven their valor. All the while, I calculated exactly how much we had earned with the raid. And the answer was obscene.

I was no stranger to wealth. It had been a very long time since I was a boy on a farm and a pound of silver seemed like an unimaginable fortune. My time in Saxony and the Mediterranean had given me a great tolerance for gold and silver and precious gems. But when I conferred with the warehouse overseers, I was compelled to do the math three times just to ensure there wasn't a mistake.

Fifty-five thousand pounds of gold, silver, and jewels.

Most of it sourced from churches and treasuries across Britannia, with six hundred from the ransom that was swiftly gathered and delivered. All of it had to be melted down into conveniently sized ingots, otherwise it'd take a dozen trips just to transport it all. It was a sum that was everything that I needed it to be. Enough that I could sponsor my projects and still fill the treasury to the brim.

It was matched by twenty-eight thousand thralls that were claimed. It was fewer than I had prepared for, but several thousand more than I would like. Unsurprisingly, the majority were women to counter the… shortage, for lack of a better word, back home. For that reason, they were important. In the years since I assumed the throne, there had been an explosion in population as our realm became more connected than it ever had been before.

Yet, it still wasn't enough. To develop the inner kingdoms, such as Norway, Sweden, Sami, or Finland -- we needed people. Migration was a solution, but the easterlands were not well populated and the population that was there mostly consisted of nomads.

There would come a day when Charlemagne's authority over the resurrected Roman Empire would not be so new. So fragile. He was already taking steps towards it. Just as the raid was a great victory for me, it was also a victory for him. The wealth we took, the slaughter on the battlefield -- all of it would feed into the narrative that he was developing. That the Christian faith was under attack.

I still played my part in that narrative. It was too beneficial not to. But I wasn't blind to what he was doing… and five years from now?

Neither of us would be so unsteady. My empire wouldn't be so new with the first generation of men being born and raised inside of a unified empire. And Charlemagne would continue to feed that narrative until it became something terrible.

Which left me to turn to a few pieces I had on the board.

"Our truce stands with Wessex," I told Hjalmar, who was seated to my right during one of the long days of feasting. "There are to be no excursions south of Hadrian's Wall. However, the Éire has no such agreement protecting it."

I found myself rather fond of Hjalmar. To my eyes, he shined blue, marking him as someone loyal. More than that, he was uniquely unambitious coupled with being exceptionally competent. He wasn't someone who would blaze a trail and ignite passion in the hearts of his men and people, but if given a task, no matter how arduous, he would reliably see it through. It was for that reason I trusted him to act in my name once more.

"Ten thousand men will be yours to command, who will remain in Geymsla." Which would open up more room for the thralls taken in the raid. "My recommendation is that you use them to secure the coast and the fort, first and foremost. However, raiding actions should be limited. For that reason, I am leaving five hundred pounds of gold and silver in the town coffers to be used at your discretion."

Hjalmar listened quietly, and offered a small nod. "You wish me to buy their good will?"

"Essentially. The next winter will be a hard one for many. Gold and bread will sate those that bend the knee, and those that don't?" It had always been the plan. But as I uttered the words, they made me confront something I didn't know how to feel about.

Being King- the Allvaldr, had changed me. I hadn't forgotten the lean times as a child, or how my own brother had succumbed to illness because he'd made sure our bowls were full while his were empty. It was not a tactic that I would have entertained as a younger man. Not as a boy in Saxony, or a bright eyed youth in Rome. But now, I gave the order because it was the most effective course of action to accomplish my goals. Which was a stable Eire during the truce.

"Those that refuse will rally. That will make it easy to sort out your enemies. None will be able to muster such a force as we fought against Ecbert, but if they do manage to unite, then take advantage of our alliance with Alba." A lighter hand would be needed in Alba. The original plan called for memories to fade a touch before we returned to their shores, but the principle was the same. It would just need to be done in stages.

Hjalmar offered one more nod, "Your will shall be done, Allvaldr."

"You have my faith in this, King Hjalmar," I said, testing the title for him. He kept his true thoughts off his face, but I saw it in his eyes -- there was more fear there than excitement. And that was how I knew he would grow into an excellent king.

...
