#7,638
Æthelwulf gazed out sullenly over the bow of Emperor Siegfried's ship, realizing that they were nearing their destination. Fog covered the sea like a blanket, obscuring the land, but he still saw the trees poking through. He wasn't sure what he expected from Denmark and the Empire of Scandinavia. No, that was a lie.

He expected savagery and debasement. They were a people who not only were without the light of God, but scorned him. If they had homes at all, then they would be made of bone and mud. Corpses would be put on display like a mockery of Hell itself. Men and women would walk naked in the streets, fighting over scraps like they were dogs.

It was why he was sullen when Denmark failed to live up to that expectation. Because what he saw emerging from that fog was no city made of mud and blood, filled with ignorant savages. What he saw, in a word, was… civilization.

And it was galling to admit.

Almost like a curtain, the fog pulled itself back as if to unveil the city of Miklagard in all of its wondrous glory. The harbor was vast. So vast that Æthelwulf had little doubt that the entirety of the Scandinavian fleet could disembark at once. That harbor was framed by tall buildings made of stone, some standing taller than his father's palace. They were capped with domed, almost ship-like roofs with chimneys emerging where the rudder would go.

There was a crowd to greet them. Or their Emperor, specifically. They gathered en masse along the vast network of larger and smaller docks, their cheers carrying over the calm waters. They were not dressed as nobles or kings, yet they didn't wear the base furs or ragged cloth that he expected. More than that, however -- there were so many. Thousands. Tens of thousands, even?

"Father says that two hundred thousand citizens dwell within the city." Æthelwulf stilled when Prince Ragnar seemed to hear the thoughts in his head, and for all Æthelwulf knew, he had. After their unexplained and impossible victory on the Red Field, Æthelwulf didn't doubt their devilish magics- "It's a common question. Miklagard earned its name for good reason. We have other cities across the empire, many built by my father's hand, but Miklagard stands as the greatest of them all."

Æthelwulf inclined his head to Prince Ragnar, not at all certain what to make of the younger man. Or his older wife, who looked at him like she was trying to decide which angle to slit his throat at every time they made eye contact.

"There will be a parade to display our spoils." Ragnar continued, and it went unsaid that he and his people would be considered amongst them. "We'll get a decent look at the city and some of its landmarks. However, should you wish, I could give you and your companions a more private tour?"

Prince Ragnar was unfailingly polite. It was… irritating in a way that Æthelwulf wasn't skilled enough to articulate. He had been taken from his home, forced to live amongst heathens, and everyone was just so… nice. It made his flesh crawl.

Still, it could be an opportunity. He doubted that he would be able to swim all the way back home, but if the opportunity arose to escape, then learning the layout of Miklagard was the obvious first step.

The regents of Miklagard seemed well prepared for Siegfried's success. Upon disembarking, horses and parade wagons were provided for what amounted to a Triumph. It was a cold comfort that he was not bound in chains or gagged, but Æthelwulf understood that he and his fellows were no less on display as the literal mountains of gold and jewels that were openly piled up in a display of grandeur. Artifacts stolen from churches and noble homes were almost unceremoniously piled up for all to see.

One wagon would have been a sight. Yet, there were dozens, all pulled by mules that were laden with more treasures. It had almost been a running jest about the sheer scope of Siegfried's theft, but when it was gathered up so, Æthelwulf really did wonder if the Emperor had looted every last spec of gold and silver from his homeland. Those wagons were flanked by the marching Ironclads, each taking a step in unison with their brothers if they weren't seated upon iron clad horses.

Æthelwulf watched the crowd that only seemed to grow during the triumph. Men, women, and children cheered with unabashed joy at the return of their Emperor. They gathered in the streets, they hung out of the windows to throw out handfuls of flower petals that rained upon them, or they danced with banners.

There was a clenching in his gut when he realized the scope of Miklagard. It was… an impressive city, but he hadn't been able to conceive how vast it really was until they began their long winding loop through it. The lines of tall houses seemed to run on without ending, and at the very edges of the city, he saw hints that construction was ongoing and had only paused to celebrate their return.

That paled in comparison to what he felt when he saw the Colosseum. It was a vast building that he struggled to believe was real when he first caught sight of it. He was no stranger to fighting pits and stages, there were plenty to be found in Wessex, but none could hold a candle to the vast arena. One so large it felt like it could seat everyone in Winchester with room to spare.

There was a surplus of art and color. Buildings painted vibrant hues while statues seemed to be erected in every other street corner with many covered in the devilish runes the Northmen preferred. That growing sense of unease only continued to swell the longer the triumph was, but it reached its zenith when they arrived at the palace and the plaza before it. It was…

He hated it. Æthelwulf wasn't even sure why at first, not until he took his place amongst his fellow hostages, presented before the plaza alongside their hoard of treasure. A crowd naturally gathered in the plaza and Æthelwulf saw a sea of faces. When he did, he understood the cause of his hate.

'I'm jealous.' He was jealous of pagans. Of those who had scorned the light of God. Who had ravaged his home.

He hated it because he'd expected savagery and instead found civilization. One that cast a long shadow over his own homeland. And that, more than anything else, was the knot of envy that formed around his heart.

"My people," Siegfried began in a booming voice that carried across the crowd. "Let there be no doubt that the gods smile upon us, as our raid and our kin in the distant Mediterranean, both found great success! Riches! Glory! Fame! We have proven beyond all doubt that together, we are strong. That we are mighty!"

The crowd, predictably, cheered. It pricked at him how fervent the cheering was. Enough so that it took a minute for them to quite down enough for Siegfried to continue.

"Years ago, I had a dream of what our future could be. A dream that was born in Saxony against the Frankish Empire. A dream that was nurtured in the Roman Empire," Siegfried continued, a weight to his voice. "Upon my return to my homeland, I began a labor that I knew would outlive me. I sought to forge an empire, binding our people from distant quarreling tribes, giving rise to cities. Kingdoms. Unity." The crowd hung on every word, waiting on bating breath for him to continue.

"I stand before you proud. Through tireless nights and with the sweat on our brow, together, we have laid a foundation that will be built upon by our children and their children," Siegfried uttered, and Æthelwulf could hear the smile in his voice. "I also stand before you to say that the labor is not yet done. We have won a great victory, that is true. We have earned a vast amount of wealth, that I cannot deny. Nor can I that those beyond our borders look at what we have built with fear and envy!"

The words almost felt directed at him specifically.

"What say you? Will you let them?" The crowd had been loud before, but now they unleashed a war cry that almost staggered him with the force behind it. This time, it took even longer for them to quiet down. "I thought not! Yet, they will try! The Romans at our borders will seek to destroy all that we have built! Because they fear what we can accomplish when we stand together! We fight together! Build together!"

"I make you this vow, my people," Siegfried swiftly continued before the cheering could drown him out. "When the Romans come… we will be ready!"

The very worst part about it?

Æthelwulf believed him.


…
​

Ragnar hadn't realized how much he missed his home until he found himself walking its halls once again. There were subtle changes from his memories, mostly the decorations that were on display -- different statues, vases, or tapestries. Still, it was undeniably his home.

Maeve, for her part, was digging her nails into his arm out of nervousness. She had a wide eyed look that Ragnar was struggling not to laugh at, like she was trying to see everything all at once and couldn't decide what demanded her attention more. He thought she had been more prepared to see his home. For his part, he had described it to her so she would have something of a warning.

He grew up around finery. Even as far back as Norland, Ragnar had long since been desensitized to lavish amounts of wealth on display. He imagined that his father looked similar when he arrived at Constantinople as a younger man.

They walked quickly down the halls for a private reunion. And an introduction. More public reunions would come in the feasts and speeches that would follow, all the kings under his father basking in the success and congratulating each other on a job well done.

A thrill raced through him when the doors opened, revealing the rest of his family-

"Father!" Radahn shouted out, not caring a wit about decorum and running forward. Bjorn was right behind him, throwing their arms around their father with large grins on their faces.

"You both have grown," Father acknowledged, a softness in his voice that Ragnar rarely heard.

"We're men now," Radahn decided, making Ragnar swallow a laugh. "So the next time you go raiding, we can come too, right?"

"... I will make you both a deal. If you study hard and train harder, the next time I go raiding, you can come with me," Father conceded, much to his younger brothers' joy. Both of them were completely unaware that Father didn't intend to go raiding for years. He likely wouldn't leave the empire again until it was time to conquer Britannia.

The soft moment was interrupted when his mother approached. Ragnar found himself meeting her gaze with some apprehension. It hadn't exactly been the plan to get married during the raid. Even these months later, he didn't regret the decision, but he also knew that it was certainly going to be a… surprise for his mother.

"And you must be my son's bride, Maeve," Mother greeted her warmly. Enough so that Maeve was a bit startled by it, but she recovered swiftly.

"I am, Allvaldís," Maeve agreed, making Mother smile.

"Please, just call me Astrid. I've never been one for ceremony," she admitted, though she tossed Father a very pointed look. "Though I would have appreciated being able to attend my son's wedding."

Oh. Father was right. She might actually kill him.

"But," Mother continued, looking back at Maeve. "Welcome to the family. We're always happy to see it grow and welcome a new member into the fold," she said, reaching out and squeezing Maeve's hands gently. That earned a more relaxed and honest smile from his wife. "And speaking of the family growing."

A knot that Ragnar hadn't realized was there melted away when a set of doors opened, revealing Aunt Morrigan. When she hadn't been there with Aunt Jill and Aunt Jasmine… it was a thought he was all too happy to dismiss, rushing over alongside Magnus and his Father. In her arms was a young child, perhaps six or seven months old.

"The gods favor you, Siegfried. Another son for your growing collection," Aunt Morrigan remarked with a dry sarcasm, passing the bundle to Father. The babe squirmed at getting passed around, looking up at them with golden eyes that were settled in an annoyed scowl. His hair was different, Ragnar noticed. All of his siblings shared their Father's blood red hair, but his youngest brother's was darker. Still red, but so dark to the point of being black, and only looked red in the light. "I have named him Hakon. He's a clever boy."

"Hello, Hakon. It's such a relief to finally meet you. I'm your father-"

"Father-" Ragnar's father nearly dropped Hakon when the infant spoke. It wasn't clean. More of a fa-ur, but there could be no mistaking his intent when he pointed at their father and repeated himself. "Father."

"T'is as I said," Aunt Morrigan continued with evident pride. "He's exceedingly clever. He takes after his father too much, I think."

"And his mother," Father replied with a grin. Despite Hakon's increasingly annoyed expression at being poked and prodded, Ragnar found that he couldn't look away from his baby brother, who held the tip of his finger in such a grip it was as if he were attempting to rip it off.

His cleverness didn't just end there. Upon being introduced to the babe, Hakon identified Ragnar as Rags. Magnus was shortened to Mags. Every word uttered was with a thick accent of a chubby child-like drawl, but there was no denying it -- Hakon was able to identify and name them.

Ragnar played with Radahn and Bjorn endlessly during Father's conquest of Scandinavia, attempting to fill their father's shoes so they wouldn't miss him as much. Hakon wasn't merely clever. Ragnar liked to think he was clever. That all of his siblings were clever. They were praised endlessly by their tutors; they met and exceeded every expectation placed upon them… Hakon was a step beyond that. If not several steps.

It was a strange feeling. One that lingered when the reunion commenced in earnest -- Ragnar embraced his sisters, finding that the months he had been gone had them grow from girls to young women. He regaled his younger siblings with tales of their adventures that were only a little exaggerated. Once she found her footing, Maeve spoke with his mother, aunts, and siblings in turn.

The family reunion didn't so much as end when supper came for an informal meal together as it shifted. Private conversations began, such as the one Ragnar and Maeve were pulled into by his mother.

"Becoming a king is no small matter, Ragnar," Mother whispered to him, taking his hand into hers. "Especially across the sea. It wouldn't be the same as taking a kingdom here. Over there… you'll be isolated. Days away."

"I know it won't be easy," he admitted. "Father has already spoken to me about my lessons in rulership." In essence, he would be shadowing him in the years to come, learning to steward a kingdom and navigate the seas of diplomacy.

By the time he returned to Alba, he would be eighteen. Hopefully, with five years of experience learning from the greatest leaders of their time would mean he wouldn't make a horrid mess of things upon assuming the throne.

"That's not the part that I'm worried about," Mother said, squeezing his hand. "I won't be able to see you so easily in Alba." That, admittedly, wasn't something he thought of when he agreed to the marriage. He just saw it as a way to bring Alba into the empire peacefully and without bad blood. Of course, such a thing would come with a cost, but he hadn't thought his mother would suffer for it. "And more than that… being a king gives you prestige. It gives your name weight. But you won't be able to use that weight and influence on the other kings of the realm. Not if you intend to become the heir."

That was another issue Father had discussed with him at length in the weeks leading up to the wedding and the ride back home. How the phrase 'out of sight and out of mind' was a very real thing when it came to rulership. Being seen was as important a part of being king as ruling well was -- and in Alba, while he wouldn't be as isolated as his mother feared, it would only be natural for his fellow monarchs to focus on their relationships within their power bloc around the Baltic Sea.

All of the conversations he had with his wife, his father, and now his mother… His mind lingered on all of them. A question that he hadn't been able to earnestly answer back in that cabin when Maeve asked him. A response that sat heavily on his tongue when his father assumed his desire to become King of Alba was a result of a grander desire to become the next Allvaldr.

"... And if I don't want to be the heir?" Ragnar asked, almost wary of her reaction. He was the eldest. That was the expectation. A constant pressure that he dealt with all of his life. A pressure that he didn't exactly mind, but…

It wasn't there.

That spark of ambition that drove his father to sail across the world to learn from the successes and failures of the Roman Empire, all so he may apply those lessons to a kingdom he had yet to conquer. Or use that kingdom to create an empire. What drove him was a desire for approval. To meet the expectations of his parents.

And that wasn't enough.

The empire demanded more. Deserved more. Someone who would take all that Father had built and bring it to new heights. Someone who didn't just want to meet his expectations but surpass them. To surpass him.

In that case, Alba was almost uniquely suited as the perfect solution for the heir apparent to step outside of the succession. He would not be shamed. He would simply be… out of sight and out of mind.

Despite his apprehension, there was only love in his mother's eyes. She gave his hand a gentle squeeze and the smile that tugged at her lips told him she already knew everything he wanted to say.

That he didn't want to be the heir.

...

#7,673
My time during the raid had been productive, securing the much needed resources and people to fuel our expansion, but I couldn't deny that it felt good to be back home. Being able to sleep in my own bed next to my wives, work at my own desk, and all the little luxuries I took for granted until they were gone returned to me. Such indulgences did come with a cost, however.

Time.

"The raids into Saxony have increased," Widukind said, seated across from me. Time had been kinder to him since he abdicated the throne, taking a role as an advisor in my court. One of the few that I trusted without reservation, even if it did come with the understanding he would prioritize Saxony above all the other kingdoms. "Not by Charlemagne's will, officially speaking."

I let out a quiet hum, "He just doesn't stop them." To that, Widukind inclined his head to me. "Reprisals will be delivered. It's only a question of how deeply we have to cut into Rome."

"The border provinces… we've always raided each other with every turn of the season. It's just the way of things, but in these last years, Siegfried…" Widukind's lips thinned. "This year, they were raiding to spill blood rather than take treasures. The garrison helps, but that just limits their damage."

"Part of that is what happened in Rome," I offered. "Tensions have risen because of it, and I doubt that they will lessen any time soon." For a multitude of reasons. My raid across Britannia had begun to spread, as well as my victory over the Christian faithful. As the Romans told the story, I had slaughtered every living thing on Britannia down to the last flea on the last rat. Or I had made mass sacrifices to herald the Christian apocalypse.

The flames of religious fervor across Rome were being stoked into an inferno. In some part as a deliberate action by Charlemagne to solidify his rule over Rome. Another hand stoking the flames was my own -- I knew the narrative that would be spun about my actions in the raid, and we had prepared accordingly. Even before the raid had commenced, priests and men of faith had traveled across the Roman Empire to polytheize.

I still found the branch of Christianity that called me a Prophet of God… distasteful. For many reasons. But it was a potent tool to use against Charlemagne, and one I wielded with deadly intent.

The very same denouncements and fervor that the Christians used to decry me and paint me as the Anti-Christ or a demon were used as evidence to prove that I was a prophet. After all, could I really have won that battle in Britannia if it wasn't God's will? Would my empire thrive as it did if I was not part of His plan?

They were unleashed upon Rome like a pox, delivering a carefully constructed message that would turn Charlemagne's weapon against him. That the Christian God had chosen me to tear down the corrupt church that profited off the misery of the faithful. That God demanded a more humble church to act as shepherds for the Christians rather than the corrupt political quagmire that served as a dumping ground for the second and third sons of nobility.

The message was spreading alongside news of my victories in Britannia. How well the message was being delivered, I wouldn't know for years, but I had already heard tales of purges across cities that proclaimed themselves Norse Christians. It was by design. After all, there were few things that spread a message like martyrs and Christianity thrived in the face of oppression.

"Meaning that it is a fine time to keep my promise to you and begin construction of that wall," I continued, watching as some of the tension bled out of Widukind. He'd expected he would have to remind me. "It won't be perfect," I warned him. "A wall that long will have its weak points, which we will use to either delay the enemy from overcoming it or force them to cross where we desire."

Widukind inclined his head, "I am well aware. It's not a perfect solution, but so long as my people are safe from Rome's raiders… that is what I care about." He might no longer call himself king, but Widukind still carried himself as one. "I had thought there might be delays given the number of projects you seem to be financing. As I understand, such a construction effort will be no small task."

It wouldn't be. Saxony was not a small kingdom, and there were swaths of it that were too exposed for my liking. What would serve as the shield against Rome would be high walls connected by a dozen forts. Costly to build, and expensive to maintain.

"The security of my empire is paramount. My other projects are important, but Saxony is where we share a border with our greatest rival. I will spare no expense to see it secure." It was a necessary expense. The rest of my borders were secured by petty kingdoms, and the Khazars had yet to recover from their civil war, though I expected they would soon. Meaning that when the time for war against Rome came, Saxony would be the doorway for our invasion or the battlefield for our defense.

Widukind chuckled. It was a warm sound, "The raid was quite the success, then."

"Jasmine has stopped scolding me about the state of the treasury," I returned with a smile. "For now, at least."

The projects I had set in motion were still going strong. The King's Road was nearing completion -- from the tip of Denmark, all the way around the Baltic Sea, to the shore of Sweden, a single road connected all of my kingdoms. Though, branches of the main artery would still be under construction for another decade, further binding the towns and cities that were being developed. Resources were being exploited, hubs of production were turning those resources into products that were then sold.

Widukind chuckled again, louder this time. "You've come a long way," Widukind voiced without prompting. "How long ago was it when you stood before me as a child in the service of another?"

"... Sixteen years, I think," I mused. Two years fighting against Francia. A year of respite in Norway and reuniting with my family. Another three years in the Mediterranean. A year as King of Norway. Another three securing my empire and forging kingdoms from squabbling tribes. Five long years of ruling them before spending a year in Britannia.

I was in my thirties. No longer a young man, even if I wasn't an old one.

I couldn't help a soft laugh of amusement from escaping me, "In a few years, I'll be the same age as my father when he died." A strange thought. Father had seemed so much older in my memories. Wiser too. For a moment I hated Horrik and Thorfin anew, realizing now just how short they had cut his life. How much more time he had to live alongside all of us.

"Back then, I knew you were destined to change things, but I never dreamed that you would change things this much," Widukind recalled fondly.

"I hadn't either. Not until my time in Rome," I admitted. "There is still more to do, I'm afraid. I won't be able to rest easily for another fifteen years at least." Probably twenty. Maybe even thirty.

It brought my thoughts toward my succession, and I had to swallow a sigh there. It was… disappointing for a number of reasons that Ragnar had confessed his lack of interest in becoming my heir to his mother, who had quietly passed his intent on to me. In part because Ragnar hadn't felt comfortable expressing such things to me. But also because he had all the makings of a fine king.

Alba would do well under his leadership, of that I was certain. Unfortunately, the kingdom of Alba was the extent of his ambition.

My other children were of course candidates to become my heir. All of them promising. Magnus had distinguished himself in Britannia. Bjorn and Radahn were still young, but brimming with potential. Scáthach and Aífe had little interest in rulership, but they still had the capacity for it. However, at that moment, my thoughts drifted to my youngest son.

Hakon was less than a year old. It would be a decade before I would even be able to tell if he had the temperament to become the Allvaldr. By that time, his siblings would be adults and likely with children of their own. It would be another decade before he would be ready to assume to throne as a man of twenty. Yet…

All my children were smart. They applied that intelligence in different ways, of course, but all of my children were immensely intelligent. Hakon, however, was an anomaly. An exceptional one. By the time he was three months old, he was already crawling. At six, he was attempting to walk. He didn't know many words, but there was a sharp awareness in his eyes and behind them was a ravenous intelligence. Within a few months, I expected him to be speaking in simple but complete sentences.

It was too much pressure to place on a child. A baby. One whose future was so unknown at this time. Still, I found myself considering him as a viable heir.

There was a knock at the door followed by a servant speaking, "King Haldur requests an audience."

Widukind inclined his head to me, rising out of his seat without needing to be dismissed. "By your leave, Allvaldr." I returned the nod, and no sooner than he left, Haldur entered with a scowl.

"Read this," he commanded, presenting a letter to me. Taking it with a raised eyebrow, it only took a few lines before I found myself scowling alongside him.

The letter was from Charlemagne. One concerning the ransom of his son Pepin.

Or the lack thereof.

"It was always a possibility," I said, setting the letter aside. Still, it was distasteful. "With the reunification of the Roman Empire, his succession has become complicated. Pepin's stay in Britannia was essentially banishment and ransoming him back just complicates his succession more."

Charlemagne had several children, many of them fathered upon his late wife. His current wife, Empress Irene had borne Charlemagne another son of the name Aurelian. A rather pointed name given that the last Roman Emperor of that name had borne the title of 'Restorer of the World.'

Which made their intent clear. Aurelian would inherit the Roman Empire.

Irene, prior to her remarriage, had most likely murdered her own son to simplify her succession. Charlemagne, however, had three sons: Charles the Younger, Carloman, who was later known as Pepin, and Louis. Pepin the Elder was a hunchback, and while he hadn't ever been formally disinherited, he had been shuffled to the side.

Now that Charlemagne had a child with Irene and he had lived long enough to escape the deadly times as an infant, it was a question of what Charlemagne would do with his other sons. Would he set them aside? Would he take his wife's route?

What would his sons do when they understood that rather than an empire that should have been theirs by right, they instead inherited nothing?

"Doesn't make it sit any better," Haldur complained with a sigh. There was a bubbling frustration in his tone. "Even with a twisted spine like that, a father should at least give a damn about his blood. For appearances' sake, if nothing else."

It had cost my brother leverage when the kings of my empire spoke of dividing the spoils. The son of the Emperor of Rome should have made a fine prize. An expensive one too. Cripple or not, asking for his weight in silver would have been a more than fair price for a ransom.

However, Charlemagne had spent the better part of two decades hiding Pepin's existence. I doubted that the common noble had known Pepin still lived long before he was banished to Britannia.

I also knew what made Haldur's ire rise about being rebuffed. It wasn't solely about the money. Nor was it his lost leverage. It was about power.

All of my kings were kept under my thumb through assets and debts. The mines that I built, the farmland that was cleared, the villages, towns, cities, and the roads that connected them all -- all of them were funded by the crown, and it was only natural that the crown would recoup its investment. That came in the form of higher taxes, percentages of outputs, and ownership of the right titles that secured my grip over the kingdoms. It wasn't something that would last forever, but I didn't need it to. Just long enough for the foundations to settle.

It limited the amount of wealth the kings could gain. All the more so as the realization had settled in that the neighbors whom they raided for extra wealth had become their allies. Or that their dreams of expansion were curtailed by the wall of lesser kingdoms that paid us homage, and were thus under our collective protection, with steep consequences for attacking them.

Some, like my brother, were chaffing under those restrictions.

"What will you do with him?" I asked, swallowing an offer. In the end, he was Haldur's prisoner, not mine. My ability to influence his thinking was limited… and now that I knew Charlemagne had formally washed his hands of his eldest son, I had less reason to.

An unhappy grunt escaped Haldur, and he sensed my position. He didn't bring this letter to me so I could see how cruel Charlemagne could be. He hoped I would offer to leverage my position on his behalf. "He's a cripple, but as far as anyone tells the story, he was half the brains in Britannia. Speaking with him myself, I can believe it." Haldur scratched at his beard before a contemplative expression appeared. As if he just now had the thought and not hours before he entered my office.

"He is clever. And every king has need of a clever fool," Haldur voiced. He was attempting to goad me into taking action, and I had to swallow a sigh.

It was tempting. The position of a fool was a dangerous one. They often served as a mouthpiece for a lord or king, saying the king's thoughts and other things a king wouldn't be allowed to say without incurring insults. It wasn't a practice I indulged in, largely because I had no need of it.

However, it was also a position of ridicule. To play the part of a fool, one had to behave as a fool.

Turning a son of Charlemagne, disgraced or not, into such a thing would be a mighty insult to the Roman Emperor. An insult that would demand a rebuttal. That told me Haldur didn't understand our position.

"I can't say that is what I would do, brother, but he is your prisoner. As is your right," I told him. Haldur swallowed a frown but offered no comment on the decision.

The war with Charlemagne was coming. That was a foregone conclusion. The only questions were when and who would make the first move?

It was something that I had anticipated for years, as I'm sure Charlemagne had. His reunified empire had enough time to bind together. My empire's foundations had some time to settle. Neither of us was ready for the war to come, and we likely wouldn't be for another decade. However, in the time between, we would attempt to goad the other into making the first move before they were ready to act.

Turning his hunchback son into a jester wouldn't be the insult that drove Charlemagne to war, but it would drive him to act.

So, distasteful or not, I would permit it.

When it was clear that I wouldn't act on his behalf, Haldur's enthusiasm for an audience waned sharply. He didn't immediately dismiss himself, but the matters we spoke of next were nothing of substance. Within fifteen minutes, I found myself alone in my office once more, feeling a degree of restlessness.

My thoughts lingered on the topic. The question of succession. Enough so that the pile of reports about increases in food production to match the surplus of population from the raid and the returning warriors from the Mediterranean couldn't hold my attention. Pushing them aside, I found myself standing up and making my way through the palace.

I needed to move around a bit to clear my head. To focus.

The gardens were the domain of my wives, who often used them as a neutral ground when meeting dignitaries. Some fresh air would do me good, I figured, strolling through them. Winter was fast approaching, so it would be some time before the flowers were in bloom again, so I savored the sight while I could.

My arrival didn't go unnoticed, "Father!" Radahn exclaimed before he just about knocked my legs out from underneath me by tackling me from behind. "Are you done being busy, yet?"

"For the moment," I said, ruffling his hair, and we walked together. Radahn took large lumbering steps to match my pace, holding my hand without a care in the world. Careless and free. It was an innocence that Ragnar never had. He had always been a reserved boy. Clever, polite, but reserved.

How much of that was simply his nature, and how much was it a result of my expectations weighing on him? I'd never thought to ask. Never considered that I needed to. My eldest was still young. He might have his armring, but he was still very much a boy who didn't realize how young he was. While I wouldn't discount him as the heir yet, as he had plenty of growing to do and could very well change his mind before I had to formally announce another heir…

But given that he was the son of myself and Astrid, his stubbornness was to be expected.

"Radahn," I spoke up, bringing my son's attention to me. "Would you want to be the Allvaldr one day?"

Even without saying a word, Radahn's expression betrayed such a visceral disgust that one would think he had just stepped in dog shit. "Yuck," he summarized his thoughts on the matter in a word and an exaggerated shake of his head. "Why would I? All you do is sit in your office all day. It's boring."

Well, he wasn't wrong. Still, I exhaled a weak laugh, accepting the answer for what it was. "Then what do you want to do?" I asked him, stroking his hair. Guilt churned in my guts when I realized I had never asked Ragnar the same thing. Or Magnus.

"I'm going to be an adventurer!" Radhan proclaimed, puffing out his chest. "Me and Bjorn decided that we're going to explore the world! Bjorn is going to explore everything to the West, and I'm going to explore everything to the East!"

There was a genuinely excited babble as he spoke quickly, almost as if he were racing to get the words out. "I want to go see the horselords! And that China place that Gyatso told me about. And I want to see what's beyond it!"

I took a breath and let it out slowly, finding myself smiling while I walked with my son through the gardens. "It sounds like a fine dream, son."

A fine dream indeed.

...

#7,699
It didn't come to a surprise to Pepin that his father had formally washed his hands of him. His father's feelings for him were rather obvious when he had a younger brother renamed Pepin. From the moment of his birth, when he'd killed his own mother as he was brought into the world, Charlemagne had shunned him. He was kept out of sight. To any and all, Pepin had been a stillborn. Of course, such a secret wasn't a perfectly kept one.

Charlemagne was soft hearted enough to let him live, at least. To let him stay in the palace, even if they rarely ever shared a room together. He was indulged when he sought to learn, granted tutors and texts. However, as his father had more children, the shadows he was hidden away in grew longer. Darker. His exile in all but name had been the end of it. Pepin never expected to set foot in Rome or see his father or any of his siblings again for the remainder of his life.

All of which held true.

What he didn't expect was to be made a fool.

Pepin looked down at the vibrant motley attire that was tailor made for him. One of several sets, all of which were inside of a trunk in the back of the carriage he rode inside of. He wasn't certain if that was thoughtful or if it just added an extra layer to his humiliation.

He had time to dwell on the unexpected turn in his life. When King Haldur departed Miklagard with his army, family, and retinue, Pepin found himself brought along. They crossed the pass that Miklagard was built at the mouth of before riding up a long road towards where he would likely spend the rest of his life. However short that might be. It was a quality road, one that looked to be of Roman make, just without a few hundred years of neglect.

It was easy on his back, at least. Leaving him with the only torment being his thoughts and company.

His gaze remained affixed out the slant of a window. They had passed through a number of villages on the road, which weaved around shores, tall hills, deep valleys… everything looked new to his eyes, in a very literal sense. The houses possessed a vibrancy free of century old wood that sagged under hundreds of layers of paint trying to make them look better than the half rotten piles they were. Houses were made of clay brick or stone, uniformly built. The people living in them were peasants, but they carried themselves lighter than the peasants of Rome or Britannia.

Probably because they thought they were being ruled over by a living god. Pepin did imagine that would improve their disposition when they were told to do something.

Their destination was in sight, and a hum of anxiety made his flesh itch. It wasn't Miklagard. Not even close. The city Siegfried was building was one of absolute absurdity. He'd call it impossible if he hadn't stayed in the city for a week to celebrate the ravishing of several petty kingdoms and a battle that would forever scar their collective memory. Even if Siegfried never stepped foot on Britannia again, a hundred years from now, a flea ridden peasant would use his name interchangeably with the Devil's.

The city of Stockholm was not the largest Pepin had seen, but given that some ten years ago there had been a fishing village in its place, it was quite remarkable. It boasted a population of some thirty thousand -- small in comparison to Miklagard, certainly, but a perfectly respectable city all the same.

It had tall walls made of stone and access to the sea, with a budding expansion growing around the gates leading into the seat of King Haldur's power. With the nature of the tall houses, the city was built up rather than wide while the land around it was cultivated as farmland, orchards, or anything else that would fit.

Pepin found himself frowning when they rode through the city in a triumph, similar to the one Siegfried subjected him to in the capital. That was to be expected. It was part of being a king. What irritated him was the palace itself. While it couldn't compare to the vast opulence of the Emperor's, it was equal to anything Pepin had stayed in. Meaning it was equal to anything in what was Francia.

The capital being so grand, that Pepin could accept with little issue. The capital was meant to be the most glorious city as it served as the seat of the empire. Some random city that served as the seat of power for what amounted to a Duke with a crown? Even if he was the Emperor's brother, it left a foul taste in his mouth. Mercifully, he was largely forgotten once they arrived at the palace, but Pepin knew that was not a mercy which would last long.

His quarters were simple, but spacious. More befitting a prince than a fool. That was something of a relief, though it did place him in a strange predicament of not understanding where he stood with King Haldur. For the low born, being made a fool could be considered an honor. Even those of lower nobility. But to a prince, even a disinherited one? That was less an honor and more of an egregious insult.

"Allow me to unpack your things, milord," a short blonde haired woman dressed as a maid quickly offered. Pepin accepted the offer with a nod -- bending over for long periods of times was as painful as repeatedly bending and straightening his back. Something that he had attempted to ignore as a younger man in a vain attempt to straighten his spine so he could be another regular boy.

Hobbling to a window, it was unbarred. Though also high enough that Pepin had little hope of survival should he try to jump. Climbing down was a possibility, however. Secure the blankets around an anchor, tie them together as a rope, and he could shimmy down the side of the palace. He wasn't sure what he would do from there, but escape was an enticing thought.

"Can I offer refreshments, milord? Wine? Ale?" The same maid spoke as she unpacked the uniform that was inflicted upon him.

"Water," Pepin accepted. "And an explanation, if you have one."

"Milord?" She asked, going still. The same stillness all servants did when something unexpected was asked of them or they weren't sure if they made a mistake or not.

"I am the king's fool, am I not?" Pepin asked, turning away from the window that was tempting to just throw himself out of and be done with it. "I am sad to say my education in my father's court didn't include what would be expected of me in such an… esteemed position."

There was a flicker of nervousness in her eyes, "I cannot know King Haldur's mind, milord, but… it… would shame him to have… an ill-trained fool." A logical answer. Perhaps he could expect a tutor on how to juggle. Or perhaps to breathe fire like a fire dancer. The prospect almost managed to sound exciting if it weren't for the fact he would be performing for an audience.

"I see," Pepin acknowledged with a small nod of his head. "But if I am to be a fool, then why are you calling me milord?" Why the address? Why this room? Why was he not paraded on the streets like a trophy?

The maid seemed uncertain for a brief second, "Because you are still a prince, milord." She bowed her head before retreating a half step, "I shall return with your water." He almost felt bad given how she half fled the room, leaving his trunk empty and open. It was beneath him to do so, but Pepin moved to close it and shove it under the bed, only to pause when he saw the trunk wasn't entirely empty.

At the very bottom was a note written in Frankish.

'You have more friends here than you know, Prince Pepin.'

His gaze lingered on the note for a long second, his mind churning through a number of possibilities. The first that came to mind was that it was a trap. The servants posed as friends and eventually co-conspirators when he decided to make a move -- whatever move that might be. He might ask for a key, or some rations, or a window of opportunity… Then, when he decided to act, he would step directly into the waiting ambush.

Or…

Or his father hadn't completely washed his hands of him. The network of spies his father built up across Scandinavia could be offering a helping hand. A potent unseen weapon that could make his stay in this land more… tolerable.

Pepin didn't know what the case was, and he doubted he would until he tested the loyalty of these so-called friends.

Plucking the note from the trunk, he brought it to his mouth and swallowed the slip of parchment to destroy any evidence of its existence. Hardly a pleasant taste, but one he had long gotten used to.

Just as he would grow used to his present occupation. From the prince of an empire to the advisor of a petty king and now, the fool of a barbarian. Few had managed to fall further than he in life…

But so long as he lived, there were chances to rise once more.


…
​

Winter came for my empire fast and hard with the weather turning for the worst mere days after the various armies departed my capital. The people were saying the gods held back winter for a few more days so I could return, but the truth of it was, we had cut it close with our return.

For so much of my life, I had hated winter. It reminded me all too much of listening to my older brother Ragnar's wet and weak coughs getting weaker by the day. Until one morning he was silent, and we all understood what it meant. I recalled the hard dirt that we had to bury his bones in. My father's furious silence. My mother's quiet weeping when she thought no one would overhear. When I thought of winter, that was what my mind turned to.

There were other memories that bubbled to the surface now, when my capital and empire was blanketed under a layer of fresh snow. Not all of them were good, such as the desecration of Verdun and the piles of corpses left in a macabre display. But, as of late, there were a few good memories to balance out the bad. My children playing in the snow. The rare few quiet moments I stole away with my wives with a warm drink and a pretty view.

I think I might even come to like winter, because it was the season where my responsibilities seemed to vanish like smoke in the wind. The number of courtiers demanding my attention dramatically reduced as most simply couldn't make the trip to ask for my time. The mad flurry of last minute talks and negotiations for the onset of winter were over as everyone made sure they had enough grain and foodstuffs to ensure their people wouldn't starve.

Given how much the population had grown because of migrations, it was a real concern even with the farming techniques and fishing fleets we had spread across the Baltic.

Leaving me with a winter morning with nothing to do but to spend time with my family.

"What does that rune mean, Hakon?" I asked the babe barely eight months old. He glanced over at the rune, a pair of carved blocks in his hands that he chewed in thought.

"Sun," Hakon answered dutifully, immediately losing interest in the rune in favor of stacking the block in a pile of similar blocks he used to teeth on. His voice was accented with a clumsy tongue and the lack of teeth certainly didn't help. Still, his answer was clear enough.

"If the child was born to any other, I would call it unnatural," an elderly Alexios spoke to me. My tutor in Rome that turned into my family's tutor was already an old man when he first arrived in my homeland. It had been a decade since. His mind was still as sharp as any I knew, but his body was failing him. "It's not just that he speaks. He retains the knowledge. Absorbs it like a sponge. The dullest of your children are at least quick. The brightest are fiercely intelligent. Little Hakon here… he is a true genius, Siegfried. Of the like I have never seen before."

I was aware. I had enough of a hand in my children's education to know what normal development looked like. This was not that. It was almost unnerving how keen his mind was, even when he smashed his blocks together because he liked the noise.

"I've started him on mathematics -- simple addition and subtraction. While I can't be certain that he truly understands the work, at the very least he's memorized the answers." At my sharp look, Alexios cleared his throat. "Prince Hakon. What is one and one?"

"Two," Hakon answered, losing interest in the blocks. While Hakon pivoted, crawling towards me and my waiting hands, I saw Alexios' pointed look over the child's head.

A clever son was a blessing. A genius was… worrying.

"I'm worried about the pressure," I admitted, placing Hakon in my lap and he played with the loose fabric of my sleeves. "He has immense potential, but too much pressure for him to realize it will do more harm than good."

To that, the old scholar let out a dismissive snort. "He is your son, Siegfried. That pressure will always be there."

I could only sigh in response. He wasn't wrong. "Stay the course," I instructed. "Teach him as fast as he can learn. Nurture his curiosity and interests. If he is to realize his potential, he needs to learn to love learning for the sake of it."

"I'll do so to the best of my ability. But, I suspect you'll be repeating those instructions to my successor," Alexios said with a graceful smile.

"Don't say that, old friend. You have more years in you yet," I replied with a grim acceptance that it likely would be but a few years.

"I do," Alexios agreed. "And I shall make the most of them by imparting all that I know with the time I have left into little Hakon. However, that means resigning from the university."

My first instinct was to refuse his resignation from the position, foolish as that was. The university in Miklagard and the second in Gotland were in their infancy, as much as Hakon was. They were a very foreign idea to Scandinavia as we'd had nothing like a university before. It was gaining momentum as my people were sending their sons and daughters to it, treating university as a place to gain an apprenticeship that they otherwise wouldn't receive.

However, even with all of the texts and knowledge gathered in their halls, it wasn't yet a place of learning. Where discoveries were made and we learned answers to questions we had yet to ask. There was no one I trusted more to oversee the university's development.

Still, I swallowed down that initial reaction even if it felt like swallowing a stone. "I understand," I admitted. If Alexios was a young man, then he'd do both. But his beard had long since grayed. His time was limited. "Have you chosen your successor?"

"A girl by the name Eivor. Married to the lad that made your crown," Alexios informed. "Started out learning how to smith, but she took a mile when given an inch. On the young side, but that means she has the energy to herd that den of squabbling cats."

"I will speak to her, but if she has your confidence, then it is a formality," I replied. Standing up with Hakon tucked against me, I heard a suspiciously loud thump down the hall which told me my younger sons had found more trouble. Alexios smiled, inclining his head to me, knowing that I had better go before those boys set the palace on fire. However, I was delayed by a sudden cry from Hakon.

"Block," Hakon requested, half lunging out of my arms for the pile.

"Which one?" I asked the boy, making him think on it for a long few seconds. Long enough that I wondered if he understood.

"Blue," Hakon declared with the force of a revelation. Chuckling, I picked up a blue block and handed it to him so he could gnaw on it in peace. Stepping outside of the room, I glanced down the hall to see that the delay had given Radahn and Bjorn time to escape. With a sigh, I trailed after them, but not before lifting the display that they had knocked over.

The servants bowed as we passed while my royal guard dutifully followed in my shadow. Sometimes I was barely aware of them. I'd never expected to, but at some point, you grew deaf to the sound of rustling chain mail. While Radahn and Bjorn had managed to escape the consequences of their actions, for now, I instead stumbled upon Jill and Magnus in a solar.

Jill wore a serious expression when she caught sight of me while Magnus craned his head back, looking equally serious. I felt the tension shift immediately with my arrival, so I broke the silence that followed the conversation I had intruded on. "What has happened?"

Her expression tightened, "The messenger has not reached you yet?"

"If he had, I wouldn't be asking," I replied, noting the weight in her tone and already knowing I wouldn't like what I was about to hear. And when she spoke, I was more right than I had about anything else in my life.

"There has been an attempt on Harun Al-Rashid's life that might still take it," Jill answered, making a stone form in my gut. "Hadi al-Gaib has been accused, and while Harun lies on his sickbed, Hadi has been declared a traitor to the Caliphate. Which stands on the precipice of a civil war."

…So much for my peaceful winter.

#7,734
"No. No, no, no." Hadi replied with a wave of his hand. "We cannot bring in Allvaldr Siegfried or his forces. That turns this from an internal issue into a war that we are not prepared for." That being said, it was quite possible that this would become a war all the same. Charlemagne was a cunning and opportunistic creature, and there were few opportunities greater than an enemy that was exhausted from fighting itself.

"We cannot accept this inquiry. If you go to Baghdad, you will not return," Sheba stressed, and Hadi agreed with her wholeheartedly. The entire situation was a mess with no correct course of action, just ones with greater and lesser consequences.

Hadi rubbed his eyes, feeling a sharp headache that had not left him since the news had been delivered. Learning that Harun had been attacked -- stabbed with a poisoned dagger, barely escaping with his life intact had been an unwelcome surprise. Learning that several members within Harun's court had named him as the assassin was even more unwelcome. The only good news he received that day was that Harun had survived, but languished on his sickbed, barely lucid in the brief moments he regained consciousness.

"We cannot afford to have a civil war," Hadi sighed.

"We can't," Sheba agreed sweetly. Always a prelude to something he deeply didn't wish to hear. "But our options are limited. Guilt is much easier to prove than innocence. The court has already named you guilty. We gain nothing by meeting with them on their terms. Accepting that means we aren't beholden to proving your innocence in their eyes. Only Harun's, should he still live. Marshall our armies, meet them on the field, and deliver their heads to the Caliph as proof."

That was the simplest course of action. An appealing course of action. Just not one without consequences.

Charlemagne's forces in Hispania had been bolstered. That in itself wasn't anything out of place. Since Hadi became Emir of Hispania they had raided and attempted to dislodge each other every year since. Charlemagne attempted to bleed him for control over the rest of the landmass while Hadi attempted to push him back to the Pyrenees Mountains. Neither had much in the way of success, beyond a pushed border here or there. The end result being their border had perhaps the most forts for every mile in the entire world.

The timing, however, was suspicious. Even if Charlemagne didn't have a hand in Harun's near assassination, he was well poised to take advantage of it. Hadi had little doubt that the moment his armies left his domain, Charlemagne would strike with as much force as he could muster. Meaning that he would either have to risk losing his domain entirely, or face the lords who named him as the assassin with an army at half strength.

"We must do something, Hadi," Sheba said, grabbing hold of his wrist, and the action betrayed how worried she was. "We cannot simply wait for this to go away."

"No," Hadi agreed, a deep frown tugging at his lips. "No, we cannot."

The internal workings of the Caliphate were something he never wished to be aware of as a younger man, but such knowledge has been foisted upon him because of his position. A position that gave him the perception of vast influence, but the reality was that he was distant from the inner workings of the court in Baghdad. What he did have was a very large army that Harun could count on.

Something the true assassins knew.

For the past ten years, he had ruled over Hispania. He remained the regent over the Egyptian territories, though that would thankfully end quite soon as Asad would soon be considered a man in the eyes of the law. However, until then, those resources were his to draw upon. As a vassal, he was exceptionally powerful. The titles Harun bestowed upon him only solidified that image.

He served as the cornerstone for Harun's power base. Present but distant. A hammer that loomed overhead, just out of sight. That lessened the other nobility's influence, allowing Harun to push through reforms to avoid unwanted strings in deals. One family in particular felt the loss in influence more keenly than others, even if they hadn't lost any official position.

The Barkmids.

They were the administrative backbone of the Abbasid Dynasty, having served as stewards for generations even before the Abbasids took power. The family was vast, well-connected, well-positioned, but not well-trusted. Not when there were so many voices telling Harun that he shouldn't, even if they hadn't done anything overt to deserve that mistrust.

Hadi had no proof that it was the Barkmids. Only the knowledge that Harun had begun to entertain the thought of removing Jafar from his position as Visier.

"We need decisive action. We cannot afford a half measure," Sheba continued, and Hadi sank into the pile of cushions he sat on.

"... I hate decisive action…" He muttered, wishing the cushions would just swallow him up. It was almost tempting to convert to Hinduism, because at least then he could blame the rotten luck of this life on his being a bastard in his last one. Blaming Allah didn't exactly seem wise, and even if he did shake his fist to the one above all, Hadi was increasingly convinced that Allah would just laugh at his misfortune. If he didn't have a hand in it.

Despite the tension, Sheba laughed. It was a beautiful sound, and he still wasn't at all comfortable with how much sway it had over him. "I know, my dear husband. But you have risen high. That comes with responsibilities."

Responsibilities he never asked for. Didn't want, either. He just couldn't refuse without insulting Harun, and Harun was the one reason why the other Emirs hadn't killed him, razed his lands, and did their best to erase him from history.

"Why can't people just… calm down?" He complained, sinking into the cushions further. Why did King Hoffer have to go kidnap the Pope and sack Rome? Why did Charlemagne whip his people up into such a religious frenzy that they started to sate their bloodlust on each other for worshiping God a little differently? Why couldn't Siegfried stop raiding entire countries to the point that he took the nails that held up their houses, and then took the houses as well for good measure? Why couldn't the Emirs see he was perfectly happy doing absolutely nothing on the fringes of the Caliphate? Why couldn't Harun do what every other Caliph before him did and just indulge in luxury and his harem?

Why did everyone seem completely determined to start a war none of them were ready to fight?

"We live in an era of greatness, Hadi. Empires are rising, and great men lead them. The world has run out of room, so one must fall." That was exactly what he was afraid of. He had done some light reading on the fall of empires, and the word that could best summarize them was 'messy'. If he were generous and used two words, then 'senseless slaughter' would also be apt.

"I'd rather live in dull times," he replied, accepting Sheba's embrace as she pulled his head to her breasts. Having a beautiful wife caused him no end of trouble, but there were times when he didn't mind. Hadi felt her chuckle before he sighed. As much as he would like to continue complaining -- and he deeply wished to complain until the sun set -- action was necessary. "Diplomacy is a dead end. Even if I could reason with them, they know they stand to gain much with my death."

Sheba nodded, running her hands through his hair.

"However, I need to know if this is a coup or not," Hadi continued. A curse of being on the fringe of the Caliphate meant news was slow to reach him. As soon as the accusation was delivered alongside the news of Harun's near assassination, Hadi had dispatched spies and messengers to gauge the temperament of Baghdad. To get in contact with Harun's mother. However, it would be weeks before he had an answer and he needed to act before then. "And if it is a coup, I need to know who set it in motion, who supports it, and who is the face."

"Then we march?" Sheba pressed, clearly wanting direct action. That was no surprise. She was chosen to be his wife because of her strong loyalty to the Abbasid Dynasty as much as she had her own noble lineage.

"If we march, then we will lose Hispania," Hadi replied. "The eastern coast is weak and Charlemagne knows it. When we are distracted, he will claim the coast down to the southern shore. We will be cleaved in half and isolated." Their current borders were well fortified, but it took one moment of weakness to change that.

"Will he be able to?" Sheba questioned, knowing how he thought by now. Despite his best efforts. "Siegfried has pillaged Britannia of all that glitters and most that doesn't. Then he went back for everything else. He humiliated Charlemagne by taking his son and giving him to his brother to be a jester. His own lands are in a brewing turmoil with the sack of Rome and the general unrest with the unification with the Eastern Roman Empire. The build up you fear could be a bluff."

"It could be," Hadi admitted. "It's likely that it is. But I fear that for all the reasons you listed, it will stop being a bluff. Few things silence detractors such as victory, after all, and I don't wish to serve him one upon a silver platter."

"That would raise the Wolf-Kissed's ire. We have an alliance," she pointed out.

"He has an alliance with Harun. Who I am accused of trying to assassinate," Hadi corrected with a frustrated sigh. "He is not beholden to defend us. Charlemagne knows this."

"But he could," Sheba stressed. "Siegfried recognizes you as a man of honor. Charlemagne also knows that. They seek to make war with each other, and Siegfried goads him. He may hesitate in fear that he will trigger a war with Scandinavia."

That was… possible. It entirely depended on how eager for war Charlemagne thought Siegfried was. And how ready Charlemagne was for that war.

The former, Hadi didn't know. He couldn't. However, he did have suspicions about the latter.

Charlemagne sought to restore the Roman Legions alongside the Roman Empire. Vast professional armies that were well armed, armored, and disciplined. A far cry from the current levies that he used to fight with. Siegfried had well and truly put an end to the days of levy armies. He proved without a shadow of a doubt that smaller but better equipped and trained armies could defeat a significantly larger force.

It was a message Hadi had heard loud and clear. Charlemagne evidently heard it too, alongside Harun. Every empire in the world it seemed was in the middle stages of reforming their military, creating standing professional armies. Which very well could be a contributing factor to the attempt on Harun's life. After all, Harun had been in the early stages of creating an army that answered only to the Caliph when the attempt came.

The Emirs feared the balance of power shifting. Charlemagne worked more slowly, treading carefully to avoid a similar fate. Siegfried, however, could blaze the trail simply because he had already so radically changed the balance of power in Scandinavia that a standing army was just one more thing.

"I suppose… if we gamble and lose, I can stop being Emir," Hadi mused, setting on a course of action. It would be a shame to waste the efforts he'd spent on keeping everyone happy so they wouldn't assassinate him. A lesson Harun really should have learned. But, Hadi imagined people would have less cause to assassinate him in the first place without the title hanging over his head like a blade.

Sheba laughed, pinching his cheek. "You aren't that lucky, my beloved. If the situation is as dire as I think, there will be plenty of emirs left short of heads and their positions left in need of filling by the end of this." That certainly made the smile slip from his face.

Still, he lingered in her embrace for a moment longer than he really should. Longer than they could afford. It was with the greatest reluctance he managed to extract himself from her arms and rise to his feet to go about doing what needed to be done. Emerging from his private chambers, he found the two men that he expected to see.

Khalid and Zafir. The former had shot up like a weed, growing from a boy to a man. He looked the part of a conquering hero. Enough so that when Khalid met dignitaries with him, it wasn't uncommon for them to mistake him for the Emir. Tall, well built, handsome, with a well groomed beard.

"Our men are ready to march," Khalid started, already knowing what decision they had come to. He probably asked the walls or something. All these years later, Hadi still didn't quite grasp how Khalid's ability worked. Just that it did, and he had an uncanny talent for knowing things he had no right to know.

Hadi nodded, the pair walking with him. "We'll gather on the eastern coast. A fleet will be gathered to transport us directly into the heartlands."

Zafir offered a sharp glance, "During winter?" It was a dangerous move, but one undercut by their ally's ability in the Mediterranean.

"King Hoffer can read the weather like no other man," Hadi replied as they walked. "And he is licking his wounds after his lost territory. He needs a victory to cement his place amongst his pirate kingdom. We are in a position to provide him one." He only knew of the Norse king's ability because of Khalid's. That, and that it was apparently bestowed upon him by Siegfried.

The implications of that were a headache that Hadi didn't want to think about, so he didn't. While ignorance could be bliss, so too could willful blindness.

"You would trust him with our lives?" Zafir questioned, sounding doubtful of the decision. However, it was Khalid who answered.

"They expect us to march," Khalid said. "It is safer that way, but longer. It gives the culprits in the capital a chance to solidify their support." Exactly right. It would also narrow the window of opportunity for Charlemagne to act with his departure. The Roman Empire was vast. Just as it took weeks or months for a message to reach Hadi's ears, so too would it take to reach Charlemagne.

Ideally, by the time Charlemagne was willing to act on his departure, he would already be on his way back home.

'Four months,' Hadi thought to himself. Winter was their shield, but come Spring, his enemies would be able to act with impunity. "It'll take a month alone to gather the troops. A week to sail to the heartlands. From there, we'll know who is a friend and who is a foe. And who is simply too cowardly to act."

Zafir nodded, accepting the reasoning with a nod of his head. "And who shall rule in your stead if you mean to answer these accusations personally?"

If the people would accept it, Hadi would place Sheba in charge. She had the mind for it. More than he ever did. "You will," Hadi answered instead, feeling a flash of amusement when Zafir nearly tripped over his own feet. "You are my right hand in all things. Respected by the army and our courtiers. Should Rome stir trouble while we are away, then there is no one I trust more to secure our backs."

"I am a maimed man," Zafir felt compelled to argue. Hadi was envious of his ability to deny a promotion. However, if he was forbidden from denying one, then Zafir had to suffer alongside him.

"An arm you lost fighting against Siegfried the Wolf-Kissed." There were some days that he still woke up in cold sweats from his brief encounters with the man. The older he grew, the more absurd it seemed that he survived their clashes. Especially with everything he said and did since their squabble on Crete.

"Take heart, Zafir. Our lord paid good money to ensure the stories of your heroism spread. None see a maimed man when they look at you. They saw a man who survived the Wolf-Kissed." Khalid seconded, making Zafir narrow his eyes into a glare.

"That was you?" Zafir muttered, annoyed but with acceptance. Which was good enough for Hadi. His lips pressed into a thin line once they arrived at their destination. A war room. One complete with maps and models of the city that served as his capital. Madrid was located near the center of Hispania and close to the border they shared with Rome. It was something of a gamble, but it gave him an advantage over Charlemagne when it came to reacting to incursions.

Avoiding the question, Hadi began to grab maps to plot the campaign. "Luckily, we're facing a temperate winter. It shouldn't impact the length of the journey; for the sake of time, we shouldn't pull from our fringes."

"We need to muddle the message before it has a chance to take root. The men will be hesitant to fight for a man who tried to assassinate their Caliph." Most likely untrue. Given how eager the people of his domain raided what had been their neighbors a decade ago, Hadi was convinced he led a nation exclusively filled with bloodthirsty warmongers.

Still, Hadi saw his point. As did Khalid, "Then let the message spread that we fight for the safety of the Caliph, and that he has made no accusation. It comes from the mouths of jealous Emirs, who muster their armies without his blessing. Even if they are honestly misled, many still overreach." A fine enough message. One that would suit their ends… and if they were particularly unlucky, it could very well be the truth.

Such an approach would naturally lend to a messy aftermath. You couldn't exactly roll back on an accusation of coup, particularly if half of the upper nobility were backing it. No matter what, the aftermath was going to be messy. Politically inconvenient at best, and a disaster in the making at worst. The Eastern Roman Empire was probing to expand, the Khazars were sorting out their succession -- a lengthy civil war could very well be the death of the Caliphate.

"We name Jafar, the Vizier, as the culprit," Hadi continued. "Every story needs a villain, and better him than one of the powerful Emirs." Harun would be displeased if Jafar wasn't truly the mastermind behind the supposed coup, but his mother would approve wholeheartedly. And Hadi was far more afraid of that woman than he was of Harun.

"He will serve," Zafir agreed, bringing stacks of parchment. Supplies, troops, equipment…

Hadi truly hated this room, but he was once more off to war.

...
