#7,762
"Emir Hadi al-Gaib," King Hoffer greeted him politely. It had been years since Hadi had last seen him, but the man really was unreasonably big. Hadi felt like a child in comparison. "Please, allow me to introduce our esteemed guest who shall be joining us this evening, Pope Adrian."

The pope didn't seem particularly happy about joining this private gathering in Sardinia. Hadi would even go as far as to say he seemed quite upset. Angry. Of the murderous variety. Still, a year of captivity would temper anyone's outbursts, and he didn't look mistreated. Just that he would rather be literally anywhere else.

"... My greetings, Pope Adrian. Peace be with you. And you, King Hoffer," Hadi said, accepting an offered seat. The pope's lips pressed into a thin line in an attempt to be as neutral as he could be. King Hoffer, for his part, simply laughed.

"I suspect peace is not what has brought you to my shores this day, Emir Hadi al-Gaib," he replied, taking a seat across from Hadi. There was a calculating glimmer in his eyes. As if he was trying to weigh how much he was worth. "No. Peace, I'm afraid, is a luxury out of your reach."

It wasn't a surprise that King Hoffer knew. He'd likely known about the accusations being leveled against him before Hadi did. So, he offered a thin smile. One not too dissimilar from the one Pope Adrain greeted him with. "Circumstances being what they are, I am inclined to agree with you." He would hardly be mustering his armies and taking a trip to Sardinia to handle negotiations personally if peace was an option. "I do hope that it goes without saying that I didn't do it."

"Of course," King Hoffer replied with a smile that didn't quite reach his eyes. "The Allvaldr holds you in high regard! I wouldn't dare think you would do something so base as attempt to assassinate your ruler." Then his smile grew a fraction, "And if you had, I would expect you to be better prepared to take advantage."

That was… something. Likely not a good something, but something nonetheless. "Then it would be my hope, King Hoffer, that you might be willing to help an innocent man clear his name and punish the perpetrators for the attempt on your ally Caliph Harun al-Rashid."

That was the wrong thing to say. Hadi saw it the moment the words left his mouth, "Ally. An interesting word to use. I must wonder where this steadfast ally was when I lost half of my kingdom." The territories of Italia and Cyrus.

"I was conducting the planned raids in Charlemagne's territory. The Caliph, I believe, was rebuffing Khalzar raids," Hadi answered, his tone even. His bitterness was expected. Counted on, even.

What he did not say was that the bitterness was entirely self inflicted. The raids Hadi had asked for were reasonable. King Hoffer was the one who escalated things to a full invasion, forcing Charlemagne to commit his forces in full. The lost territory, the evaporation of the core of his army… the blame for all of it could be traced back to Hoffer's own feet. However, kings weren't renowned for their ability to be self aware. Quite the opposite. So, King Hoffer needed someone to blame for his… misfortunes.

"However, if we had been made aware of the scope of your ambitions… While I cannot speak for the Caliph, I, of course, would have adjusted my plans. Expanded them in scope to push Charlemagne to the Perynes Mountains and threatened to go beyond them in the hopes he would go on the defensive to allow you to consolidate your territorial gains."

Hadi had told a number of lies during his life. However many was anyone's guess, but he was confident that it outnumbered the number of truths he had uttered by a factor of… at least ten. The words that just came out of his mouth were likely the single greatest lie that he had ever spoken. Because when he'd learned that King Hoffer was radically altering what should have been a simple raid, Hadi had simply smiled, thought, 'What a fool,' before taking a key fortress on an important hill.

He had no interest in battle. Even less interest in facilitating King Hoffer's kingdom of pirates that occasionally turned their fangs to his merchant vessels and coastal villages. Officially, King Hoffer disavowed such actions, but the fact of the matter was that he had a loose grip on his kingdom to begin with and it only got worse when that bastard Hjalmar took fifty thousand Norsemen back to Siegfried. The core of King Hoffer's support had been gutted.

Something they both knew.

"How regrettable," King Hoffer replied, his tone entirely neutral. He didn't fully believe the lie, but he didn't exactly doubt it either. Simply because it was true -- Hadi had prepared for a small raid. The kind of force needed to carry out that make-believe plan would require more prepared resources than he had. "As are our present circumstances."

"So they are," Hadi agreed.

There was a terse silence that fell over the room. Hadi watched King Hoffer ponder the information as well as his options. Which were limited. While he enjoyed an alliance with the Caliphate, it wasn't in the same scope as the one made with Scandinavia. Such protections came with strings that King Hoffer had refused. All the same, what alliance they did have wasn't likely to outlive Harun as Caliph.

"Your enemies are many," King Hoffer broke the silence. "Three Emirs have denounced you. They name you an assassin. An usurper. More shall join their chorus if they haven't already."

Hadi inclined his head to the king, "So they do."

"As our nations are close, they beseeched me to take action. To invite you to my hearth, betray you, before delivering you to them." He continued in an idle tone. Hadi did not react to the provocation, but Khalid did. He tensed, a hand resting on his scimitar as he looked to those in the room to gauge their threats.

"I hope they offered you a high price for your honor and dignity," Hadi replied, earning a bark of laughter from King Hoffer. It sounded genuine.

There was a faint twitch of his lips, a smile being smothered. "They offered me wealth. Trade concessions. And men."

"A high price," Hadi acknowledged. King Hoffer had need of them all. While his grip had always been weak over his dispersed kingdom of islands, he had been able to solidify control because a significant portion of his warriors were Norsemen as he was. Hot blooded idiots, but that was just something else they had in common. Serving a master who looked different, had different customs, and spoke a different language wasn't unthinkable, but for many, they wanted to see themselves reflected in their ruler.

King Hoffer still had supporters. Some ten thousand Norsemen remained, and while he'd lost the battle in the end, the wealth plundered from Italia had made him a living legend, and so many powerful chieftains offered him nominal support. However, his grip on islands like Crete or even Sicily was wavering. His authority challenged by pirates and warlords. Unless something drastic happened relatively soon, he would lose control over them entirely.

It was something Hadi rather looked forward to, if he were to be honest. Pirates were bad enough, but pirates with the resources King Hoffer commanded? They were a nightmare. Sheba had likely cursed them a thousand times and when she heard they had been crushed outside of Rome, she'd laughed so hard she had tears in her eyes. And while it was outside of his purview, Hadi did know that Harun desired control over the port of Norland -- influence primarily, but direct ownership would be preferable.

"A price that I would see matched," King Hoffer replied. Hadib would give him that much -- he preferred the direct request for a bribe.

"I cannot in good faith promise that I can match it," Hadi replied. "I cannot speak for the Caliph or what reward he might bestow." It wasn't what King Hoffer wanted to hear, but he didn't interject. "However, I can say this -- Caliph Harun al-Rashid intends to keep his father's promise. He will take the whole of Anatolia, and in doing so, it would be prudent to retake Cyrus."

There was a glimmer of interest, but not enough. King Hoffer wasn't a fool. He understood that territorial gains was not what he needed when he was losing his control over the territory he already possessed. "Additionally, I will be committed to pushing the Romans out of Hispania at the same time. An opportunity that Allvaldr Siegfried will surely not let go by, and while I cannot speak to what his plans are, I am certain he will give Charlemagne cause to look North. This would grant you an opportunity to retake your lost lands in Italia, if not the whole peninsula."

Which was the kind of victory that King Hoffer needed. Nothing washed away the stain of defeat like victory, after all. What's more, with the taking of Anatolia, King Hoffer's people would have far greater ease sailing into the Mediterranean from the Black Sea. That, in turn, would allow him to rebuild his support base.

"A fine picture you paint," King Hoffer replied. "When could I expect this opportunity?"

Hadi had no earthly idea. "This near assassination will have complicated matters, but so long as it is resolved cleanly, the timeline of five years should be held." That earned a twitch, telling Hadi that was too far out. He wanted something more immediate. "Which, I admit, is less than ideal. While I cannot speak for the Caliph, I am allowed to speak for the resources and concession of my own domain. Even if they are a lesser bounty than you would receive from my enemies."

King Hoffer hummed thoughtfully, stroking his long blonde beard. "You are an honest man, Hadi al-Gaib. I respect that." Hadi heard a but coming. "How many men can you muster?"

"... Twenty thousand in the short term," Hadi decided to answer.

"So, fifteen thousand," King Hoffer deduced. The true number was closer to seventeen thousand, but the fact remained that he was being generous with his estimation. "That would be a hundred ships. More for cavalry."

Hadi inclined his head ever so slightly, still waiting for the but. "I came here seeking quick passage to the Caliphate heartlands. Ideally using your ships." He admitted, and King Hoffer nodded, expecting nothing less.

"Our priests asked for an omen on the eve of your arrival. The gods look favorably upon the venture, as they have provided a passage for the journey." An outright lie, of course. But, then again, he had no idea how whatever magics were involved worked. He could be telling the truth. Hadi wasn't curious enough to find out. Or, he could simply be lying about the opportunity.

"... Your gods are kind," Hadi replied tersely. Something King Hoffer smiled at.

"At times," he replied. "But they are, as a rule, greedy. As am I." At least he acknowledged it. "The price your enemies offered was greater, but not high enough to buy my honor. What's more, while you are outnumbered, I will not wager against a man who faced the Allvaldr and survived to tell the tale."

Hadi couldn't take it any longer, "But." He supplied for the pirate king, and for the first time, his smile reached his eyes.

"But," King Hoffer agreed. "There are certain men and crews within my domain that I would see… removed. You will aid me in this." So that his hands would remain clean. If they just so happened to die in the fighting then it was the will of Allah. Or the gods.

Hadi wasn't particularly enthused by the idea of doing King Hoffer's dirty work but… what was the saying? Better the evil he knew than the ones he didn't?

"It can be arranged," Hadi agreed. All the more, he would hardly weep for dead pirates.

With that, they clasped hands and the deal was struck.


…
​

Mobilizing an army was not a quick affair. It took time for supplies to be gathered, moved to a depot, stored and recorded. It took time for men to make their way from their villages and towns. Men got lost, either willfully or by accident. Somewhere in the process there would be a clerk working with too little sleep, leading to an error in the ledgers. Then there was pay to consider -- honor and glory were fine, but most preferred gold for putting their lives on the line.

However, if there had to be a silver lining about sharing a border with Emperor 'The only good heathen is a dead one' Charlemagne… then it was the fact that his nation was well prepared for war. He had well trained militias he could draw from, his supply depots were already full, and it only took a few strokes of a quill to set everything in motion.

There was no such thing as organization within an army. It was just that some armies were less disorganized than others. Hadi took pride in very little, but he did that his army managed to be assembled and depart from his shores within a month. The 'gods' continued to smile upon them because their trip from Hispania to the Abbasid Caliphate was without incident even if the weather wasn't always clear.

They first sailed to Sicily, weathering a storm that lasted for two days before setting out once more. They stopped again on Crete for another day, riding out something less than a storm but the sea was too rough to sail safely. Inside of a week, Hadi's army of twenty-five thousand men disembarked upon the shore of the Damascus region, bolstered by seven thousand mercenaries 'volunteered' by King Hoffer.

Of course, their arrival was not a secret. Hafi was sure by the time they departed Hispania, the Emirs and Jafar had already learned of his intentions. However, a week was not enough time to muster an army. It wasn't enough time to march and group up.

Siegfried seemed to enjoy his grand battles where he was outnumbered a hundred and one. Hadi, however, had a very different approach to war. He was not whatever Siegfried was. He didn't possess his abilities or unnatural talents. He was a simple man with simple intentions -- kill the enemy before they could kill him. They were divided by distance, so Hadi would defeat as many as he could before they had a chance to unify.

"You have history with Emir Ismail, do you not?" Khalid questioned as they marched from the shore and into Damascus proper. It was not a rich land, but most of the trade from the Abbasids through the Mediterranean flowed through its ports.

It really was a wonder that old man was still alive. A decade ago, he was pushing ninety. He had to be close to a century old by now, and it seemed he lived purely to spite Hadi. "Less with the man and more with his family," Hadi corrected. "I was a… less than responsible younger man who often found myself in brothels. As one does when spending so much time there, I… befriended a few of the prostitutes."

Khalid snorted softly by his side, "Lady Sheba is an ocean away. She will not overhear you."

Oh, what a poor foolish boy. "Half of my attendants are her spies that I know about. The other half are spies I haven't confirmed." Hadi corrected with a small shake of his head. The boy would learn. While his status of being a descendent of the Sword of Allah remained obscured for now, he knew Sheba was already planning matches. "Anyway, one day, an arrogant braggart arrived, already drunk and quite rude. Wealth does not smooth over a problematic personality, but with his status of… I don't even know. The great-great-great grandson of the Emir? Between it, and gold, he was under the impression that he could do whatever he desired."

His tone was light. Casual. But Khalid was too sharp eyed to not notice how his grip tightened on the reins. It seemed so very long ago, but it felt like it had been the defining moment of his life. It had been the event that had his father entirely give up on him, not quite banishing him from the family but only by a hair. After everything -- befriending the Prince, now Caliph, his many near death experiences, the dozens of assassination attempts… by all rights, it shouldn't stand out in his memory as it did.

But he could still smell the sweat, alcohol, and incense of his favorite brothel. A place where he could drink, gamble, and shamelessly break every tenant of Allah with women who were as clever as they were beautiful. And they were very beautiful. Hadi, as a younger man, was convinced he would die there and that he would die content.

He was losing a board game with one of his favorites when he heard the scream. Alcohol must have given him courage, because he erupted onto the scene. There, he saw Inara, his friend and companion, beaten bloody with a burn scar across her face and eye. He also saw the man standing over her with a red hot blade.

Rage was not anger. Anger could be reasoned with. It could be controlled. Rage was insanity, and it was insanity that possessed him when he demanded a duel. It was insanity and alcohol that gave him the courage to fight it. And despite all odds, he had won.

At the time, Hadi had been lesser nobility, not even Sheikh. Distantly related or not, the bastard was the blood of high nobility. Killing him was out of the question. So, Hadi took his sword hand and the same eye he took from Inara.

So, Emir Ismail's ire was… understandable. If inconvenient.

"Did you ever see her again?" Khalid asked, seemingly hearing everything that wasn't said. A real annoying habit of his, but one Hafi had grown used to.

"Never," Hadi admitted. "I tried once, but by then, she was gone. My father got me a position in the army…" he shrugged. It was hardly the most satisfying ending, but life was rarely satisfying.

The battle would be over far more than a clever and beautiful woman, this time. But, days later, when he stood across a battlefield with two familiar faces at the head of an army twelve thousand strong? When one of those faces was missing an eye?

Well, it felt a little personal.

...

#7,784
"Yahya," Hadi greeted Harun's trusted attendant first, standing underneath the noon sun. It had been some time since he had last seen Yahya. A few years at least. He looked more like his father now -- the same cheekbones, the same beard, the same nose and eyes. Just a younger version of him as Jafar already had whitening hair when he first met him a decade ago.

It was difficult to gauge in what capacity Yahya was here. Hadi had blamed his family because it was convenient. He imagined that would be something of a sore point. But if the Barmakids really had been responsible for Harun's near assassination, then it was a question of how high his kin were attempting to elevate themselves.

However, if they weren't behind it, then there could be a path toward a peaceful resolution. However unlikely that might be.

"You've at last overeached, mutt," Yusuf, the something something grandson of Emir Ismail, remarked with a delighted grin. "I've awaited this day for a long-"

"Who are you, again?" Hadi asked with a small frown, knowing already that the passing remark was going to get inside Yusuf's head. Given that they were about to fight a battle, there was no place that Hadi would rather be. Let him get angry. Let him make mistakes. And when the battle was done, he could take his head like he should have done years ago.

Exactly as Hadi hoped, Yusuf stilled in a way that told Hadi he didn't know how to reply. He was struck speechless.

"Hm. Anyway, Yahya," Hadi continued addressing the Barkmid, whose lips thinned. It was evident enough what Hadi was doing. The Barmakids, for all of their influence, didn't have an army. Or, at least they didn't. Meaning that the fifteen thousand men -- ten thousand infantry, three thousand light cavalry, a thousand heavy cavalry, and a thousand archers split between horse archers and traditional archers. All of them answered to the pissant next to him. A man that Hadi knew was both a hot-headed idiot and burdened with a very prickly pride.

"Does the Caliph still live? Or has your father puppeted his corpse?" Hadi continued, searching Yahya for a clue. Something to hint at an answer one way or another. Rumors in Norland and beyond swirled with deliberate intent, making it impossible to tell if Harun still lived or if he had passed from his injuries. As something of a connoisseur of misinformation, Hadi had been impressed and frustrated in equal measures that he couldn't get an accurate answer.

The last thing he had heard that seemed remotely truthful was that Harun was recovering in Baghdad. That was weeks ago.

"I'm not inclined to answer the questions of assassins," Yahya rebuked, offering nothing. His face didn't twitch, he sat still on his horse, and his tone was deliberately flat. "To think that the Caliph trusted you so. He named you a friend, elevated you beyond your station, and defended you from your many detractors. And you repaid his generosity with a poisoned blade in the back."

A blade in the back. That could merely be a turn of phrase, but he had heard thousands of renditions of how Harun had nearly been assassinated. The rumors ranged from his eating a poisoned apple, to assassins hiding in the walls, to a beautiful woman sneaking into his bed. Again, with deliberate intent, someone had made sure that it was impossible to tell truth from fiction.

"I do not deny that our Caliph was betrayed, but not by my hand," Hadi returned. "That, I lay at your feet, Yahya. If you did not wield the blade yourself, then your incompetence allowed for our Caliph to fall to an assassin's blade." There was something in his eyes. A shift. The remark struck a nerve, but Hadi wasn't sure how or why. "You, who Caliph Harun al-Rashid, trusted above all others. You either betrayed him then, or you do so now by standing against me."

"You? Who answered accusations of treason by mustering your army?" Yahya returned the accusation, but there was a coil of anger in his voice now. "If you were as innocent as you portrayed yourself, then you would have submitted to the summons."

Hadi laughed. Loudly and mockingly. It wasn't even a fake laugh. "There is no one that must fear the law more than an innocent man," Hadi rebuked. "As you say, the Caliph spoke for me against my many detractors. Those same detractors now name me an assassin and usurper. I am hurt that you thought me to be so foolish, Yahya."

"Then submit yourself now. To me. Despite the accusations you have levied against my family, I am prepared to speak for you. I shall guarantee you safe passage," Yahya offered. He sounded sincere, but that didn't mean a damn thing. If his family truly was behind the attempted assassination, then it would be impossible for Yahya to not know of it.

Meaning that even if he hadn't wielded the blade, he had given another the opportunity.

Yahya grew up together with Harun. He was the reason why Harun was so resistant to the thought that the Barmakids couldn't be trusted. Harun had full and complete trust in his lifelong friend. And there were likely odds that Yahya had betrayed him regardless.

If he was willing to do that, Hadi thought it was likely he would be willing to just lie about the promise of safe passage.

"No," Hadi replied, his tone even. "I will have the truth of the matter, and I don't trust you to give it to me." Even if he were to submit right now, Hadi wouldn't believe whatever he had to say. There would always be a doubt in the back of his mind. That was just the cold truth of it.

So, he would defeat Yahya here. Capture him. And when he reached Baghdad and Harun, he would leave that messy decision for the Caliph to decide.

"Enough," Yusuf interjected when Yahya began a retort. "You asked who I am -- I am the man who will defeat you on this day. I am-"

"I'm not interested," Hadi interjected, turning his horse around. Next to him, Khalid was trying and failing to stifle his chuckles. All the more when Yusuf shouted threats after them, promising a fate worse than death. His threats were creative enough that Hadi was convinced he'd stolen them from someone else. "Are you ready?"

"I am," Khalid answered. "We have the edge in numbers. And Yusuf is in control of the army. Given his temper, I doubt that Yahya will be capable of quelling his rage before the battle. Especially when you insulted him by ignoring him to speak to Yahya." That was the plan.

"... And Yahya?" Hadi asked, uncertain if he truly wanted the answer.

Khalid glanced his way for a quiet moment, likely sensing that Hadi didn't really want an answer. Still, he needed it. "Guilty."

Hadi wished that he was surprised, but he wasn't. "I see," Hadi replied. It would seem that they wouldn't have to withdraw any accusations once this mess was cleaned up. Even still, he would have preferred being wrong.

He and his guards returned to his assembled army. Twenty-five thousand men. Eighteen thousand infantry, two thousand archers, and the remaining five thousand was an uneven mix of heavy and light cavalry. Of their infantry, seven thousand men were Norse mercenaries, with their captains and commanders marked for death by King Hoffer. The reason for each varied -- from simple ambition to actively undermining his authority.

It was tempting to renege on his end of the deal. But it simply wasn't worth it as King Hoffer would go to great lengths to get his revenge if he did. So, in the days leading up to the battle, he planned around how to best uphold his end of the bargain while maintaining as much strength as he could.

The battlefield was one ideal for cavalry. It was a large flatland with little in the way of shrubbery. For that reason, every footsteps sent up a cloud of dust, and a great many feet caused enough of a stir to make it difficult to see through. A tactic that Yusuf undoubtedly intended to take full advantage of. Hadi was no different.

It was clear that Yahya did not have the influence on the army that he desired. If he did, then the army would withdraw to link up with the armies of the other Emirs. His spies informed them where they were, and their numbers. Altogether, they would have an army of seventy thousand. As it was, he had a numerical advantage of ten thousand over Yusuf.

There were two possible reasons he refused to withdraw. The first was that he feared Hadi would ravage his lands with raids, but Hadi doubted that was it. The other and more likely option was that Yusuf just hated Hadi that much, and was convinced that he could win despite the long odds. In either case, it suited him just fine. Ideally, he would fight three battles where he had the advantage in numbers. Just how he liked it.

Once more at the head of his army, Hadi gave the nod and the war drums began to beat. While far from the standards of a professional army, the core of his was a force that lived in a state of perpetual skirmishes with Charlemagne or his Paladins. They were experienced and disciplined. Something that showed in the march over the field. They moved as a unified whole in perfect synchronization.

The light cavalry rushed out first, skirmishing with Yusuf's own light cavalry and horse archers. As predicted, they kicked up a screen of dust ahead of both armies. A screen that Yusuf undoubtedly used to reshuffle the position of some of his units, identifying his left wing as the weaker of the two. Naturally, that was the wing where Norse mercenaries were.

It was, perhaps, dangerous to rely on old impressions of Yusuf. People did change, after all. But even in that brief meeting, Hadi saw that all of his worst personality traits had only grown more prominent in the time since he'd known him. It was a gamble.

One that paid off, as erupting from the cloud of dust was Yusuf's heavy cavalry. A full commitment to destroying his left wing as fast as possible.

"I… have fought too many clever enemies," Hadi muttered under his breath. He sat back with the reserve forces, allowing him to see the full scope of the battle. Yusuf had taken the bait. His cavalry charge was devastating on the mercenaries. They didn't crumple, but they wavered dangerously.

However, with their heavy cavalry engaged, it left his infantry free to march forward. Once more, Hadi gave the nod, everything proceeding within expectations. The signal rang out and the rest of his army advanced with all haste in a general charge.

Under normal circumstances, it would be unthinkable. He was leaving behind an entire wing of his army to be ravaged. Not only did it risk being routed, it exposed him to Yusuf's right wing. It would be free to swing around and strike his center on the sides and rear. There were two things that turned what would traditionally be a foolish risk into a reasonable gamble.

Hadi was well prepared for the clash that followed in the dusty air. His men knew what to expect when the surprised enemy was counter charged. Just as the dust in the air obscured the enemy, it also protected Hadi's army from their eyes. A great clash rang out across the field as men shouted to pretend they weren't afraid.

He might have better command over the situation if he led from the front, Hadi knew. But that meant being near a bunch of people who really wanted him dead. So, he was perfectly content being surrounded by people who really wanted to protect him. It seemed far safer that way.

In his place at the front was Khalid, who for some insane reason, preferred being in the thick of things. Perhaps it was the best way to use his ability. Hadi didn't know, and he didn't ask. Even if he did, Hadi doubted he would be able to understand his reasoning.

"Send in the reserve left," Hadi instructed, going more off the timing than what he could see. It would take around six minutes for the reserve to cross the field. Eight for additional maneuvers. "Have them go wide and bypass the engaged left. When they do, they are to turn their formation forty degrees and charge."

The order was relayed and carried out with three thousand men in reserve marching forward. The dust was bad enough that he couldn't see how bad the mercenaries were doing, but thus far, they hadn't fled. Or if they did, they hadn't fled in Hadi's direction. He watched the reserve force obey instruction, and in his head he saw the flanking maneuver.

By now, Yusuf would have ordered his men to pounce on his unguarded center. He would order a mass push to distract it, while his right wing would swing in. Three thousand men would be outnumbered, but in the dust, their true numbers would be obscured. What's more, while his center would be flanked, the reserve men would strike them in the back, pinning them between two forces.

It would make doubt sink in. 'Was this the left?' 'Was the cavalry charge rebuffed?' 'If we're outmanuvered on the right, then what do I send to alleviate the pressure?'

War was not a game. Those who compared it to one were fools. But that wasn't to say that they weren't similar. Knowing the enemy was an integral part of battle. Knowing what they knew, suspecting what they suspected, all of it allowed Hadi to predict how they would react.

Yusuf was a prideful man. One with a grudge. A man who took this battle despite having more reasons to refuse it. When he would sense the battle was turning against him, he would do two things. Perhaps three.

First: he would ignore all good sense, understand that he had been outwitted, and withdraw. Perhaps not quit the field entirely, but he would need to accept that his right was compromised and addressed it accordingly.

Secondly: he would whole heartedly believe that he could turn the situation around with a personal hand.

Thirdly: he would command his bodyguards to join him on a counter charge against his outflanked right to relieve the pressure. To that end, he would command the skirmish cavalry to commit to a flanking maneuver.

"Tell Khalid it is time," Hadi decided, giving his heavy cavalry the order. Yusuf's cavalry was entirely engaged, giving them a window of opportunity for a singular decisive blow. Where that blow would be landed was a decision Hadi would leave in Khalid's hands. However, he knew what the result would be.

Khalid led the cavalry charge, choosing to strike at Yusuf's unprotected left. While Hadi couldn't see it in its entirety, the sound of the charge striking was a devastating thing. The signal quickly rang out to mark that the left wing was collapsing, caught between a hammer and an anvil.

"Send in the reserves. Have the light cavalry hunt," Hadi relayed his final orders of the battle, knowing that it was won even before the dust cleared. Yusuf's left and right flanks faltered and with a final push, his center routed.

It was not a surprise to see a dust trail in the distance. He knew it belonged to Yahya and Yusuf, along with what forces they could flee with. Which would be the cavalry.

As for the battlefield itself, once the first surrenders came, many others followed. The heavy cavalry finished its ravaging of the mercenaries to find that it was surrounded on all sides, so they needed little prompting. Hadi drank the sight in and…

"Good," Hadi voiced, urging his horse forward. The injured were being sorted, but with how quick the battle was, there weren't many. Perhaps a few hundred on the extreme end, discounting the mercenaries.

He had no true gift for public speaking. Nor any particular desire to. However, a lesson he had learned was that when something was said often mattered more than what was said. So as the defeated men were gathered up, near twelve thousand in total, he spoke.

"You have been lied to!" Hadi shouted out, riding amongst the men. "Through no will or awareness of your own, you have been party to treason against the Caliph! You have served one of his would-be assassins, who muster now to reach out for his throne out of petty ambition!"

Most of them wouldn't really care. What they would care about was this.

"So I offer you this chance for atonement. Join me, and we shall rescue the Caliph from their grasping hands! From those who would snuff out his life in the name of greed!"

Most wouldn't care about the Caliph. Or the Caliphate. To the average man, it didn't matter whose ass warmed the throne. So long as life didn't grow more complicated for them, they would accept a dog as Caliph. They might even prefer it, as dogs knew of loyalty.

However, Hadi had just handily defeated them. Never mind his advantage in numbers. In their eyes, he was the likely winner. Thus, the Caliph was the likely winner. Meaning that fighting against Hadi would have consequences -- executions, loss of land, and so on. The Caliphate wasn't exactly known to look favorably on traitors or treason.

On the other hand, fighting with Hadi? That meant rewards. Money, titles, land… it was a simple equation.

"Al-Gaib!" Hadi wasn't sure who first shouted, but it didn't take long for the chant to spread. "Al-Gaib! Al-Gaib! Al-Gaib! Al-Gaib! AL-GAIB!"

In no time at all, the chant was deafening. Enough so that Hadi could barely hear himself think. He had more to say, but it seemed unneeded. He had underestimated how unpopular Yusuf was by a considerable margin. Still, it worked in his favor. The mercenaries had lost an estimated three thousand men, though there were a few names that still needed to be crossed off yet.

They'd gained more than they lost. From twenty-five thousand, they were now thirty-four thousand. Most of the additions were infantry, as Yayha had taken the cavalry with him. Which was a shame, but unavoidable. To win the battles to come, he needed more men than horses.

He made the rounds, doing what was expected of him. Nodding at the right times, offering compliments, and assuring the various minor nobles that no, he didn't begrudge them for fighting against him. Even though they likely would have roasted his head on a spike if he'd lost the battle. Magnanimous and generous.

Of course, he didn't trust the army further than he could throw them. They had already betrayed one master after all. The moment the winds blew against him, Hadi was prepared for a similar betrayal.

Until then? He would use them for all they were worth.

It was a time-consuming affair. Enough so that he had little time for anything else, much less joining the celebrations for their victory. The hour was late when Hadi stumbled into his tent, his eyes bleary with his bed singing a sirens song to him.

Or, perhaps that was the woman seated upon it.

"I'm married," Hadi replied instantly, suddenly alert. The woman wore a veil, making her face difficult to see, but he was something of an expert on beautiful women. And the woman was undoubtedly beautiful. Enough so that it would cause him no end of trouble, so he really hoped she stumbled into the wrong tent.

"I'm sure Sheba will appreciate your faithfulness," the woman replied with a hint of a smile in her voice. "However, that is not why I am here. I carry a message from Al-Khayzuran, the Queen Mother, for your ears."

Hadi swallowed a groan. Whatever the message was…

He was certain that he wouldn't like it.

...

#7,800
Lot of names get thrown out in this chapter. Here is something of a reference to make things a bit easier for you.

Jafar Barmakid
Yahya (son)

Emir Ismail of Damascus (Does not like Hadi because of a duel)
Isa (Emir of Isaid)
Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Qasim (Emir of Dulafid)
Hasan (Emir of Zaydid)

Emir Divdad of Sajid (Co-head of conspiracy)
Al Muwaffak ibn al-Mutawakkil (Emir of Basra)
Ahmad ibn Malik (Emir of Attab)

Emir Asad of Egypt (Hadi's ward)

Al-Khayzuran (Harun mom)

…

Being an Emir was an immense privilege. Less than a dozen bore the title, and even amongst his peers, his domain was vast. Powerful. And it was on the very far reaches of the Caliphate, so he enjoyed freedoms unknown to the other Emirs. Emir Bassam of Syria was a rich man, but his territory was comparatively small. It was also a territory tightly controlled because of its proximity to the heartlands of the Caliphate.

When it became clear that Harun was attempting to murder Hadi with kindness and favors, Hadi had found himself… tripping the fat, so to speak. With his meteoric rise from an absolute no one to one of the most powerful men in the Caliphate, he had no shortage of enemies. Some who were jealous of his rise, others hating him fiercely because he overpassed them, and a few who despised him as a matter of principle. In the first year of his rule alone, he must have survived at least a hundred assassination attempts.

Well, it felt like a hundred. It was closer to three.

The point being, with such a plethora of reasons for his subjects to want him dead, Hadi began to rein in his worst habits. He was a married man now, so no more brothels. He had never been a particularly devout Muslim, but Allah frowned upon wine for some reason; thus he would abstain. That was enough to convince Hadi that Allah hated him in particular, because there were few things more miserable than having a banquet with people who already hated you while staying completely sober.

He had gotten used to it over time. Even appreciated it. His position wasn't entirely devoid of its amusements or advantages. He had come to care for his wife, and he liked to think she was at least a little fond of him in turn. It was also very nice that people had to tip-toe around him now, instead of the other way around.

However, there were moments like these that made him long for wine and his days of absolute obscurity. Because the moment he laid eyes on the woman in his tent, he could already tell he was going to loath the conversation that followed.

"You claim to be here on behalf of Al-Khayzuran," Hadi began, eyeing the woman warily as he moved to his desk. A knife was in a secret compartment, which he was ready to grab while he sat down. "What proof do you have of this claim?"

The woman seemed pleased by his caution, watching him from behind her veil, "Lazy. Content. Cynical. These were the words my master passed to me to convince you of my identity."

There were few people that Hadi genuinely feared. Siegfried was one of them, even if that fear had faded as they were nominally allies. Another was Al-Khayzuran, Harun's mother. He'd met her the first time as a humble Shiekh, fresh from their defeat at Ravenfeast but victory over the Romans. It had been that meeting where she summarized him in three words.

He had met her two times since, and she was no less terrifying with exposure. Khalid denied that she was like him, who could gaze upon something and know its innermost secrets. But never before, and never since, had he been so exposed. The well-crafted mask he wore as naturally as breathing was ripped off with ease.

But, because of those three words, he'd risen as high as he had. Al-Khayzuran trusted him because she knew that Hadi didn't even want the power he had as a Shiekh. That, in turn, had Harun dumping more and more responsibility upon him until he landed in this mess. Damn it all. Maybe he should just rebel. Maybe then he could get some peace and quiet.

Hadi pushed the thought away with a sigh, "You are who you claim." He acknowledged with a nod of his head, some of the tension easing out of him. "Does Harun still live? Is Al-Khayzuran safe?" He questioned sharply, bracing himself for the answer. "What is your name?"

"This one is named Tahleela el-Sadri, Emir Hadi al-Ghayb," Tahleela answered with a bow. "The message is thus: Caliph Harun al-Rashid lives. His strength is recovering, but he and the Queen Mother are imprisoned inside the palace under the guise of protection. The servants and guard have been purged of loyalists. Should the battle turn against the traitor Jafar, my master believes that they will be slain outright."

Relief and concern warred in Hadi's chest. Relief that Harun still lived. That his corpse wasn't being propped up and wrung of all use before being discarded. But concern overshadowed his relief because he was in a precarious position. Hostage in his own palace. Baghdad was as much Harun's seat of power as it was Jafar's. He had a wealth of influence in the city -- control over the servants, the city guard, keys to the treasury, and lesser appointments at court.

The Barmakids had no lands. No armies. However, their position of servants to the Abbasid dynasty had granted them a wealth of influence, which they'd used to pull off the coup. However…

"Jafar is the face of it, but who is his backing?" Jafar didn't have the power to become Caliph. Hadi had no doubts he orchestrated the coup, but the people and the Emirs wouldn't accept him as Caliph. The most he could hope for was to be granted an Emirate with wealth, armies, and titles, so his family would have hard power to support their soft power.

"A collection of Emirs, one you have already bested. Emir Ismail of Damascus and Emir Divdad of Sajid are the heads of the conspiracy. Each of them has recruited their own followers, quarreling for the throne even as they work to usurp it." At that, she unveiled a scroll of parchment that she presented to him. "Jafar serves as an intermediary between them, playing both sides against each other for the promise of greater rewards and to keep them from descending into pure chaos."

On the scroll was a list of his enemies.

Emir Isa of Isaid and Emir Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Qasim of Dulafid supported Emir Ismail.

On the other side of the conspiracy were Emir Al Muwaffak ibn al-Mutawakkil of Basra and Emir Ahmad ibn Malik of Attab, who supported Emir Divdad.

Meaning that of the eleven Emirs, six of them were attempting to usurp the Caliphate. He and his former ward, Asad, were loyal. The remaining three were waiting to see which way the wind blew before committing. It was a less than ideal situation. It would seem that the Emirs were not fond of Harun's efforts to curtail their powers and influence.

If there had to be a piece of good news, then it was that most of his enemies were divided and far removed from each other. Emir Isa of Isaid controlled the territory around Mecca. While Mecca was important, the lands around it were not. Harsh, sparsely populated, with a desert between Hadi and whatever army Isa could muster.

On the other hand, the half of the conspiracy that supported Divdad was far more localized around the Arabian Peninsula. That would be a problem. While not all Emirates were created equal, there was no such thing as a weak Emir. They could summon thousands of men to their banners, if not tens of thousand. Hadi was an extreme outlier on how much power an Emir could traditionally command.

Between those three, he would face an army thirty to fifty thousand strong. Perhaps more. It entirely depended on how desperate they were. Worse, since they were so tightly grouped together, he had little hope of marching fast enough to attack them before they could group up.

"Emir Ismail and his son Yusuf have been diminished with the loss here," Hadi ventured slowly, putting together parts of ideas to create a halfway coherent plan. "That would unify them under Divdad's leadership. What is his temperament?"

"Cold." Tahleela answered, and that was the last thing that Hadi wanted to hear. Rash men made much better enemies.

"The men who support him?" Hadi tried, looking for an angle that turned his plan from impossible to merely a long shot. He searched his memory. "Ahmad of Attab. I recall that he is the ambitious sort."

"Your memory serves you well," Tahleela confirmed with the barest of nods. "He cares little for the truth of Caliph Harun al-Rashid's near assassination. He merely seeks to put an end to the efforts to diminish his own standing. He, and many others."

That was something to use. Support was conditional. There was always a first amongst equals, and there were few who chaffed more than those who looked at their peers and thought they should be the one in charge. When there was a shift in that hierarchy? Someone like Ahmad would always take a step forward to fill it. It was just a question of how he could convince the man that it was his own idea.

"Is there any one being misled? Any who earnestly believe that I am responsible and that they serve the Caliph's will?" A little much to hope for, but apparently not too much.

Tahleela offered a deep nod, "Emir Abd al-Aziz. At least, that is our belief." That was a relief. In that case, the plan was possible. A thoroughly terrible idea, but possible. "What is your intention, Emir Hadi al-Ghayb?"

Hadi's fingers drummed on his desk, pulling together details and half-formed ideas into a coherent plan. "First… I shall strike Divdad directly. A forced march into the heart of his territory." A risky maneuver, but with it, they will have lessened the leadership behind the coup. All the better, by his recollection, Abd al-Aziz and Ahmad of Attab were no friends.

It would have to be fast, however. Before they have a chance to earnestly join forces. Even with all haste, they wouldn't be able to stop at least one or two armies joining forces. It would require the right battlefield and a pinch of luck, but it was a battle they could win.

"And second?" Tahleela questioned, earning a small smile from Hadi.

"I shall kidnap the Caliph."


…
​

Upon the morning, before they had a chance to earnestly celebrate the victory, his army began its long march into the heartlands of the Caliphate. A small army of scouts rode ahead of them, to ensure that they didn't march into an ambush, and also to keep an eye on the new shifting lines amongst the rebelling Emirs.

With Yusuf's defeat, Emir Ismail was diminished. His support wavering. Emir Isa was a desert away, and Hadi had already sent missives to Egypt to rally up some troops. They wouldn't be used in the conflict, not unless something went well and terribly wrong. Beyond how horribly wrong everything already was, of course. They were just another factor for his enemies to consider as Egypt was perhaps the second most powerful Emirate.

While he didn't have access to his spy network, Al-Khayzuran had her own that she had opened up to him. Word of his victory spread a bit faster than Hadi would have preferred. All of the lords, nobility both high and low, had kept a close eye on the battle, so word spread like wildfire. He made a concentrated effort to disperse the truth with false rumors -- that his victory had been far more narrow, that his losses were grievous. How effective it was, there was no way to tell.

In the end, he saw the cracks he hoped to see. Emir Ismail was pushing against Divdad while Ahmad of Attab attempted to usurp his place in the alliance. Hasan flirted with supporting Ahmad, while Abd al-Aziz remained steadfast. Where it really counted was the fact that support was being frozen for Divdad.

If they joined forces in earnest, they could boast an army many thousands strong. Perhaps a hundred thousand strong if they threw caution to the wind. As it was, as Hadi tore through the heartlands, purchasing supplies as needed rather than carrying them to avoid the extra weight slowing them down. Well, he said purchasing, but it was mostly looting with a promise of repayment that he was going to foist on Harun.

An army that could have been a hundred thousand strong was instead divided. Split up by political machinations and distance. Something Hadi took full advantage of more than a week later, his arsenal covered in saddle sores, but they were in position.

"Hadi…" Khalid began, once they arrived on their chosen battlefield. Or, rather, the battlefields.

"I know," Hadi replied, already knowing what Khalid was going to say. No need for special powers for that. "Believe me. I know."

At his back were twelve thousand men. Another twelve were elsewhere, marching on Khalid's command. The remaining ten thousand? They were marching towards Baghdad underneath a commander Hadi trusted enough to hold the siege, but not enough to win the three pivotal battles that were coming.

It was a risk to spread his forces. A substantial one. It was, however, necessary.

Abd al-Aziz and his eight thousand men were rushing to Baghdad instead of reinforcing Divdad. Al Muwaffak ibn al-Mutawakkil marched to join Divdad with fifteen thousand additional men, reinforcements which wouldn't be arriving due to Khalid marching to battle him. Meanwhile, Emir Ismail- or, rather, Yusuf, had joined up with Hasan. Combined, they numbered twenty thousand strong with the cavalry Yusuf had managed to salvage from the battle.

Leaving the lone force before him to be the combined might of Divdad and Ahmad. An army that could have been as many as a hundred thousand strong was instead fifteen thousand. Ten thousand levied from Divdad's holdings, with the remaining five thousand commanded by Ahmad.

"You are needed elsewhere, Khalid. Have a little faith. I only pick fights that I know I'll win." He was a coward like that. Because, despite being outnumbered by three thousand men, he wasn't truly outnumbered. It could even be argued that he had the advantage. "But only if you win your battle."

The pieces on the board were divided but not so much that they couldn't unify. When their enemies learned that he'd divided their forces, they were going to pounce on the isolated armies. Yusuf would be eager to avenge his loss, but he might not be in control over the army. He remained afar for now, but only because his rivals were battling his enemies.

"Be careful, Hadi," Khalid said after a moment, gazing off in the direction of the Divdad army. They were not yet in sight, but he knew their composition. Ten thousand infantry. Three thousand archers. Two thousand cavalry, one part heavy, two parts light. "The path we walk is a narrow one."

Hadi inclined his head to his trusted right hand before they went their separate ways.

His twelve thousand men marched onward to a battlefield that wasn't of their choosing, as it was a vast flatland with not so much as a hill to be found, or a river. It was within Hadi's expectations when they arrived. His men marched out according to his orders.

Eight thousand infantry, five hundred archers, and three thousand and a half cavalry. Two thousand light skirmisher cavalry and a thousand five hundred heavy cavalry. Which he, rather unfortunately, would be at the head of. A messenger was sent out when both armies took to the field, but Divdad apparently wasn't feeling too talkative given he merely shot an arrow at Hadi's messenger.

It mattered little, even if it would have been nice to rile up the peer commanders. Inflame tension and work a divide between them. A divide that was already there as when the enemy army arranged itself in its battle lines, it was quite clear who commanded which part. Ahmad's control was concentrated on a single wing.

Lies were a useful thing on the battlefield. Misdirection was better. Things didn't need to be true for others to believe them to be. And sometimes, a lie could become the truth if given the opportunity.

Hadi had no doubt in his mind that Divdad, wherever the man was amongst the army, noticed how Hadi arranged his. A concentration of skirmisher cavalry on the right flank. Where Ahmad was. The anemic Norsemen guarding Hadi's own flank, while the majority of his infantry was concentrated on the center and left wings.

An odd arrangement, to be sure, given that Divdad's right wing had the largest amount of infantry in it. A suspicion would be planted in his mind. An opportunity in Ahmad's.

With a call to arms, Hadi first sent forth his skirmishers. There was dust in the air, but nothing compared to what had been kicked up during his battle with Yusuf. They charged forth, unleashing arrows and javelins into the right wing. And they were answered in turn by a volley of arrows. Some fell, but more wheeled around for another pass.

The sheer volume of his skirmisher cavalry undercut Divdad's own archers, forcing them to shoot from the back ranks of the army. Where they were less effective by half. Yet, Divdad did not dare to unleash his own skirmishers. Not when the same flank they sat on was mirrored by Hadi's heavy cavalry.

Instead, he committed to the natural course of action. He had the advantage in numbers. It would be better to use them.

A distant horn blew and Divdad's army began to march across the field. They weren't professional troops, but Divdad's domain now bordered the Khazars after their mad Roman gold-fueled dash towards their northern border, so they were drilled better than the average levy. An equal to Hadi's own force. Better, even.

But it was in that action the cracks began to show. Hadi's skirmishers delayed Ahmad's advance, making it lag behind the entire army as his horsemen darted in and out, harassing the flank with a single-minded commitment. It wasn't an effective use of his skirmishers. They would be better used along the entire army, weakening the men's resolve. After all, seeing a friend with an arrow in the eye put quite a damper on one's spirits. It was ideal for what he had in mind.

The divide widened, both physically and metaphorically.

Ahmad felt singled out. Like he was being left behind, sacrificed to arrows and javelins for the sake of convenience. Ahmad likely thought that Divdad was doing the exact same thing that Hadi had done to the Norse mercenaries.

Divdad, however, suspected betrayal. With Ahmad's forces tied up, he was facing a far more even fight than he wanted. Worse, he was doing it by attacking Hadi's position in the field. By all accounts, it looked like a farce. That Hadi had deliberately weakened his left wing, knowing that Ahmad would not reach it.

How openly Ahmad confessed his ambitions was anyone's guess, but if Divdad wasn't a fool, then he would have at least some kind of inkling. A spark of suspicion that was catching fire after being fed kindling to nurture his doubts.

Hadi had his archers step forward, unleashing a volley into the mass of approaching men. He didn't have many of them, giving most to Khalid for his own battle. Some men fell, but most didn't and simply marched onward. At least until a point.

The gap between the right and the center widened, driving things to a tipping point. A point where Divdad would either have to halt his advance to secure his right, or simply abandon it to commit to the advance.

The moment Divdad decided to commit was the moment the lie became the truth. Ahmad saw that he was being abandoned. Sacrificed upon the altar of victory. Something that he did not take with grace. Through the swarm of skirmishers, Hadi saw Ahmad pulling back. Retreating from the field, refusing to be a sacrifice for a lesser man.

Of course, that confirmed his treachery in Divdad's eyes. A deal brokered before the battle, or simple opportunism. It mattered not.

In truth, it didn't matter. Because the moment that Ahmad retreated?

The outcome was decided.

...

#7,812
Jafar Barmakid
Yahya (son)

Emir Ismail of Damascus (Does not like Hadi because of a duel)
Isa (Emir of Isaid)
Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Qasim (Emir of Dulafid)
Hasan (Emir of Zaydid)

Emir Divdad of Sajid (Co-head of conspiracy)
Al Muwaffak ibn al-Mutawakkil (Emir of Basra)
Ahmad ibn Malik (Emir of Attab)

Emir Asad of Egypt (Hadi's ward)

Al-Khayzuran (Harun mom)

…
The reaction to Hadi's victory, and to Khalid's, was as expected. His sudden arrival, followed by a series of defeats, had taught the Emirs a painful lesson -- alone, they were vulnerable. There was strength in numbers. Safety. Abd al-Aziz, upon realizing that he would not be able to lift the siege on Baghdad, swiftly retreated.

Divdad managed to escape after his army's defeat, but his relief was short-lived. Ahmad captured him and his remnants, and apparently Hadi was quite bloodthirsty, as Hadi had him killed as well. The truth of it, as far as Hadi could tell, was Ahmad had him killed to quietly absorb control over the odd four thousand men that had escaped with Divdad. Leaving Ahmad with a combined host of nine thousand men.

He retreated to where Yusuf and Yahya gathered, towards the region of Armenia. The land was treacherous with mountains, making it no place for a battle. Hadi was yet unsure what their total number would be. Isa remained a desert away, essentially a non-factor in the battle to come. With the string of defeats, Hadi expected some desertions. After all, men preferred to fight for winning causes.

Still, he put their combined force of forty thousand. Maybe more, maybe less. Meaning that they were evenly matched. In theory, at least.

Hadi was content to let them gather their strength and kick their wounds. The nature of the war had changed with his victories. He had the initiative. Their claim to power was that they were acting on behalf of the Caliph. That they were punishing a traitor. It was a narrative that Hadi fed into simply because it left them with a singular course of action. They had to attack.

Particularly when he was besieged the capital with forty thousand men.

"I can't say that I expected these circumstances when I returned to Baghdad," Hadi admitted to Khalid. He did expect to return one day. Only that it would be clapped in chains once Harun realized he had promoted a fraud. It was a beautiful city, the little he could actually see of it from behind the tall walls.

Baghdad was a statement of power from the founder of the Abbasid dynasty. There was none like it anywhere else in the world. A perfectly round city, guarded by walls and a deep moat, with the palace resting in the very center of it. It was no fortification turned center of power. Quite the opposite. It was almost exposed in a way that pricked at Hadi as entirely unacceptable. Because someone like him would do what he was doing without much difficulty.

That was the point, Hadi knew from his quiet discussion with Harun. It was a testament of power. The capital of the caliphate was exposed because none could reach it. At the very least, Harun had conceded it was a dangerous confidence that bordered arrogance.

It possessed four gates, each on a central axis. As it was a city to mesmerize any who visited it, Baghdad was not built to confound an enemy. For that reason, four central roads connected the palace to the gates. However, within the city itself was a second wall. An intentional barrier to keep out the poor and undesirables from the wealthy and nobility. A third wall was erected around the palace itself. Or rather, the impressively large garden surrounding the palace, with the palace itself having its own mostly aesthetic walls.

Meaning, just because it wasn't a conventional city didn't mean it would be easy to take. Not that he desired as such. Hadi imagined Harun would be quite cross with him if he sacked his capital.

"I would be quite worried if you had," Tahleela mused with a touch of amusement. The three of them resided in his tent. Hadi himself stood behind a table with a map of Baghdad upon it. His army was divided into twelve parts -- groups of five thousand were placed around each gate, with smaller groups placed in the space around the city. "I suppose this is where you intend to kidnap the Caliph and his family?"

He was going to regret that choice of words. He might already. "We cannot afford a siege for several reasons. To begin with -- Baghdad is well provisioned. We are not. Harun estimated that Baghdad could survive two years under siege with proper rationing. I estimated five, because most Caliphs would expel the poor and sick as their opening move."

Tahleela remained a mystery to him. She was an intelligent woman. Sharp. She could never meet Sheba, that was certain. She offered nothing about herself, but from what he could glean, she was fiercely loyal to the Abbasids and enjoyed Al-Khayzuran trust.

"Secondly, I cannot risk putting Jafar into a corner," Hadi continued. He saw that she understood by the flash of violence in her eyes at the mere thought. "When Yusuf and his army march, I will have to give battle. Winning would be as disastrous as losing."

Jafar would realize his attempted coup failed. Whatever he sought to achieve with it would be lost. He might lash out. Burn the whole Caliphate to the ground by slaughtering the hostages in his possession. Or, if a steadier hand prevailed, he would use Harun as leverage.

After all, Hadi had no proof of duplicity. Only Khalid's word. Thus far, Jafar had behaved accordingly as his position of Visier demanded, if one set aside the fact he was the cause of Harun's impairment. It was entirely possible that to accept Harun's release, he would need to spout the story that it all was just a misunderstanding. That bygones were bygones. Water under the bridge.

In that case, it was possible that Jafar could remain as Visier. It entirely depended on how lucid Harun was.

In any case, it was entirely unacceptable.

"Once we have kidnapped the Caliph, such a battle will prove unnecessary, yes?" Tahleela questioned, a certain grimness in her tone that told Hadi she suspected the answer already. "The traitors must be dealt with, but I fear the Romans at our door just as much. They have already seized Antioch and the surrounding territories. As Charlemagne rises the Roman Empire to west, the Eastern half champions a reclamation of the East."

Hadi was aware. Painfully so. But that hadn't been his problem, so he was mostly unconcerned with it.

Irene spouted rhetoric about the eagle rising from the ashes. How it wasn't that long ago Rome had controlled the Levant. How it had encompassed all of the Mediterranean Sea. Such an expansion was well beyond their means, but wouldn't stop them from trying. Seizing Antioch and Cyprus had been a strong indication of intent.

The rallying cry that followed was that the holy land of Jerusalem was in the hands of heathens. It paired well with the religious fervor that spread over the Roman empire, the flames being stoked into an inferno because they somehow managed to justify their outward expansion by feeling threatened and persecution.

"Unlikely, I'm afraid," Hadi admitted, wishing it could just be that simple. But no, it couldn't be. Hadi was convinced it couldn't be specifically to spite him. "After kidnapping the Caliph, all that he shall say in my defense will be suspect. It shall be a trivial thing for the lords to twist everything as a result of duress."

If he felt like being fair -- which he absolutely did not -- then he could admit that he would have his doubts too if he were on the other side of things. Odds were, no matter what, he would suffer a dark mark on his reputation in the eyes of many even after restoring Harun to power. There would be doubts and whispers that followed him that he kidnapped the Caliph and restored him to power for… something. Hadi didn't know.

They would, though. Those that scheme as naturally as they breathed would fill in the blanks themselves, convinced Hadi got something out of the arrangement. But, if he was lucky, then he woukd never have to deal with that kind of intrigue again after cleaning up this mess.

He could go back home.

To his wife.

Their children.

And live out the rest of his life in peace.

Hadi nearly smiled at the thought, but restrained himself because it would give the wrong impression as they were talking about kidnapping the Caliph. He cleared his throat, "We must secure Caliph Harun al-Rashid, his mother, his children, and his harem before we fight the traitors. The siege is only bait to spur them into action."

Unwise action. Which was why Divdad had to be removed from the equation. Now the host was, theoretically, being led by Yusuf and Ahmad. Both ambitious, prickly, and prone to rash action. As far as enemies went, they were his favorite kind.

Tahleela nodded slowly, her expression betraying nothing. "There are passages in and out of the city. Including to the palace itself," she began and Hadi was unsurprised. After all, it only made sense to have a few ways out of what appeared to be a corner. "However, their danger is that Jafar is also aware of them. He helped oversee the construction of Baghdad, after all." Also expected, but Hadi really wished that Harun's relatives would be a little more paranoid.

"But?" Hadi tried, hoping that there was one coming.

"But-" What a relief. "-There may be one we can use. It was a passage that we may be able to use. One built by smugglers that Caliph Harun al-Rashid's father discovered, had them executed, but did not destroy the tunnel. I am unaware if Jafar knows of it. And it is into the city. There are still many walls to the palace."

That was a complication, admittedly.

"It's a start," Hadi decided before his gaze slid to Khalid. His ward turned right hand offered a knowing smile. There was no mistake in what Hadi would ask.

He would go himself, but the truth of it was… the truth was he was a middling swordsman. The war depended on him. If rescuing Harun failed, and Hadi was captured, then that was it. Jafar would win in every way that matters. Whereas Khalid…

"I understand, Hadi al-Ghayb," Khalid assured him, but it still twisted his guts into knots. "I am up to the task, but not alone. I will need… ten men, I believe."

His confidence was convincing, but Hadi couldn't tell if it was for his sake than not. "Have them. What else do you need?"

"A distraction. How large is the garrison?" He questioned, sounding like he was putting the plan together.

"Five thousand, nominally. Jafar has put weapons in the hands of an untrained militia to bolster their numbers to fifteen thousand," Tahleela answered.

Khalid nodded, "How much time would I have?"

"Two weeks. Three, if we're being optimistic." It was winter, after all. That would slow them down a fair bit, both in regrouping and the following march. While Arabia did not experience the brutal winters of the North, particularly the far north the Scandinavians described, it was not uncommon for them to see snow. Nor did it change that marching for miles on end in the cold, particularly when you were not equipped for it, was a thoroughly miserable experience.

Khalid mulled that over for a long few seconds before his chin dipped in a nod, "It should not take that long."

He was confident. Enough so that Hadi wanted to believe him as a matter of principle. "You will have your distraction," he promised, knowing that all of it rested on Khalid's shoulders.

He could only hope that he put his faith in the right hands.

…

Khalid ibn al-Walid found himself in a small, cramped tunnel heavy with the scent of smoke due to the torch he carried in one hand. Behind him were ten men who followed in relative silence, all loyal to Hadi. Thus the Caliphate.

There was a sharp hiss as moisture from above dripped into the torch; the tunnel itself was steadily flooding, the stagnant water already coming up to his ankles.

They followed the tunnel carved from stone for some time, but through the darkness beyond his torch's light, Hadi spied their destination. A rough set of carved stairs leading up to a wood covering. The hiss was stronger when Khalid plunged the torch into the water, similarly plunging the tunnel into absolute darkness. It made the faint light that streamed in from the gaps in the floorboards that much more apparent. Pushing up against the boards, the hatch lifted with a squealing hinge in dire need of an oiling.

Pulling himself up, Khalid instantly found the gaze of an elderly woman in the cellar they arrived inside of.


[Jasra el-Nasrallah

Age: 65

History: Orphaned at a young age. Raised by Rifaah al-Qazi until the age of sixteen, she was then wed to Haashim al-Dajani for the dowry of a silver ring, five chickens, and a goat.



Her marriage with Haashim was a peaceful one, resulting in three children. Two lived to adulthood, with four grandchildren produced from the union. Haashim passed fifteen years ago, leaving her eldest son, Mamoon, to maintain ownership of the inn. Mamoon does not have a head for numbers, or good business sense, leaving her to run the inn as she had with her husband.



Has been aware of the smuggling tunnel for some time. Her husband was part of the smuggling ring. Did not fill the tunnel out of fear it would arouse suspicion.



Fears your arrival. Understands that even should she scream, she is not likely to be heard.]
​

Hadi did not understand Khalid's gift, for all that he tried to. Perhaps the only one who truly could was Siegfried, as their tale was a similar one. From the moment of his birth, he could look upon anything to learn its history. Secrets that he could not learn naturally were revealed to him within his mind, not as a whisper but as if he had learned it from a page.

He improved with time. Should he wish, it would be trivial to look deeper. To learn the complete history of her life. The lives of her children. Or he could learn specific things, such as her favorite food, what flowers she found the prettiest, or her opinion on something.

Khalid rarely used his gift in such a way. And never without cause. It… took something from him, in a way. Not physically. It was an easy gift to abuse. He could look at someone and learn their innermost secrets, fears, desires, and hopes. To do so freely would rob him of his chance to learn such things naturally as their relationship deepened.

In this case, however, it was prudent. "Good evening," Khalid greeted her with a polite bow. "I ask that you forgive our trespass. Please, allow me to offer compensation to make amends," he said, taking out a small coin purse. Jasra looked to it, then to his face, and then to the men that continued to emerge from the smuggler's tunnel in her cellar.

"... there is nothing to forgive, child. Do you require a room?" She asked, reframing the bribe and Kahlid's smile widened.

"We do. You have our sincerest thanks, my lady," Khalid assured her, paying her a generous amount for the rooms. And her silence. She accepted the coin with a knowing look.

"We have supper. Hot and cold," She informed after a moment of debate, choosing to treat them as common guests. Khalid saw why she was in charge of the in.

"Something hot sounds lovely," Khalid decided, choosing to follow when she made a gesture to. The last man out of the tunnel closed the hatch behind them before joining them inside of an empty in. That, Khalid suspected, was their fault. Few travelers when there was a war. Fewer when the city was under siege.

"It'll just be a moment," Jasra assured them, disappearing into the kitchen. Khalid took a seat at a table, and he was joined by the others. It was a strange thing to be looked to for guidance. He understood why Hadi disliked it, even though he was quite good at it. However, he offered none until Jasra and her granddaughter arrived with bowls full of warm stew.

"My thanks," Khalid said, looking down into the bowl. The ingredients were fresh and it was untainted. The others only ate when he took the first bite. "Could I trouble you with a few questions about Baghdad?"

"You may, young man. Though, my eyes are dim and my hearing fades, so I cannot promise any answers," Jasra replied. "I suppose the siege has your curiosity?"

"Among other things," Khalid replied, taking another bite of stew. Hadi's cooks were excellent, but there were times when Khalid found himself wistful for the days of simple travel foods. His days as Alim, a common peasant with only one man aware of his heritage. "How have things been since the siege began?"

Jasra offered a small scoff at the question, likely due to his own part in it, but she answered all the same. "Things have been… difficult. Vizier has strangled the city in the name of rooting out traitors who had a hand in Hadi al-Ghayb's attempt on the Caliph's life. That 'milita' he assembled aren't much more than a band of thugs, but they've set up checkpoints every five feet, it feels like. Just so they can rob you under the guise of an inspection."

Unfortunate to hear, but useful. As luck would have it, Hadi had foreseen something along these lines and prepared a sizable purse for the purpose of bribes. "Is travel between rings permitted?"

"If you have a pass. Which I don't have. And I doubt you do either," Jasra continued, with a small humph. She was correct in that estimation. "The only ones that do are guards and merchants. The nobility too, I suppose, but I haven't seen any of them."

Khalid took another bite of his stew, mulling over the information. Again, it was less than ideal, but well within expectations. Jafar would naturally strangle the ability to move within Baghdad, as it was a means to strangling information coming to and from the city. When every creature inside the palace belonged to him, it allowed him to spin whatever story he wished. His lies became the truth to all who heard them because they had no other means of learning what happened inside the palace.

However, such measures were not perfect. There were some who would bow their heads, feigning obedience while they plotted behind his back. There would be more who obeyed out of fear, or because they saw Jafar as the eventual victor. Something that would change with the siege and Hadi's string of victories. Then there would be those who were simply greedy whose loyalty could be purchased for a heavy enough purse.

It seemed right that Allah had granted him the ability to distinguish one from the other.

...
